text.0_Introduction, 0_Paragraph: The flood of commentaries and multitude of explanations, streaming, surging, and passing from age to age through the rivers of the Prophets and the brooks of the Writings—the abundance of explanations and translations issuing, emerging, and springing up daily in our generation upon the mountains of Scripture, its lofty fields, like waves over the furrows of the land—bear witness that souls yearning to understand Scripture and uncover its mysteries have found no satisfaction in the waters of the well that princes dug, that the nobles of old excavated with their scepters and their staffs. Therefore, they search for and dig other wells, seeking water. This is the sign and proof that this generation—a generation wise in its own eyes, examining the root of every matter and probing the utmost limit of everything—has not found enough to satisfy it, nor can its spirit rest content with the commentaries produced by the generation of its fathers. Thus, the search has greatly increased and inquiry has grown exceedingly intense, seeking to uncover the mysteries of the Holy Scriptures and solve their riddles; and therefore, commentators spring up in city after city like the grass of the earth.
text.0_Introduction, 1_Paragraph: Indeed, the hearts of the early sages were open as wide as the entrance to the Temple’s great hall. They knew the wisdom of the language, comprehended its ways, understood its paths, and attained knowledge of holy things and understanding.
text.0_Introduction, 2_Paragraph: Yet because they were the pioneers in this work, and the land before them was a wilderness, a land unsown, they applied themselves with immense diligence and labored greatly: digging in the valleys, hoeing the mountains, and breaking up the soil of Scripture, explaining difficult words and unraveling the meaning of its statements, opening their locks with the key of the plain, literal sense, so that they would no longer remain sealed riddles, like a fierce people whose obscure speech cannot be understood. Thus, from the time Rashi, of blessed memory, sowed in that land and reaped a hundredfold, and Hashem blessed him and it yielded a harvest, until Kimḥi came and ground fine flour in the mill and baked unleavened cakes, the commentators’ entire occupation and the fruit of their toil consisted solely in establishing the rudiments of understanding—the meanings of words and their grammar. In these endeavors, they did not turn to bringing forth the offspring of sublime ideas, which soar with mighty strength above the heights of Divine expression, towering above their counterparts born upon the knees of the human spirit and human understanding as the heavens tower above the earth.
text.0_Introduction, 3_Paragraph: Therefore, every reader and student who applies heart and mind to understanding Scripture will recognize that not only do many expressions, entire passages, and even whole prophecies still remain veiled, their intended meaning shrouded, while even the explanation of their statements and the meaning of their words remain tightly sealed and covered in darkness; even those prophecies that appear at first glance to have been explained and interpreted have not truly been clarified or made plain. We realize this when we consider that these masters of expression, these princes of holiness, spoke with understanding through the spirit of Hashem; when we remember that it was no human spirit, but a Divine spirit, a mighty and holy spirit, that spoke through them, with His word upon their tongues—a sublime spirit, exceedingly majestic, far above the human spirit. Even the human spirit rises aloft in the soaring flight of feeling to the heights of eloquence, and, in the soul’s exaltation, flies upon the wings of poetry through the potent force of imagination and the stirring of human emotion. If even then the soul gathers strength and rises in its power to speak sublime things, how much more when it is filled with power, with the spirit of Hashem, with justice and might, when Hashem bestows His spirit upon it, and through the power of the God of gods it speaks wonders and utters words from the Most High! “How, then,” every thoughtful reader will ask, “can the dishes the commentators have prepared for us please our palate, when they season the delicacies of the seers and the eloquence of men of the spirit with the insipid juice of purslane? How can we behold the daughters of man—their songs—perfect in beauty, their expressions dripping with grace and pleasant words, a golden necklace about their throats, while the daughters of the Most High walk in gloom, their garments torn, their expressions feeble, their speech obscure, their language halting and devoid of understanding? How can our souls accept the instruction of their interpretations if, according to them, the expressions of Scripture appear so impoverished and exceedingly ill-favored—withered, thin, and scorched by the east wind—and even the good, full ears of grain are swallowed by the thin and poor ones?” Such are the questions thoughtful readers ask, and such is their bewilderment.
text.0_Introduction, 4_Paragraph: Yet this is not what I would discuss with you now. I have not called you here to seek your favor and ask you to incline your ear to hear my remarks on the commentaries upon those books of Holy Scripture composed in poetry and elevated language—to acquaint you with the shortcomings of those commentaries, or to tell you how I have prepared the highway, cleared it of stones, and established a new path, which shall be called the Way of Holiness. This is neither the time nor the place to discuss these matters. Bear with me a little, for the vision awaits its appointed time, and there are yet words to be spoken on God’s behalf in the introductions to those books, each in its proper place and season. For now, I have come only to awaken your ear to listen as a learner, and to explain what moved me to sow and plant in this plot, the first to bear ripe fruit: the Former Prophets, whose contents take the form of narrative and account, expressed in plain statements. Perhaps you might imagine that nothing can be added here to the words of the commentators, since the matters are simple and readily understood by any student with discernment—what new word could possibly be heard concerning them? Therefore, I shall place in your hand a plumb line, a balance, and just scales, so that you may weigh matters in the scales of your understanding and see that these passages, too, follow winding paths: you will not know their hidden and sealed intent until you find in my words a lamp for your feet, and in my commentary a light for your path.
text.0_Introduction, 5_Paragraph: Even if you compare these historical narratives with secular histories written in every generation by learned men versed in the events of their times, recording the fortunes of nation after nation from ancient days, the reader will already find that, according to the commentators’ interpretations, these sacred books appear inferior to the works of skilled writers who wield the pen of a ready scribe in such matters, standing far below them in every particular. For anyone writing a historical record must fulfill the following conditions for the work’s excellence and beauty: 1] The writer must keep a definite purpose before his eyes, a goal according to which he arranges his narrative. He may connect the events and occurrences he records through the relationship of causes and effects, taking care to place before each effect the causes that brought it about. Or he may portray the course of events as they advance or recede, linking time, place, and circumstances within the chain of history, together with the many peoples and nations, regions and countries, and the transformations they underwent amid the turn of events. Or he may aim to portray the moral or political condition of nations through the events arising from that condition, whether bringing kindness or chastisement. The writer must observe an inviolable rule: every detail included in his narrative must accord with the purpose toward which he directs his attention. 2] He must preserve the proper order, neither placing what is later in time or causation before what is earlier, nor postponing what should come first; all the more must he avoid confusion and disorder. 3] He must weigh his words in just scales, neither giving the reader too little explanation nor multiplying words without purpose. 4] He must choose discerning language, clear and pure, and words pleasing and agreeable to the listening ear. Yet when we examine these sacred books, as interpreted by the commentators, by this standard, we find: 1] The purpose toward which their authors directed their narratives is clear and evident: to show how Hashem’s constant Providence accompanied the people close to Him throughout these generations; how they rose or fell, prospered or declined, according to their good or evil deeds; and how all their affairs were governed in a wondrous, miraculous, Divine manner—besides the lessons in morality and conduct, Torah and faith, woven into the narratives. Nevertheless, throughout these accounts we find many matters that miss this purpose, intermingled with numerous stories whose inclusion serves no apparent end, whether for morality or conduct, Torah or faith. 2] Much of the material appears jumbled and unordered, placing later events first and earlier events afterward. At times the narrative leaps from one subject to another, introducing in the middle matters wholly unrelated to the subject at hand, or taking up an event preceding the one under discussion, continually turning back and forth. 3] It repeats words and matters unnecessarily, offering many words and little substance. 4] It employs strange expressions and poorly chosen language; sometimes it takes up a subject and abandons it, beginning without completing it. You will find many such perplexities in every section if you read the questions I have set out concerning each subject. Through the window of these questions you will look upon the scene, and your heart will understand that deep waters—hidden counsel—lie in the depths of these narratives, and a man of understanding can draw them out. You will draw living water, pure, cool, and flowing, from the wellspring of explanation I have dug; you will give their fill to all the trees of Hashem, the cedars of God in Eden, the garden of God. You will water the wilderness, the parched land, and the desert plain, and it will blossom like the lily. You will refresh your weary soul, and it will be like a watered garden, like a spring whose waters never fail, and you will be filled with Hashem’s blessing. Your soul will bless me too, for after bringing every hidden matter under scrutiny, my commentary stands fully ordered and secure. In it I have made the crooked straight and the rugged places a plain: there is no repetition, no omission, no confusion, and no disorder. For all these passages are filled with wisdom and abundant understanding, and the words themselves testify that they are the words of the living God, spoken through the spirit of God by men of the spirit; and the tablets are the work of God.
text.0_Introduction, 6_Paragraph: I have arranged my commentary with utmost brevity and in simple language, so that every reader may move readily through it and grasp its meaning correctly, provided he reads attentively and does not rush. I also turned to the commentators who interpreted Scripture after Kimḥi—those mighty men of old, men of renown—but found none who strove to breathe life into the verses through their plain meaning except the distinguished Rabbi Isaac Abravanel and the circle of his contemporaries. I drew pearls from the depths of their words wherever their explanations commended themselves to me, and gathered them into my work under their names. The other commentators turned to homiletical interpretation, with which we are not presently concerned, while the commentators of the latest generation offer nothing new; some have been carried away by the east wind and feed upon wind.
text.0_Introduction, 7_Paragraph: As I bring my words to a close, I spread my hands to Hashem: Send Your help from on high, and sustain me from Your sanctuary. Guide me in Your truth, and uphold me with a willing spirit. Let Your face shine upon Your servant, and graciously grant me Your Torah. Even unto old age and gray hairs, O God, do not forsake me, until I proclaim Your might to this generation and Your holy words to all who are to come. And I shall praise Your name for Your kindness and Your truth.
text.0_Introduction, 8_Paragraph: Signed on the 26th of Tammuz, 5626, in Luntschitz, Meir Leibush Malbim.
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(1) Why does he describe Moses as “the servant of Hashem” and Joshua as “Moses’ attendant” here in particular, more than elsewhere?
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 0_Verse, 1_Comment: And it came to pass. This means that as long as Moses was alive, Joshua could not cross the Jordan for two reasons: 1] Joshua could not command the army during Moses’ lifetime. 2] Crossing the Jordan was impossible because of the oath that Moses would not cross it. After Moses’ death, however, both these obstacles were removed, and therefore, Hashem said to Joshua. He explains that Joshua merited both prophecy and leadership of the people because he had been Moses’ attendant, for serving a sage is greater than studying under him (Berakhot 7b). He calls Moses “the servant of Hashem” to indicate that even after his death he continued to bear this title, as our Sages said: “Just as he stood and served here, so he stands and serves there” (Sotah 13b). This means that the righteous person who works only to perfect himself ceases his service at death. But one who works for the perfection of his generation and future generations both acquires merit and brings merit to others, down to the last generation. The service that continues through his influence even after his death is attributed to him, as it says, “And his righteousness endures forever” (Psalms 111:3). Thus, even after Moses’ death, he remained “the servant of Hashem.”
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(2) Why did He say to him, “Moses My servant is dead,” when he already knew this? And the repetition, “to them—to the children of Israel,” is unusual wording.
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: Moses My servant is dead. Thus, the two obstacles mentioned above have been removed: 1] Previously, crossing the Jordan was impossible; now, arise and cross the Jordan. 2] Previously, you could not take the lead; now, arise and cross at the head, with all this people following you. (For, as explained, wherever the pronoun is repeated explicitly, it is the principal focus of the statement.) To the land. He says: Although you will command the army, and conquerors ordinarily give the conquered land the name of the commanding general or conquering king, who has the right to divide it and do with it as he pleases, this land will be different. Rather, to the land that I am giving to them—and He specifies, to the children of Israel. The pronoun repeated before the noun indicates that it is specifically for the children of Israel, not for you.
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Every place. This verse already appears in the portion of Ekev (Deuteronomy 11:24). Our Sages explained (Sifrei, there) that it means: Even if you tread upon places outside the Land of Israel to conquer them, they will become yours, and the sanctity of the Land will apply there. But from the wilderness, etc., shall be your border—that is the territory you are commanded to conquer, whereas conquest outside the Land is optional. Moreover, you may not conquer territory outside the Land until you have conquered the Land of Israel. It is already known from the words of our Sages (Sifrei Devarim 7) that had Moses crossed over and conquered the land, they would not have needed warfare; wherever their feet trod, their enemies would have fallen slain before them. Thus, He told Moses, “Every place upon which the sole of your foot shall tread”—by merely treading upon it, you would acquire and conquer it, and it would become yours. Although sin caused them now to require warfare, the word of Hashem would not return unfulfilled. He therefore says that even now, every place upon which the sole of your foot shall tread, etc., I have given to you, as I spoke to Moses. This, however, depends upon the condition that from the wilderness, etc., shall be your border—that you conquer the whole Land of Israel. This, in turn, depended upon their improving their deeds, as it says, “These are the nations that Hashem left to test Israel through them” (Judges 3:1). Since He saw that their hearts were not wholly devoted to Hashem, He left some of the nations to test them. Had their hearts been wholly devoted to Him, so that they required no testing and could conquer their entire territory, matters would then have been as they would have been under Moses: they would have needed neither sword nor warfare.

text.1_, 0_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: No man shall stand. He promised him two things: 1] No man shall stand before you—to assume authority or speak against you. (Know that there is a distinction between yityatzev lefanekha, with the letter lamed, which denotes an inferior standing before a superior on equal footing, as in “He shall stand before kings” (Proverbs 22:29) and “Who, then, can stand before Me?” (Job 41), and yityatzev befanekha, which denotes rising up to fight against someone, as in “No man shall stand against you” (Deuteronomy 7:24; 11:25).) He promised him that throughout his lifetime he would lead the people, and no one would raise his head independently of him. 2] Regarding his attachment to the Divine, as I was with Moses, so I will be with you—to cause My Divine Presence to rest upon you through miracles and wonders, as with Moses. He explains: Corresponding to the first promise, He says, “I will not let go of you,” meaning that I will hold your right hand to strengthen you continually. Corresponding to the second, He says, “I will not forsake you,” so that My holy spirit will not depart from you. For the opposite of physical strengthening is loosening one’s hold, as in “I held him and would not let him go” (Song of Songs 3:4), while the opposite of the resting of spiritual influence upon someone is abandonment.
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(6–9) Why does He repeat the exhortation to courage and strength three times? Why does He add the word “very” the second time? What does He mean by “Have I not commanded you?” Why does He repeat His admonitions to observe the Torah? And why does He first say, “So that you may act wisely,” and afterward, “For then you will prosper, and then you will act wisely”?
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: Be strong. He now explains His words. Corresponding to the first promise, “No man shall stand before you,” you must strengthen yourself and take courage. (The initial awakening of valor is termed ḥizzuk, strength, while its maintenance and persistence, which constitute steadfastness of heart, are termed immutz, courage. This is the distinction between them everywhere.) For help from above comes in proportion to human preparation. He explains, “For you shall apportion the inheritance,” and this requires strength, so that no one will stand before you in matters concerning the inheritances, over which quarrels and disputes will arise. He explains that Joshua should strengthen himself and not fear for three reasons: 1] On account of yourself, for you, and no one else, will apportion the inheritance. 2] On account of those receiving it, namely, this people, the chosen people. 3] On account of the inheritance itself, namely, the land that I swore to their fathers; and My oath will not go unfulfilled.
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Only. Corresponding to the second matter, attachment to the Divine, concerning which He said, “As I was with Moses, so I will be with you,” you must strengthen yourself even more, for true might consists in conquering one’s inclination. He also means that physical strength depends upon spiritual strength through observing the Torah. He explains that this strengthening consists of: 1] Observing—guarding yourself against violating the prohibitions. 2] And doing—fulfilling the positive commandments. Only in accordance with all the Torah—meaning that you should observe them not because your reason dictates them, but because the Torah commands them. Thus He says, which Moses My servant commanded you. Nor is it sufficient to observe only part of the Torah, for you must observe the whole Torah.
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: Do not turn aside from it—from the book. “To the right” refers to adding; and to the left, to subtracting. That is, you must neither add to it nor subtract from it.
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 6_Verse, 2_Comment: So that you may act wisely wherever you go. He explains that the commandments of the Torah differ from human laws in two respects: 1] Most human laws lack a rational basis that leads to the desired end. The Torah’s commandments, however, are rational commandments leading toward happiness and perfection. Thus He says, “So that you may act wisely.” 2] Even rational human laws encompass only general principles, not every detail and aspect of conduct. The Torah’s commandments, however, teach a clear path through all the ways of human life. Therefore He says, “Wherever you go.”
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: It shall not depart. He explains that there is another condition besides practice: contemplation and study of the Torah. 1] It shall not depart from your mouth—engaging in learning and reviewing the Torah’s laws and commandments. 2] And you shall meditate upon it—continually reflecting upon and examining the Torah’s theoretical teachings. The purpose of contemplation and study must be practice: to observe the prohibitions and to fulfill the positive commandments, and only in accordance with all that is written in it. For even the teachings received through the Oral Torah will, upon examination, be found written and indicated in the Written Torah, according to the rules of language and the principles by which the Torah is interpreted.
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 7_Verse, 1_Comment: For then you will prosper. There is a distinction between prosperity and wise conduct. One who consistently uses his reason and understanding to choose good means leading to the desired end is called wise; one whose fortune favors him, so that he consistently attains his desired end by chance, is called prosperous. The wise person has a keen and penetrating intellect, enabling him always to choose the most direct route to his goal. The prosperous person enjoys good fortune and a favorable configuration of the stars. He says that through studying the Torah, you will prosper, for Hashem will continually turn your fortune toward the good; and you will also act wisely, using your intellect to choose what is good. Furthermore, you will prosper in worldly matters and act wisely in matters of the soul.
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Have I not. He has commanded him to be strong in distributing the inheritances and observing the Torah, but has not commanded him here to be strong in warfare against his enemies. He therefore answers, Have I not commanded you?—meaning: I have already commanded you to strengthen yourself in warfare, as it says, “He commanded Joshua and said: Be strong and courageous” (Deuteronomy 31:23). Corresponding to “Be strong,” He says, Do not be terrified; and corresponding to “Be courageous,” which means maintaining strength in the heart, He says, Do not be dismayed—meaning: Never fall from your level of resolve.
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 8_Verse, 1_Comment: For Hashem your God is with you wherever you go. Even when you go to war against the enemy, Hashem your God is with you to deliver your enemy into your hand. Therefore, He did not say, “For I am with you,” since this refers back to what Moses told him: “Hashem is the One Who goes before you; He will be with you” (Deuteronomy 31:8). Here He repeated what He had spoken through Moses.
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And Joshua commanded. I shall explain (in verse 12 and in chapter 2, verse 1) that before the word of Hashem came to him, Joshua was afraid. He spoke with the Reubenites and Gadites, asking them to go ahead as armed troops to assist him, and also secretly sent spies to investigate and gather information. He intended to wait until the spies returned. Now, however, upon hearing the word of Hashem, he took courage and no longer wished to wait for the spies, but commanded that the following proclamation be made:
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Prepare provisions for your journey. For on the morning of the second day they departed from Shittim (3:1). Preparing the provisions consisted of grinding the manna in mills and pounding it in a mortar.
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(12) Why does he alter the word order, placing the noun before the verb? The usual narrative wording would be, “And he said to the Reubenites,” for such is the rule of the language.
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 11_Verse, 1_Comment: And to the Reubenites. Hebrew ordinarily expresses the past by using future-tense verbs prefixed with a vav, which converts the future into the past: and he said, and he saw, and he separated, and he called. This applies specifically to narrative statements that preserve the chronological sequence of events, and is called the sequential past. But when the text wishes to recount something that began or occurred before the event previously narrated, it uses the verb alone and always places the noun before the verb. This is called the anterior past, as the grammarians have written. Thus Rashi explains “And Adam knew” (Genesis 4:1) as “he had already known,” and “And Hashem remembered Sarah” (ibid. 21:1) as occurring before He healed Abimelech. We have already discussed this in various places. Accordingly, since it does not say, “And Joshua said to the Reubenites and Gadites,” it is clear that the text does not follow chronological order here. Rather, and to the Reubenites he said means that he had said this previously. That is, even before the word of Hashem came to him, Joshua had been considering how to conquer the land. Being afraid of the war, he told the Reubenites and Gadites to cross over armed before their brothers, and likewise sent spies—all because of his fear and apprehension. Thus, the entire account from here until chapter 3 took place before the preceding event, when Hashem spoke to him. For when Hashem saw that he was dismayed at heart, He told him to cross the Jordan without waiting for the spies he had sent, to be strong and courageous, and not to rely upon the might of the Reubenites. Therefore, immediately after this Divine address, Joshua commanded the people to prepare provisions, for within three days they would cross the Jordan, although he did not then know that the spies would return within those days. This resolves the difficulty concerning the reckoning of the three days, as will be explained at the beginning of the next chapter.
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(13–15) Did not Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, stipulate with them (in the portion of Mattot) only that they should cross over armed and remain until the conquest was complete? Why, then, did Joshua add that they must remain until after the land had been apportioned and settled? Why does he repeat, “Hashem is granting you rest” and “He has given you this land”? And why does he say again, “Which Moses gave you beyond the Jordan,” words that appear superfluous? According to the rules of the language, he should have said, “You shall return to the land of your possession, which Moses gave you, and take possession of it” (as I explained this rule in my commentary on the Sifra, Vayikra 1, concerning the phrase “Which is at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting”).
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 12_Verse, 1_Comment: Remember the word. He refers to what is stated: “I commanded you at that time, saying: Hashem your God has given you this land to possess it; you shall cross over armed,” etc., “Only your wives and your little ones,” etc., “Until Hashem grants your brothers rest as He has granted you” (Deuteronomy 3:18–20). That is, in the condition he stipulated with them, he said, “And the land shall be subdued before Hashem, and afterward you may return” (Numbers 32:22; likewise verse 29), obligating them to remain only until the conquest was complete. In Deuteronomy, however, he recalled commanding them to remain there until the division of the land. Although he had not originally stipulated this, he said that fairness required them to do so. There is another reason for this, as I explained in my Torah commentary on the portion of Mattot: Moses repeatedly stipulated that they should go armed “before Hashem,” as it says, “Every armed man among you shall cross over before Hashem,” and “The land shall be subdued before Hashem” (ibid., verses 21–22). For he thought that the conquest would take place miraculously, in which case they would need to remain only until the conquest was complete. In Deuteronomy, however, he saw that the warfare would follow a more natural course. Therefore, he said, “You shall cross over armed before your brothers,” without specifying that they would cross “before Hashem.” They consequently needed to remain until the division was complete, when warfare would cease entirely. Joshua likewise explains here: Hashem your God is granting you rest—meaning that you enjoy two benefits: 1] Rest, for your wives and little ones dwell peacefully and no longer wander from place to place. 2] And He has given you this land, which you requested. He clarifies his meaning as follows:
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Your wives, your little ones, and your livestock shall remain in the land. They will not wander like your brothers’ wives. Therefore, fairness requires that you cross over armed before your brothers. (According to our explanation that “before your brothers” means the warfare would follow a natural course, he specifies that the mighty warriors should cross over. Had they crossed “before Hashem” in miraculous warfare, the entire people would have needed to cross, not specifically the mighty warriors.)
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Until Hashem grants your brothers rest as He has granted you. You must remain here until after the division of the land, so that they will have rest and an inheritance just as you do. Corresponding to “Hashem your God is granting you rest,” he says, “Until Hashem grants rest”; and corresponding to “He has given you this land,” he says, “And they too shall take possession,” etc.
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 14_Verse, 1_Comment: Which he gave. This means that he gave it to you only on this condition: that you would take possession of it if you did not abandon your brothers.
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: All. This means: You need not remind us of Moses’ command, for your own command is sufficient for us to act accordingly. And not only in this matter, which fairness obligates us to fulfill, but also wherever you send us, we will go, provided that:
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: Only if Hashem is with you as He was with Moses. Then you will have the same standing in our eyes as your teacher. And not only this, but also:
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: Any man who rebels against your command shall be put to death. In accordance with the law governing rebellion against royal authority. They said, “Anyone who rebels”—doing the opposite of what he was commanded—and also, “Who does not obey”—failing to do what he was commanded. For rebellion concerns violating a prohibition, while disobedience concerns failing to carry out a positive command. They said, in whatever you command us—even in a minor matter, he is liable to death under the law governing rebellion against royal authority.
text.1_, 0_Chapter, 17_Verse, 1_Comment: Only be strong. Provided that you show the strength befitting the leader of the people. Notice that they, too, mentioned the two things Hashem had told him: “No man shall stand against you,” and “As I was with Moses, so I will be with you.” Concerning both, they told him, “Be strong and courageous,” as I explained above.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: And he sent. This occurred when Joshua spoke to the Reubenites and Gadites, before Hashem spoke to him and before he proclaimed, “Prepare provisions for yourselves,” as I demonstrated (in the preceding chapter, verse 12). This resolves the commentators’ difficulty concerning the calculation of the three days, which does not accord with the time required for the spies’ journey and return. In fact, the spies had departed several days earlier.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 0_Verse, 1_Comment: And Joshua sent. He comes to answer the question that arises here: How could Joshua send spies after seeing the evil that resulted from the mission of the spies in the days of Moses? He answers that there were five differences between Joshua’s spies and those of Moses. 1] The spies sent by Moses were sent at the people’s request, as it says, “All of you approached me and said, ‘Let us send men ahead of us’” (Deuteronomy 1:22). Therefore, when they returned and brought back an evil report, the people relied upon them. Here, however, Joshua sent the spies on his own initiative, not at the people’s request. 2] Moses sent them from the wilderness of Paran, which was far from the land, and they were uncertain about the nature of the land and their ability to conquer it. Joshua, however, sent them from Shittim, which was on the border of the land. He had no doubt whether they would enter it; he sought only to determine the most advantageous place from which to conquer it. 3] Moses sent twelve scouts, whereas Joshua sent two men as spies. By this I mean that I have already explained in my commentary on the Torah (in the portions of Miketz and Shelach) that there is a distinction between a scout and a spy. A scout seeks what is good—whether the land is good, whether its inhabitants are mighty, and similar matters—whereas a spy seeks the land’s vulnerable points, from which it may most readily be conquered. I also explained that there are two kinds of missions. If the people send scouts to determine whether the land is good or bad—meaning whether it is worthwhile to wage war for it—they send a leader from every tribe. They will not rely upon men of lesser standing, nor will one tribe rely upon the emissary of another tribe. Each tribe will send a man whom it trusts to determine whether the land is suited to that tribe and its occupations, according to whether its members are farmers, shepherds, merchants, or seafarers. It was for this purpose that Moses sent men to scout the land, not to spy it out. He therefore sent a leader from every tribe, and for this reason their mission led to that great calamity. But when a spy is sent—after the people have already resolved to conquer the land, merely to identify its vulnerable points and determine from which direction it may most easily be conquered—one or two ordinary men are sent. Such a mission is undertaken solely by the commander of the army, who wishes to know from where he should launch his attack. Joshua therefore sent only two men, not twelve; ordinary men rather than tribal leaders; and spies rather than scouts. There was consequently no possibility here of their bringing back an evil report. 4] He sent them secretly—that is, in silence, so that no one knew of the matter except Joshua himself. 5] Saying, “Go, inspect the land, and Jericho.” The principal object of their mission was Jericho and the surrounding territory, since they would enter by that route and wished to know how it could be conquered.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 0_Verse, 2_Comment: And they went. It was for this purpose that they went.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 0_Verse, 3_Comment: And they came to the house of a prostitute named Rahab. This involved a twofold strategy. 1] To prevent anyone from recognizing them as Israelites, they entered the house of a prostitute. The inhabitants of Canaan knew that Israel was a people that detested sexual immorality, so it would never occur to them that Israelite agents would assemble in a prostitute’s house. 2] Because her name was Rahab, and she was famous by name among the leaders of the land—as it says, “Rahab enticed through her name” (Megillah 15a)—the secrets and private affairs of the land’s leaders were revealed to her, and through her they could investigate everything occurring in the land. Therefore, they went nowhere else, but lodged there.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(2) How could Joshua tell them that they would cross within three days? Perhaps the spies would be delayed for many days; how did he know that they would return from scouting the land immediately? If we say, following Ralbag, that he sent the spies earlier, the order of the verses becomes difficult: After the officers made their proclamation, Joshua spoke to the Reubenites and Gadites, and afterward sent the spies. All the commentators also wondered about the matter itself: How could Joshua send spies, forgetting that in the days of his teacher the spies had caused weeping for generations? If Moses did not do this until the people pressed him and he consulted Hashem, how could Joshua, after the calamity that resulted, do so on his own initiative? Furthermore, how could the messengers abandon their assigned mission of investigating and searching the land, enter the house of a prostitute, and lodge there? And how could they have acted so unwisely that the king of Jericho discovered them immediately on the very first night?
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: Behold, men. They understood that the men were spies for three reasons. 1] They had entered the city even though it was tightly shut, with no one going out or coming in. Thus it says, Behold, men have come. 2] They knew that the purpose of their journey was confined to Jericho alone. Had they been merchants traveling from place to place, they would have lodged near the gate so that they could continue their journey at daybreak, since during the siege the city gates would not be opened until full daylight. Thus it says, They have come here. 3] They came at night, unlike ordinary travelers, who enter while the light is still good, especially in a time of danger. From this they concluded that the men were from the children of Israel and that the purpose of their arrival was to search out the land—to learn its secrets through the prostitute. There is a distinction between one who searches out the land and a scout or spy: one who searches investigates a single place deeply in order to discover people’s thoughts and secrets. These men likewise went only to search out one particular place.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(3) Why the repetition: “who came to you” and “who entered your house”?
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 2_Verse, 1_Comment: Who came to you. That is, although they may tell you that they came to you for prostitution, know that the purpose for which they came was to enter your house, because they came to search out the entire land. They intend to investigate within your house the secrets and affairs of the whole land, which is the meaning of “searching out,” as explained above.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(4–6) Why does Scripture relate her concealment of them twice? And why does it first say, “She concealed him,” in the singular, and afterward, “She hid them,” in the plural?
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 3_Verse, 1_Comment: And she took them and concealed each one. There is a distinction between concealing and hiding. One who is concealed stands in a place where the eye cannot see him—even though he is not covered by any covering or by earth, but merely stands off to the side. (This is the opposite of the verb “to look,” as some Hebrew roots can denote both a thing and its opposite.) One who is hidden, however, is covered from above by a covering or by earth. When the king’s messengers arrived unexpectedly, Rahab had no time to hide the men beneath the stalks of flax and cover them. She could only conceal them—that is, place them off to the side in secluded corners so that they would not immediately be seen. Nor could she place both of them in one spot, for if they were discovered together, the searchers would recognize them as the two spies. She therefore placed each man separately in his own corner. Even if they discovered one of them, they would not think he was one of the spies, since they knew that there were two spies; and in any event, the other man would escape. Realizing, however, that they would find the men if they searched the house, she acted cunningly and wrung her hands, declaring that spies had indeed been there but had just departed and fled, so that the messengers would hurry out of her house and pursue them. Thus she said, Indeed, the men came to me—that is, the matter is exactly as you say, and the men came in precisely the manner you described, for immediately upon arriving they questioned and investigated matters as spies do. As a second indication, she said, But I did not know where they were from. If known men sometimes came and inquired about the affairs of the land, one might attribute their inquiries to chance. But these were strangers whose origin was unknown; what reason could they have for investigating the affairs of this land? Moreover, the fact that they concealed their place of origin and did not reveal where they came from demonstrated that they were spies.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: (Third proof) And it was time for the gate to be closed. They departed and disappeared just as the people were preparing to close the gate, behaving like fugitives. (Fourth proof) They went out in the darkness and gloom and did not carry a torch in their hands, for they fled to escape. (Fifth proof) I do not know where they went. Just as they concealed the place from which they came, so they concealed the place to which they were going. All these were clear signs that they were spies. Therefore, pursue them quickly, because: 1] It is proper to pursue them, since they are certainly spies. 2] You will certainly overtake them, and therefore you should not delay in pursuing and capturing them. (6) But she. After her cunning had succeeded in removing the messengers from her house, she feared that they might return to search for the men again. Therefore, she brought them up to the roof and hid them—“hiding” denotes covering something—by covering them with the stalks of flax that she had arranged there. They had already been laid out beforehand, so no one would suspect that men were concealed beneath them. The commentators explain “stalks of flax” as flax stalks, the expression being constructed like “crimson worm” and “worm of crimson.” It may also mean that the stalks had already been beaten but not yet combed, so that the flax fibers remained mixed with the woody stalks. Accordingly, Scripture uses the feminine form “arranged,” because “flax” is a feminine noun. Others explain that this was a kind of flax growing on trees, called “cotton” in the language of the Mishnah; ordinary flax, to which the prohibition of sha’atnez applies, grows from the ground, while cotton is called “tree flax.”
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(7) The final word “after them” is superfluous, since she had already said, “Pursue them.” Furthermore, Scripture does not explain who closed the gate. If Rahab closed it, why did she lower them by a rope? She could simply have opened the gate for them.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: And the men pursued. Meanwhile, they pursued after them, as they supposed, along the road to the Jordan.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 6_Verse, 2_Comment: And they closed the gate. The sense of the verse is: They closed the gate behind them, after the pursuers had gone out. The word “after them” is used as in, “And he closed the door behind him” (Genesis 19:6). After the pursuers went out, they closed the gate behind them from the other side, so that if the spies had not yet left the city, they would be unable to escape from it.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: And she went up to them. For they were hidden beneath the flax, and she went up to them to remove the covering and speak with them.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(9–11) Why the repetition: “Terror of you has fallen upon us,” “all the inhabitants of the land have melted away,” “we have heard,” and “our hearts melted”?
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 8_Verse, 1_Comment: I know. She first spoke generally: I know that Hashem has given you the land. She now explains how she knew this, based upon two things. 1] For terror of you has fallen upon us. The defining characteristic of “terror,” distinguishing it from other terms denoting fear and dread, is that terror always arises from one’s conception of the exalted stature and might of the object feared, not from the possibility of harm that it may cause. Thus, she means that terror of your greatness and exalted stature has fallen upon us. 2] And all the inhabitants of the land have also melted away from fear of the harm that you will bring upon them. She explains that her statement, “Terror of you has fallen upon us,” referring to awe of their exalted stature, was based upon this: (10) For we have heard how Hashem dried up the waters of the Sea of Reeds before you. Her statement, “All the inhabitants of the land have melted away,” was based upon hearing what you did to the two kings of the Amorites, whom you utterly destroyed, leaving no living soul.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And when we heard. Ordinarily, when a nation comes from the ends of the earth to destroy other lands, the inhabitants initially tremble and become afraid upon hearing reports of it. But when that nation approaches the border of their land, the inhabitants arouse themselves and encourage one another to fight against it. Here, however, this did not occur. Both when we heard, at which time our hearts melted because of the report, and even now, when you have approached the border of this land, no spirit of courage has arisen in any man to summon the people to arms, for they have all despaired of fighting. They know that Hashem your God is God in the heavens above and upon the earth below—and who can fight against and defeat such a mighty God?
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(12–14) Why did she repeat, “with my father’s household, kindness,” and “give me a true sign”? And why did they say, “We will deal with you with kindness and truth”? What is the distinction between these expressions? Furthermore, regarding their statement, “If you do not reveal this matter of ours”: If, as the commentators explain, this refers to the sign of the scarlet cord, they had not yet given her that sign.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 11_Verse, 1_Comment: And now. She said: Although after you cross the Jordan you will not leave any soul alive, swear to me now, before you cross the Jordan, for at this stage they were permitted to accept converts who made peace with them. Thus our Sages said (Jerusalem Talmud, Shevi’it 6:1): “Joshua sent three proclamations,” etc.; whoever wished to make peace could do so. Moreover, she had converted and accepted the kingdom of Heaven, as indicated by her words, “For Hashem your God is God,” etc. She specified three elements in the required oath: 1] Swear to me—for an oath taken according to another person’s understanding cannot be annulled. 2] Swear by Hashem—this is a more solemn oath, since it is taken using the Explicit Name. 3] Since I have shown kindness to you—an oath taken according to another person’s understanding in return for a favor that person performed cannot be annulled.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 11_Verse, 2_Comment: And you shall show. That is, I request the oath primarily for my father’s household, for with them you will be acting with kindness, since you are under no obligation to repay them for any favor. But you are obligated to spare my life, and this is called not kindness but truth. I therefore ask only that you give me a true sign—a sign between you and me by which you will recognize my house at the time of the conquest. She now explains the kindness they are to show to her father’s household: Her father—?
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: And you shall keep my father alive. 1] They must spare them and not kill them. 2] And you shall deliver our lives from death—you are obligated to protect us so that others do not kill us. She also alluded to their saving their very souls from spiritual death by converting them.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Our lives. They told her that this, too, was an obligation imposed upon them by law: to surrender their own lives to death in place of theirs.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 13_Verse, 1_Comment: If you do not reveal this matter of ours. That is, because you did not reveal our matter—although we informed you that we were spies, you did not report us to the royal palace. Therefore, saving your lives falls under the category of truth, as the repayment of an obligation. And it shall be, when Hashem gives us the land, that we will deal with you with kindness and truth—with truth by preserving your lives, and with kindness by granting you abundant gifts and honor.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: For her house was in the wall of the city. That is, it stood outside the city wall, with the wall itself forming one wall of her house. Therefore, it says that “her house was in the wall, within the city wall.” Her house was also recessed into the wall, so that the wall surrounded it on three sides, while she had a window opening freely toward the outside. Thus it says, “She dwelt in the wall.” This explains why her house did not collapse when the wall fell, as will be explained below (6:20), for they then lived in a house attached to the city wall but situated outside it.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And afterward, go on your way. That is, you will not need to take a circuitous route; simply descend from the mountain to the direct road and continue along it.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(17–20) This entire statement should have been spoken to her privately upon the roof, at the time of the oath, rather than after she had lowered them through the window, when there was a danger that their words might be overheard—for walls have ears. Furthermore, what did they mean by saying, “We are free from this oath of yours,” which indicates that the oath was not binding upon them? How could this be, seeing that they had initially sworn without any condition? How could they subsequently attach a condition to their oath? Moreover, according to the commentators’ interpretation, they should have said, “We wish to be free from the oath,” rather than making the categorical statement that they were free, which implies that the oath had never taken effect at all.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 16_Verse, 1_Comment: We are free. Since their original oath had been made without any conditions, if her family were to mingle with the inhabitants of the city, they would be obligated to save everyone in the city. They therefore told her: Know that we are free from your original oath, which you made us swear. That is, the oath was imposed upon us under compulsion, since we were in your power, and an oath taken under duress is not binding. Nevertheless, we now swear to you a second time—when we are no longer under compulsion—but conditionally: the oath will apply only to the members of your family who are found inside your house and do not go outside. If anyone goes outside, we are free of responsibility. It will also apply only if you bind the cord of scarlet thread, so that we can identify the house by that sign, and only if you do not disclose the sign; otherwise, everyone might bind a scarlet cord to his house. Thus, we are free from the first oath, which was unconditional, because you made us swear while we were under compulsion, as explained above. At first they said, “If you do not reveal this matter of ours,” in the plural, because this included the members of her household, who knew that they were spies but did not report them to the royal palace. Here, however, they refer to revealing the sign, which she alone knew, and therefore say, “If you do not reveal,” in the singular. We have explained that elevated language commonly denotes forceful entities through masculine grammatical forms. Therefore, they said “this oath of yours,” using the masculine zeh rather than the feminine zot, and pronounced “you made us swear” with a kamatz rather than a ḥirik. This indicates that both the oath itself and the one imposing it acted upon them with force, compulsion, and necessity—qualities represented by the masculine form. They were therefore free from it under the law governing oaths taken under duress.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: And she tied it. She did so immediately, lest they afterward notice anything suspicious.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: What had befallen them. There is a distinction between korot, unforeseen occurrences, and motza’ot, natural outcomes. Something whose cause is unknown or unusual is called a chance occurrence, whereas something arising from an evident and immediate cause is called an outcome. Therefore, regarding Jacob it says, “They told him everything that had happened to them” (Genesis 42:29), using korot, because there was no apparent reason for them to have been accused of being spies. Here, however, Scripture uses motza’ot, because it is natural for spies searching out a land to be detected; what befell them had a readily apparent and understandable cause.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: And they said. The conclusion of their report was that Hashem had given them the land, as demonstrated by His having miraculously delivered them.
text.1_, 1_Chapter, 23_Verse, 1_Comment: And that all the inhabitants of the land had melted away before them. This was evident from their seeing how frightened the king of Jericho was and how diligently he searched for them, as well as from what they learned from Rahab.
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: At the end. This was on the ninth of Nisan, as explained above, for the words “within three days” mean at the end of three days.
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: When you see. The Ark always journeyed after two tribal divisions, and the Levites always carried it. But now, when you see two changes—1] the Ark, etc., meaning that it travels first; and 2] the priests carrying it—you must not proceed as usual, when the first two divisions began the journey. Rather, you shall set out afterward.
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(4) His statement, “So that you may know the way, for you have not passed along the way,” etc., is unclear. It would make sense had he said, “For you have not passed along this way before.” But it is not reasonable to say that they required a guide because they had not traveled along any road yesterday or the day before. Moreover, he should have said, “For you have not passed along the way for many days.”
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 3_Verse, 1_Comment: But at a distance. Ralbag explains that because the Ark was showing them the way, it had to remain at a distance so that everyone could see it and know to follow it. If it were close to them, not everyone would be able to see it. Thus it says, so that you may know the way, etc. This is also evident from the opinion of the author of the cantillation marks, who placed the etnachta on the word “by measure.” According to Rashi’s interpretation, however, in which “so that you may know” refers back to “and you shall follow it,” the etnachta should have been placed on the word “to it.” Regarding the words for you have not passed along the way since yesterday and the day before, their meaning appears to be as follows: When Israel intended to enter the land in the days of Moses, it is written, “The Ark of Hashem’s covenant journeyed before them a three-days’ journey to seek out a resting place for them” (Numbers 10:33). According to Rashi, this was the Ark containing the fragments of the Tablets, and it always traveled in this manner. According to Ramban, however, there was only one Ark, and it traveled this way only then, when they intended to enter the land. It went three days’ journey before them like a warrior advancing before the camp to terrify the enemies. Its purpose at that time was therefore not to show them the way—for they then had the pillar of cloud—but to conquer the land, and for this reason it traveled three days ahead. Scripture therefore explains that its purpose in journeying now is to show you the way, not to conquer the land as in the days of Moses. The proof is: For you have not passed ahead along the way since yesterday and the day before. Had the Ark been going forth to conquer, it would have needed to set out beforehand along the road, together with the Levites accompanying it, since yesterday and the day before—that is, a journey of three days. Since its present journey is intended to show them the way, they must not approach it; rather, do not come near it, maintaining a measured distance of about two thousand cubits.
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(5–6) How did Joshua know that Hashem would perform wonders, when Hashem did not reveal this until afterward? And if he already knew it, why did Hashem later tell him, “This day I will begin to make you great”? He already knew this beforehand.
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 4_Verse, 1_Comment: And Joshua said, etc., Sanctify yourselves. When Joshua saw that the priests would carry the Ark that day, he knew that Hashem would perform wonders for them. Thus our Sages said (Sotah 33b): On three occasions the priests carried the Ark—when Israel crossed the Jordan, when they encircled Jericho, and when they returned the Ark to its place, the Holy of Holies, in the days of Solomon. On all these occasions, open miracles occurred: the fall of Jericho’s wall and the descent of the fire in the days of Solomon. Joshua thought that these miracles would be performed through Israel’s agency. Thus he said, Hashem will perform wonders in your midst. He therefore commanded them to sanctify themselves, so that the wonders might be performed through their merit and power. But Hashem informed him (verse 7) that the wonders would be brought about through His power and by means of the Ark of the Covenant.
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said. This occurred on the tenth of Nisan.
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: Carry. He commanded: 1] That the priests should carry the Ark, rather than the Levites. 2] That they should cross before the people, as explained above (verse 3).
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: This day I will begin to make you great. Hashem informed him that the wonders would not be performed through Israel’s agency. Rather, even before they approached the Jordan, its waters would turn backward before the Ark of the Covenant and Joshua, and from this they would recognize the greatness of his merit.
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: For as I was with Moses, etc. Just as the splitting of the Sea of Reeds occurred through Moses and by virtue of his power, so would this occur through Joshua. A miracle was not necessary merely to enable them to cross, for the Jordan is not so large a river that they could not cross it without a miracle. Jacob said, “For with my staff I crossed this Jordan” (Genesis 32:10), and the spies likewise crossed it without a miracle.
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: And you. Therefore, you shall command the priests carrying the Ark that when they reach the edge of the Jordan’s waters, they must stand there and not cross the Jordan, for the waters would recede only before the Ark; once it emerged from the Jordan, the waters would return to their place. He means that they were to stand at the eastern edge, as will be explained (4:11).
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(10–13) Regarding the words, “By this you shall know”: If they refer to the statement, “Behold, the Ark of the Covenant is crossing before you into the Jordan,” it is difficult to understand how this would show them that He would drive out the Canaanites before them, for until then the Ark of Hashem had also traveled at their head. But if they refer to the statement, “And it shall be, when the soles of the feet of the priests come to rest,” meaning that from this miracle they would know that He would perform other miracles for them in conquering the land, why did he interrupt the passage with the words, “And now, take for yourselves twelve men,” thereby cutting the statement into separate pieces? The commentators explain that the command, “And now, take for yourselves twelve men,” is itself the command that Hashem gave Joshua below (4:1–2). But this is exceedingly difficult: 1] If so, the words stated below, “Hashem said to Joshua,” belong here; why were they written out of place? Their strained interpretation that it means, “Hashem had already said,” does not accord with the rules of the language. In that case, Scripture should have said, “And Hashem had said to Joshua,” as it does above (1:12). Moreover, the words, “And now, take for yourselves,” should have been written at the end of the statement, since they concern an entirely separate matter.
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 8_Verse, 1_Comment: “And he said,” etc., “Come near,” etc. “And he said,” etc., “By this you shall know.” He told them in the name of Hashem that by this—namely, by the fact that the Ark of the Covenant, Hashem of all the earth, is passing before you into the Jordan—they would know, etc., for two reasons. 1] From the fact that the Ark of the Covenant is passing before you, you will know that the living God is in your midst and that He will surely drive out, etc., for it resembles a king going before his people to conquer the land for them. 2] From the fact that Hashem of all the earth is passing into the Jordan, which demonstrates that He is Hashem of the land. Just as gatekeepers open doors and do not close the gates before the ruler of the country, so the Jordan will open the gates of the land, and the King of Glory will enter through them. From this, too, you will know that He will surely drive them out, since the land belongs to Him. (Our Sages said (Leviticus Rabbah 10:9) that He compressed all of them between the two poles of the Ark. He told them, “By this”—that is, from the fact that you see yourselves all compressed together here—you shall know that the living God is in your midst. This contains an intelligible idea. The resting of the Divine Presence within Israel can occur on two levels: 1] Hashem may be among them like the heart within the body, surrounded by all the limbs. 2] He may be like the brain situated in the head of the body, intellectually encompassing the entire body. The Guide has already explained (part I, chapter 73), in comparing the greater world with the smaller world, that in the greater world, whatever is more important encompasses that which is less important, while the earth, the lowest of all, is encompassed by everything. In the human being, however, the reverse is true: that which is most important is situated in the center and surrounded by everything else. When Hashem is like the heart, surrounded within them, He governs through concealed Providence by means of natural intermediaries, and His Providence is surrounded by the world and by the natural order that covers it. But when He is like the brain, encompassing nature and governing it, He conducts the world through an intellectual and freely chosen order rather than a natural one—that is, through miraculous and wondrous governance. This is the distinction between “filling all worlds” and “surrounding all worlds” mentioned by the thinkers. At such a time, nature, materiality, and their conditions are entirely suspended. Therefore, here, when their King went at their head rather than being surrounded within them, He compressed them all between the two poles of the Ark, so that they were all encompassed by Him; and space, which is one of the conditions of physical existence, did not separate them. He told them: By this you shall know that the living God is in your midst—the God Who gives life to everything through His spiritual influence—and that He will drive out the Canaanites through miracles and wonders. The proof is that He passes before you as Hashem of all the earth, Who alone governs everything.)
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And now. Since the miracle will be performed through the Ark:
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 11_Verse, 1_Comment: Take for yourselves twelve men. So that they may serve as witnesses to the miracle.
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 11_Verse, 2_Comment: One man from each tribe. That is, each man shall represent his tribe. He shall be one of the tribe’s leaders, so that his presence there will be regarded as the presence of the entire tribe.
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: And it shall be, when the soles of the feet of those carrying the Ark of Hashem come to rest, etc. That is, through the power and holiness of the Ark, the waters of the Jordan shall be cut off—there will be a division and separation between the waters. Only the waters descending from above will be cut off; they will turn backward and stand like a heap, contrary to the nature of water. The waters flowing downward from that point, however, will continue descending naturally. Thus it says, They shall stand in a single heap. At the splitting of the Sea of Reeds, the miracle occurred on both sides, and the waters stood like two walls, because the waters of the sea flowed on a level plane. The waters of the Jordan, however, flowed from higher to lower ground, so their nature needed to be altered only on the upstream side. Therefore it says, “The Jordan turned backward” (Psalms 114:3).
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And it came to pass when the people set out. Scripture relates that by the time the priests reached the Jordan, all the people had already departed from their tents, so that those carrying the Ark were before the entire people as they journeyed from their tents.
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 13_Verse, 1_Comment: The Ark—the Covenant. It is sometimes called “the Ark of the Covenant” because the Tablets, which constitute the covenant, were placed within it. At other times, the Ark itself is called “the covenant of Hashem” (below, verse 17), because it is itself Hashem’s covenant. Likewise, the expression the Ark—the Covenant means that the Ark itself was the covenant, and it became a banner raised aloft.
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And when those carrying the Ark came, etc., their feet were immersed at the edge of the water. Although the Jordan ordinarily overflows all its banks throughout the harvest season, nevertheless:
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And they stood. This means that the miracle was twofold: 1] The waters descending from above ceased flowing and stood in a single heap, as explained above (verse 13). 2] Very far away. That is, the waters did not spread laterally toward the place where a city named Zarethan stood. Had the waters spread naturally across the surrounding area, they would have swept away the inhabitants of that city. Thus, the miracle also occurred across the width of the Jordan: the heap of water remained far from the people of the city situated beside Zarethan, and the city’s inhabitants suffered no harm.
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 15_Verse, 1_Comment: And the waters flowing downward were exhausted. This occurred naturally: because they were cut off and separated from the waters upstream, they naturally continued flowing until they were depleted.
text.1_, 2_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: And they stood. Scripture relates all the details of the miracle. 1] The priests stood firmly upon dry ground. That is, although naturally, even if the depths dry up, some water will inevitably remain in hollows and channels, leaving the ground muddy, here the miracle was that they dried completely, so that the priests could stand firmly upon dry ground. 2] Israel likewise stood upon dry ground. 3] The miracle continued until the entire nation had finished crossing, etc. (Do not incline your ear to the words of Ralbag, who wrote here as follows: “It is proper that we investigate here the resolution of a considerable difficulty arising from this miracle. Our Sages have established that miracles do not bring anything fundamentally new into existence. Therefore, Rava found difficulty in the verse, ‘But if Hashem creates a new creation’ (Numbers 16:30): Is it not written, ‘There is nothing new beneath the sun’ (Ecclesiastes 1:9)? He resolved the difficulty by explaining that the miracle merely hastened the earth’s opening of its mouth. The explanation is that over a long period this can naturally happen to the earth when smoky vapor is confined within it, as explained in the Book of Signs; the miracle caused, in no perceptible interval of time, what nature ordinarily accomplishes over a long period. The same applies to the transformation of the staff into a serpent. But Hashem does not create something fundamentally new among all existing things. Therefore, He could not make something simultaneously a staff and a serpent, nor produce something whose existence contradicts itself—for example, a square whose diagonal equals its side; a triangle composed of straight lines whose angles total less or more than two right angles; cold fire; or anything similar. Since this is so, and it is the nature of water, whenever it actually exists as water, to seek the lowest place, it would appear that this miracle occurred in a manner that cannot properly be attributed to Hashem. It may therefore be said that causing water not to flow is not something fundamentally new, since this already happens when something prevents its movement. It is possible that, miraculously, God created in the air adjacent to the water a dense, transparent substance that prevented the water from descending. Alternatively, Hashem may have created a powerful wind that drove the water toward that place and prevented it from descending.” These are his words. But he has equated things that are not equal. It is indeed true that we do not describe God as producing something self-contradictory, such as a round square, or causing one object to be both black and white simultaneously. Likewise, the Sages agreed that “there is nothing new beneath the sun.” Their meaning is that after the first absolute Creation, when He created existence from nothing, He would not again create something from nothing, but would produce one existing thing from another through the transformation of forms, as we have explained in many places. Therefore, Rava questioned the words, “If Hashem creates a new creation,” because the term “creation” properly denotes bringing something into existence from nothing, as explained in our commentary on Genesis. Altering the nature of an existing substance, however, is not the production of something from nothing, but merely a change in the nature and properties of something that already exists. Hashem does this whenever necessary, and it is called a miracle because He alters the customary nature of the substance. Through His wonders He cools fire, arrests the sun, and causes flowing waters to stand like a heap. All these are merely alterations in a substance’s natural quality or motion, which are attributes of the substance rather than the substance itself. Furthermore, even according to his own approach, Ralbag failed to understand the matter here. Water’s downward movement is not an intrinsic property of the water itself, as heat and burning are intrinsic properties of the element of fire. Rather, it results from the pressure of the air, which weighs upon the water and forces it downward. Water can rise as vapor and make the clouds its chariot; it can also remain suspended in a vessel whose upper opening is sealed, when the air does not press upon it from above. It is therefore evident that water’s descent results from an external cause, not from its own nature. If the air hovering over the water were removed at the place where the waters were cut off, the flowing waters would necessarily stand like a heap, just as water rises within a tube from which the air has been removed by an air pump. Why, then, should the waters not stand still before Hashem of all the earth? Scripture also makes clear that it was not a wind that restrained the waters, for in that case they would have spread sideways toward Adam, the city beside Zarethan; nor was it a dense, transparent substance, for it would have been adjacent to the priests’ feet and they would have perceived it. Scripture says, “Do not be excessively wise; why should you bring desolation upon yourself?” (Ecclesiastes 7:16).)
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(1–2) I have already explained that the plain meaning of the words “Hashem said” indicates that He spoke to Joshua only now. If so, how had Joshua previously selected twelve men on his own initiative? Furthermore, above (3:12) it says “one man for each tribe,” using the prefix lamed, whereas here it says “one man from each tribe,” using the prefix mem. Why this change?
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: Take for yourselves. In addition to the twelve men whom Joshua had selected above (3:12) to serve as witnesses to the miracle, Hashem commanded him to select twelve men. Joshua had selected one man for each tribe. The use of the prefix lamed indicates that each man would stand in place of his tribe; he therefore had to select the leader of each tribe, as explained above. Hashem, however, said, Take for yourselves from among the people, for these men did not need to be leaders. He required one man from each tribe. The prefix mem indicates only that each man should come from a particular tribe, not that he should represent his entire tribe. (For this reason, above Scripture used the singular “man,” whereas here it uses the plural “men.” The singular form there indicates that they were equal in leadership and prominence, as I have explained frequently in my commentary on the Torah.)
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And command them, saying, “Take for yourselves from here.” That is, they were to point out with a finger the precise place from which the stones should be taken, which had to meet two conditions: 1] From the midst of the Jordan, not from the side near its bank. 2] From where the priests’ feet stood—that is, from beneath their feet. He commanded them to carry the stones across the Jordan with them and deposit them at the place where they would lodge.
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And Joshua called. Since Joshua had already selected twelve men on his own initiative, he summoned them to perform this commandment as well, for each one was from a different tribe, in accordance with the word of Hashem.
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Cross over. Since they were standing at the bank of the Jordan, he told them to cross over into the Jordan, to the far side of the Ark. (He certainly indicated to them that they should take the stones from beneath the place where the priests stood.)
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 4_Verse, 1_Comment: And each of you shall lift up for himself. Hashem’s words, “Take for yourselves twelve stones,” could be understood to mean that they should take all twelve stones together and carry them on poles, which would enable them to carry heavier stones—as stated in Sotah 34a, “It is traditionally known that every load a person lifts upon his shoulders,” etc. Joshua therefore clarified that each man was to lift a separate stone and carry it upon his own shoulder. (See my commentary on the Sifra concerning the verse “You shall bring your offering” in Leviticus 1:2.) He explained the reason: There were to be twelve stones corresponding to the number of the tribes, for each tribe constitutes a distinct entity.
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(6–7) Why does he repeat, “So that this may be a sign among you,” and, “These stones shall be a memorial for the children of Israel forever”? It also appears that the sign was to be “among you,” meaning within that generation, whereas the memorial was to remain forever. Why did Joshua repeat these matters a second time (verses 21–23)? Here he says, “When your children ask tomorrow,” implying that they would question the people of that generation, and likewise, “What do these stones mean to you?” But in verse 21 he says, “When their children ask their fathers,” implying future generations, and does not include the word “to you.” Here he says, “You shall say to them,” whereas in verse 22 he says, “You shall inform them.” Here he says that the waters were cut off before the Ark of Hashem, whereas there he says that Hashem dried them up before you, without mentioning that it occurred because of the Ark. There he recounts the event at length—“Israel crossed on dry ground,” etc.—whereas here he speaks briefly.
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: So that. He further explains the purpose of taking the stones: they were to serve as a sign. This statement is repeated below (verses 21–22), where it says, When your children ask their fathers in time to come, saying, “What are these stones?” you shall inform your children, saying, “Israel crossed this Jordan on dry ground.” These are two distinct statements. Here he says, When your children ask tomorrow, implying that the children of that generation would ask you; likewise, the words What do these stones mean to you? make clear that this passage concerns the question asked by the contemporary generation. Below, however, Scripture discusses the questions of future generations and therefore does not include the word “to you.” The stones served both as a sign and as a memorial. The sign was intended as an indication for that generation, whereas the memorial was intended to preserve the event for the final generation. Since the contemporary generation witnessed the miracle with their own eyes, they did not require a memorial, but they did require a sign—so that they would not imagine that the Jordan had been split through their own power and merit. The stones taken from beneath the feet of the priests carrying the Ark served as a sign that the Jordan was split through the power of the Ark and the holiness of the Tablets of the Covenant contained within it. Thus it says, When your children ask tomorrow, saying, “What do these stones mean to you?” They will ask you why you require a memorial, since you witnessed the event with your own eyes.
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And you shall say to them. Here Scripture does not say, “You shall inform them,” as it does below (verse 22), because both they and their children already knew what had occurred.
