Rather, you shall explain to them that the stones are needed as a sign, so that we may know that the waters of the Jordan were cut off not because of us, but before the Ark of the Covenant of Hashem and through its power. The proof is that when it passed through the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan were cut off; this serves as a sign that the waters were cut off because of the Ark. Besides serving as a sign for the present generation, these stones shall also be a memorial for the children of Israel forever. That is, in future generations, whose members did not witness the miracle, they will serve as a memorial to the miracle itself. Joshua explains this second purpose—that the stones should serve as a memorial for later generations—below (verse 21 through the end of the passage), as will be explained there.
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(8) Why does he repeat, “As Joshua commanded,” and “As Hashem had spoken to Joshua”?
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 7_Verse, 1_Comment: And they did so. There was a difference between the wording of Hashem’s command to Joshua and that of Joshua’s command to the people. Hashem’s words did not explicitly state that each man should carry one particular stone, while Joshua’s words did not mention that they should carry the stones with them to their lodging place. Therefore, Scripture says that they acted “as” Joshua had commanded and carried twelve stones—that is, they carried them in the manner Joshua had commanded, each man bearing one stone upon his shoulder. They likewise acted as Hashem had spoken to Joshua, etc., and carried them with them to their lodging place.
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And twelve stones. After they removed the stones from beneath the priests’ feet, Joshua set up other stones in their place. These stones also remained as a memorial at the site where the miracle occurred.
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And the priests stood. That is, they remained standing at the eastern bank of the Jordan until the entire matter was completed. This appears to refer to what is stated: “Call Joshua, and present yourselves in the Tent of Meeting,” etc., “And Hashem said to Moses, ‘Behold, you are about to lie with your fathers,’” together with the entire passage that follows (Deuteronomy 31:14 onward). Hashem commanded Joshua to speak these words to the people.
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(11–18) After saying, “The Ark of Hashem and the priests crossed over,” thereby apparently completing the account, why does Scripture return and say that Joshua commanded the priests to come up from the Jordan? Had they not already crossed it? Moreover, the verses indicate that the priests stood at the eastern edge of the Jordan, as it says, “When you reach the edge of the waters of the Jordan, you shall stand in the Jordan,” and this is stated explicitly in 3:15. If so, Scripture should have said, “They crossed the Jordan.” “Coming up” denotes ascending from the place where one is standing onto the adjacent bank, whereas “crossing” denotes passing from one bank to the other. [For this reason, our Sages said (Sotah 35a) that Joshua actually commanded them to come up onto the eastern bank. The earlier statement, “The Ark of Hashem crossed over,” occurred afterward, through a miracle in which the Ark and its bearers flew through the air. According to this explanation, however, the events are related out of chronological order, whereas our purpose is to make the crooked straight according to the plain meaning.] After Scripture has stated that all the people crossed together with the Ark, why does it return to relate that the Reubenites and Gadites crossed, when they had marched ahead of the people? Finally, the wording indicates that the words (verse 18), “The soles of the priests’ feet were lifted onto the dry ground,” form the predicate of the sentence—that is, it was then that their feet were lifted. [Otherwise, Scripture should have said, “And it came to pass when they came up,” etc., “that their feet were lifted,” etc., “and the waters of the Jordan returned.”] How, then, is the verse to be understood?
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 10_Verse, 1_Comment: And the Ark of Hashem crossed over. The Ark then crossed from the eastern bank, where it had stood until that point, to the western bank. (The term “crossing” applies to passing from one edge to the other, although they did not leave the Jordan until afterward, as stated in verse 16, “Come up from the Jordan,” referring to their subsequent ascent from the western bank.) The words “before the people” mean “in the sight of the people.”
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And they crossed. Until this point, the Reubenites and Gadites had traveled according to the order of the tribal divisions. From this point onward, they began crossing at the head of the people, as Moses had said, “You shall cross over as advance troops before your brothers” (Deuteronomy 3:18). They are called ḥamushim because they customarily divided themselves into units of fifty men, each with a commander of fifty at its head; and they are called ḥalutzim, advance troops, because they separated themselves from the rest of their brothers to go to war. Not all of them went, for the Reubenites and Gadites alone numbered more than eighty-three thousand.
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Before Hashem for battle. This too formed part of the condition Moses stipulated with them (in the portion of Mattot): that they cross over before Hashem—that is, for His sake—and not as men relying upon their own strength, as I explained in my commentary.
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Hashem made Joshua great. For they saw that the miracle occurred primarily on Joshua’s account, as explained above (3:7).
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And they came up. That is, they ascended from the western bank of the Jordan onto dry land. Therefore, Scripture says, And they came up, rather than “and they crossed.” The reason they required an explicit command was that, after Joshua had told them, “You shall stand in the Jordan,” they were not permitted to leave on their own without authorization.
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: And it came to pass when they came up. Scripture relates three miracles that occurred here. 1] There is a distinction between ḥaravah and yabbashah. A place may be called ḥaravah in reference to the fact that water had previously been there, even though it has now dried completely. Thus, the statement, “All Israel crossed on ḥaravah,” describes the drying up of the water that had formerly been there, although the Jordan had become completely dry, as stated in verse 22: “Israel crossed this Jordan on yabbashah.” Alternatively, even a place where there had been no water may be called ḥaravah if it is not completely dry but remains damp and muddy. The Jordan, where the miracle occurred, dried completely; but the bank of the Jordan, which is always damp and where no miracle occurred, was merely ḥaravah—damp ground. Thus it says, And it came to pass when the priests came up, etc., that the soles of the priests’ feet were lifted onto the ḥaravah. That is, as they ascended, they moved from the yabbashah—the completely dry ground in the middle of the Jordan—to its bank, which was ḥaravah and still somewhat damp. 2] Immediately when they came up, the waters of the Jordan returned to their place. 3] And they flowed as yesterday and the day before. Since the waters had accumulated in layers, one upon another, they should naturally have surged down all at once when the miracle ended and spread laterally beyond the riverbanks. The miracle was that they descended gradually until they flowed as they ordinarily had before.
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: And the people. Scripture also relates that this miracle occurred on the tenth of Nisan. The verses describe at length the place and time of the miracle and all its details in order to refute the deniers, who might claim that it occurred when the waters had naturally dried up, or that Joshua knew how to calculate the times when the waters would rise and fall—what is called “ebb and flow.” Scripture therefore specifies that the miracle occurred on the tenth day of the month, when the Jordan ordinarily overflows, and identifies the location, which remained recognizable through the stones even in the prophet’s time. At that place, the waters never dry up, nor do they rise and fall with the waxing and waning of the moon. Scripture further proves the miracle from its precise duration: It began at the exact moment when the soles of the priests’ feet came to rest and ended at that very instant when they departed. Nor can it be said that Joshua calculated how long the priests should remain in the Jordan, for Scripture says, “The people hurried and crossed.” The people therefore completed the crossing earlier than might have been expected, yet everything still coincided at the precise instant. From this they knew that the hand of Hashem had done it.
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 18_Verse, 1_Comment: And they encamped at Gilgal. According to our Sages (Sotah 36a), they traveled sixty mil that day.
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(20–24) The statement that Joshua set them up at Gilgal is unclear, for Scripture already said (verse 8), “They deposited them there.” The other differences between this passage and what Joshua said above (verses 5–7) have already been noted there.
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 19_Verse, 1_Comment: Joshua set them up at Gilgal. Verse 8 relates that those carrying the stones deposited them at the lodging place without arranging them. Here Scripture relates that Joshua set them one upon another, building them upward and forming them into a monument. We have already explained that these stones served both as a sign and as a memorial: a sign for the present generation, who knew of the miracle, and a memorial for future generations, so that they would remember it, as stated in verses 6–7. Those who carried the stones deposited them for the purpose of the sign, while Joshua erected them as a memorial for future generations.
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said. That is, besides serving as a sign for the present generation, it would serve as a memorial when your children ask in time to come—in future generations.
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: And you shall inform them. Through this memorial, you shall make known to them that Israel crossed the Jordan. Here, the purpose is not to specify the cause through which the miracle occurred, as in verses 6–7, but to commemorate the miracle itself. Although it occurred through the merit of the Ark, it was nevertheless performed for Israel’s sake.
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: Who dried up. Just as He dried up the waters of the Sea of Reeds before us—meaning before Joshua, who had participated in the Exodus from Egypt—so He dried up the waters of the Jordan before you, the generation entering the land. Both occurred miraculously, and both served two purposes: 1]
text.1_, 3_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: So that they may know. The nations should recognize the hand of Hashem and fear Him with the fear of punishment. 2] Israel should recognize His wonders and fear Him with the awe inspired by His exaltedness. He also means that the miracle previously performed at the sea was repeated at the Jordan for two reasons: 1] So that the nations of this land, who had not witnessed the splitting of the Sea of Reeds, would also recognize the hand of Hashem. 2] So that you may fear Him all the days. For this reason, He repeatedly manifests His power and might in every generation. The word yiratem, “you feared,” is unusually vocalized with a kamatz beneath the resh. According to Radak in the Mikhlol, it follows the paʿal conjugation and uses the past tense in place of the future.
text.1_, 4_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Make for yourself sharp knives. Targum Jonathan translates this as “sharp scalpels.” The adjective is placed in construct with the noun it modifies, as in “the bitter waters” (Numbers 5:18) and “the third generation” (Genesis 50:23). In Genesis Rabbah (31:8), it is explained as “blades of stone,” interpreting tzurim as in, “Zipporah took a flint” (Exodus 4:25). That is, since Joshua also instructed them at that time to purify themselves from corpse impurity, as our Sages stated (Yevamot 71b), he could not circumcise them with an iron sword. A metal implement or sword assumes the same degree of impurity as the corpse that contaminated it and would therefore render them impure again, as explained by Rambam (Laws of Impurity from the Dead 5). He consequently circumcised them with flint, which is not a metal implement.
text.1_, 4_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: And circumcise, etc., a second time. A great multitude had already been circumcised together at the Exodus from Egypt, and now they were circumcised a second time. According to what we shall explain—that the tribe of Levi never ceased practicing circumcision, either in Egypt or in the wilderness—the words “a second time” mean that only those who had been circumcised on the first occasion were now to be circumcised again, but not the tribe of Levi.
text.1_, 4_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(4–7) How is it possible that all Israel was uncircumcised, as the verses here appear to indicate? The tribe of Levi, as well as those who were under twenty years old at the time of the sin of the spies, entered the land, and they were circumcised. Moreover, does not the Midrash state that the tribe of Levi observed the covenant of circumcision even in the wilderness? Why did Moses’ court not compel them to undergo circumcision? If it was because the north wind did not blow for them, did our Sages not say that regarding a danger commonly disregarded by the public, “Hashem protects the simple”? If it was because they did not know when they would travel, why did Moses not inform them, whenever they remained in one place for many days, that it was now safe to circumcise? Moreover, if this was the reason, how did the tribe of Levi circumcise its children throughout all those years? The verses themselves are also repetitive and seemingly superfluous, and cannot be explained without considerable strain and forced interpretation.
text.1_, 4_Chapter, 3_Verse, 1_Comment: And this is the reason. That is, this was the reason Joshua circumcised them, and he circumcised only those to whom this reason applied. It is impossible to say that they were all uncircumcised, for those who were under twenty years old when the spies were sent had been circumcised and entered the land. Nor had the decree been issued against the tribe of Levi. The Midrash likewise states (Numbers Rabbah 3:6) that the tribe of Levi did not cease practicing circumcision in the wilderness, as it says, “They preserved Your covenant” (Deuteronomy 33:9). Joshua therefore needed to circumcise only the sons who had arisen in place of their fathers—that is, those whose fathers died in the wilderness because of the sin of the spies. The commentators explain that this generation’s justification for neglecting circumcision was that they continually wandered along the way and did not know the day of their next journey. They therefore feared to circumcise because of the danger to the child, as it says, “To circumcise and then set out is dangerous for the child” (Nedarim 31b). Our Sages said (Yevamot 72a) that it was because the north wind did not blow for them. The tribe of Levi, however, together with the righteous among Israel, disregarded these concerns and circumcised their sons. Regarding the absence of the north wind, the Talmud says (there) that nowadays, since the multitude commonly disregards this danger, “Hashem protects the simple.” Regarding the weakness caused by traveling, they could remain outside the cloud until they recovered, relying upon Hashem’s Providence. Moses our teacher was punished for failing to circumcise his son, as it says, “And it came to pass on the way, at the lodging place” (Exodus 4:24), and Zipporah circumcised him while they were traveling. Only those whose hearts were not wholly devoted to Hashem sought excuses and did not circumcise their sons. Moses’ court could not compel them, because they possessed a plausible justification. Scripture therefore explains here whom Joshua circumcised and why: All the people who came out of Egypt, all the men of war—meaning those who were more than twenty years old—died along the way. The underlying cause of their death had already existed when they came out of Egypt, for they had not yet purified themselves from the impurity of Egypt and its corrupt beliefs.
text.1_, 4_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: For they were circumcised. All those who came out of Egypt were circumcised. Of these, Joshua did not circumcise those who entered the land—namely, the tribe of Levi and those who had been under twenty years old.
text.1_, 4_Chapter, 4_Verse, 1_Comment: But all the people born, etc., they had not circumcised. That is, their fathers had not circumcised them, for the verb “circumcise” in the simple conjugation is always transitive.
text.1_, 4_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: For. Why did they not circumcise their sons, and why did Moses’ court not compel them to do so? He answers that the court could not compel them, for they traveled for forty years, etc. They were continually wandering through the wilderness and therefore had a plausible justification for neglecting circumcision because of the weakness caused by travel. Had their hearts been upright, they would have disregarded this concern, as the tribe of Levi did when circumcising their sons. But the reason they were made to wander through the wilderness was until the entire nation had perished, etc.—those who did not obey the voice of Hashem and were not righteous. The proof is that Hashem swore to them that He would not show them the land, for He knew that they were unworthy of it.
text.1_, 4_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And their children. These were the children born to them in the wilderness, whom He raised up in their place, as it says, “But your little ones, whom you said would become plunder—I will bring them in,” etc. (Numbers 14:31). Joshua circumcised them, for they were uncircumcised, because their fathers had not circumcised them along the way. That is, their fathers had a plausible excuse arising from the journey, during which they continually wandered. Joshua did not need to circumcise the tribe of Levi or the children born to those who had been under twenty years old at the time of the decree, for they were righteous and had already circumcised their sons.
text.1_, 4_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: And they remained in their places. Since until then they had been concerned about the danger posed by traveling, they did not move from their place until they had recovered.
text.1_, 4_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: This day I have rolled away. Their neglect of the commandment of circumcision resulted from their not yet having purified themselves from the abominations of Egypt, where the people were uncircumcised, as indicated above (verse 5) by the words “on the way, when they came out of Egypt.” This day I have rolled away this disgrace from upon you. Uncircumcision was considered a disgrace, as it says, “To give our sister to a man who is uncircumcised, for that would be a disgrace to us” (Genesis 34:14). That is, they had inherited this disgrace from Egypt.
text.1_, 4_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And they offered the Passover sacrifice. For while they were uncircumcised, they could not offer it.
text.1_, 4_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(11–12) Rashi, following the words of our Sages (Kiddushin 38a), explains that “they ate from the produce of the land” means that they ate from the new crop on the day after the Passover—namely, the sixteenth of Nisan, after the offering of the Omer. This does not accord with the plain meaning, for everywhere in the Torah, “the day after the Passover” means the day after the slaughtering of the Passover sacrifice, which is the fifteenth of Nisan. Furthermore, why does Scripture first say “from the produce of the land” and afterward “from the yield of the land”? If this interpretation is correct, it should have said, “The manna ceased when they ate from the produce of the land,” making the phrase “on the next day” superfluous. The wording would also be unnecessarily lengthy, for it should simply have said, “The manna ceased on the day after the Passover, and they ate unleavened bread and parched grain from the yield of the land of Canaan.” Finally, the phrase “in that year” is imprecise, since from that time onward they continued eating the land’s produce forever.
text.1_, 4_Chapter, 10_Verse, 1_Comment: And they ate from the “stored produce” of the land. According to the plain meaning, there is a distinction between stored produce and the current crop. Stored produce is the land’s yield from the preceding year. It is called avur, “that which has passed,” because the land has once again passed through its fruit-bearing cycle. The current crop, however, is the produce of that particular year, which the land brought forth during that year. Throughout the Torah, “the day after the Passover” means the fifteenth of Nisan, the day following the slaughtering of the Passover sacrifice, as in, “On the day after the Passover, the children of Israel departed” (Numbers 33:3). The verse means that on the fifteenth of Nisan they ate unleavened bread to fulfill the day’s commandment, and parched grain as a delicacy, both taken from the stored produce of the land—the old crop. They could not eat from the new crop because the Omer had not yet been offered. (Incidentally, Scripture informs us that as long as they still possessed manna, they did not eat ordinary produce. They ate it on that day only to fulfill the commandment of unleavened bread, together with a small amount of parched grain as a delicacy. Thus it says, on that very day.)
text.1_, 4_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And the manna ceased on the following day. Because they had begun eating from the stored produce of the land, the manna ceased on the day following that day—that is, on the sixteenth of Nisan. Since they no longer had manna and the Omer had now been offered, they ate from the crop of the land of Canaan that year. The words “that year” modify “the crop”: They ate from the crop that had grown during that year, meaning the new crop. (This accords with the interpretation of Rabbeinu Tam cited by Tosafot in Kiddushin 37b and Rosh Hashanah 13a. The Talmud there likewise explains: “This is well according to the one who says that ‘in your dwellings’ means wherever you dwell, for then we understand why it is written, ‘They ate from the stored produce of the land on the day after the Passover’: They ate on the day after the Passover, but previously they did not eat. Evidently, they first offered the Omer and only afterward ate. But according to the one who says that ‘in your dwellings’ means only after conquest and settlement, why did they not eat immediately? They did not need to, because they were sustained by the manna in their vessels.” The Talmud’s inference does not arise from the words, “They ate from the stored produce of the land on the day after the Passover,” but from the statement, “The manna ceased on the following day”—the sixteenth of Nisan—“and they ate from the crop of the land of Canaan.” This is the meaning of its words, “They ate on the day after the Passover, but previously they did not eat.” In the language of the Sages, “the day after the Passover” refers to the sixteenth. That is, on the sixteenth they ate from the new crop, but not previously. For Scripture says that “they ate from the stored produce of the land on the day after the Passover”—on the fifteenth, which the language of the Torah calls “the day after the Passover,” they ate from the old crop. Only on the following day, the sixteenth—which the language of the Sages calls “the day after the Passover”—did they eat from the crop of the land of Canaan. The Talmudic commentators understood the statement “They ate on the day after the Passover” as referring to the “day after the Passover” mentioned in Scripture. In truth, however, it employs the terminology of the Sages, who call the sixteenth “the day after the Passover.” This resolves Tosafot’s objection there to the interpretation of Rabbeinu Tam.) The passage in the Jerusalem Talmud may be explained similarly. Regarding Rabbi Ishmael’s opinion that the prohibition against eating the new crop took effect only after conquest and settlement, Rabbi Bun bar Kahana objected: “‘They ate from the stored produce of the land on the day after the Passover’—did they not eat on the sixteenth?” Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Yose then objected: “But is it not written, ‘On the day after the Passover, the children of Israel departed from the land of Egypt’? Did they not depart on the fifteenth?” (Jerusalem Talmud, Ḥallah 2:1). Both challenge Rabbi Ishmael’s position. Rabbi Bun asks: Scripture says that they ate from the stored produce of the land—the old crop—on the day after the Passover, the fifteenth, but not on the sixteenth, when they ate from the new crop, as it says, “The manna ceased on the following day”—the sixteenth—“and they ate from the crop of the land of Canaan.” Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Yose strengthens Rabbi Bun’s objection, lest one argue that Scripture’s “day after the Passover” means the sixteenth of Nisan, as it does in the language of the Sages, in which case nothing could be inferred from this verse. He therefore proves that in Scriptural language, “the day after the Passover” is the fifteenth.
text.1_, 4_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(13–15) It is exceedingly difficult: If the man appeared to Joshua through a prophetic vision, so that Joshua knew this was a revelation of an angel of Hashem, how could he have wondered whether the angel might be assisting Israel’s enemies? Had not Hashem promised to be with him, neither letting go of him nor forsaking him? But if the man appeared to him in an ordinary manner and Joshua did not recognize him as an angel of Hashem, why did Joshua approach him alone rather than send one of his men to ask the purpose of his arrival? How could he ask a solitary man, “Are you for us or for our adversaries?” What assistance could one man provide? And why did Joshua bow to him immediately upon his claiming to be an angel? Perhaps the man was deceiving and mocking him. Furthermore, what was the purpose of this entire vision?
text.1_, 4_Chapter, 12_Verse, 1_Comment: And it came to pass when Joshua was at Jericho. This occurred when he went to conquer Jericho and was in the surrounding area of the city. (Our Sages said (Nedarim 56b): From here it is derived that a city’s outskirts are regarded as part of the city.) Before the word of Hashem was revealed to him—as it says, “And Hashem said to Joshua” (6:2)—he saw the angel who regularly serves as the intermediary through whom prophecy reaches the prophet. He saw: 1] The form of a man. 2] That the man held a drawn sword in his hand. 3] That he stood facing him. Joshua recognized that he was an angel, for those to whom angels appeared in prophetic visions could recognize them as such. He also understood why the angel appeared with a drawn sword: This indicated that the coming prophecy would concern the war against Jericho, which they would conquer by the sword. He did not understand, however, why the angel stood facing him. If he had come to march at their head and fight the enemy, his face should have been directed toward the enemy, not toward Israel. Divine assistance granted to Israel in warfare can take two forms: 1] Limited assistance, in which they must fight with their own swords and bows, while Hashem strengthens and encourages them so that their hearts do not falter and gives them the power to achieve victory. 2] Great assistance, in which they need not fight at all; Hashem fights for them, while they merely pursue the enemy and strip the slain. Had Joshua seen the angel facing the enemy, he would have known that Hashem intended to grant them a great deliverance, with the angel himself fighting the enemy on their behalf. But because he saw the angel facing Joshua, he thought that the angel had come merely to strengthen the hands of the Israelites who would themselves do the fighting, which would be only limited assistance. He therefore asked him, Are you for us? That is, have you come merely for our sake, to strengthen us while we ourselves fight, or for our enemies? Have you come to fight directly against our enemies?
text.1_, 4_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said, “No.” He answered: Do not remain uncertain about this, for in truth, I am the commander of Hashem’s army. That is, I have not come alone; countless hosts of the celestial army accompany me, going forth to fight the enemy, and I am the commander who marches at their head. You saw me standing with my face toward you because I have now come for the first time. The battle has not yet begun; I have come merely to communicate a prophetic message to you. When Joshua saw that the angel was speaking to him, he fell upon his face and asked, “What does my lord say to his servant?”
text.1_, 4_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said, etc., Remove your shoe. That is, the word of Hashem will soon be revealed to you, and you must remove the garments of materiality from yourself, preparing for the prophecy that I have come to convey to you and making yourself ready to receive the prophetic influence. Our Sages said (Genesis Rabbah 97:3): “‘Now I have come’—but in the days of your teacher Moses, I came and he did not desire me.” For both Moses’ prophecy and his miracles occurred without the mediation of an angel or any other emissary, as is well known.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And He said. Hashem then told him that, notwithstanding all this, He would deliver Jericho into his hand, together with its king and armies, although they were mighty warriors. Joshua would not prevail through strength, but through a miracle.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(3) Why does Scripture repeat both “You shall march around” and “encircle”?
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 2_Verse, 1_Comment: And you shall march around. The Ark was not to circle the city with Joshua alone; rather, all the men of war were to march around it.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 2_Verse, 2_Comment: Encircle. There is a distinction between going around and encircling. “Going around” may refer even to an incomplete circuit, whereas encircling denotes only a complete circuit around all four sides, as I explained in my commentary on the Torah concerning the words “around the altar” (Leviticus 1:5). He adds that they must encircle the city on all four sides.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And seven. The advance guard marched before the priests, while the priests carrying the shofars followed the advance guard and preceded the Ark, as stated in verse 9.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 3_Verse, 1_Comment: And the priests shall sound the shofars. This means throughout all seven days. It was their practice to sound a tekiah on a day of rejoicing and a teruah on a day of battle against an adversary, as it says: “When you go to war,” etc., “you shall sound a teruah,” etc.; “and on the day of your rejoicing,” etc., “you shall sound a tekiah,” etc. (Numbers 10:9–10). He informed them that the priests would now sound a tekiah as a sign of rejoicing and victory.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: When they sound a prolonged blast—when you hear it. That is, immediately together with the great shofar blast, the people shall raise a teruah, so that the two sounds will intermingle and follow one another without interruption. This will clarify the verse below (verse 16).
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And Joshua summoned. I have already written that when this Divine communication came to him, he was with the Ark and the people before Jericho, for he intended to begin the battle. Until then, the Levites had carried the Ark; he now commanded the priests to carry it, because once wonders were to be performed through it, it was fitting that the priests should bear it, as stated above (3:5).
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(7) What is meant by “Pass on and march around”? Where were they to pass?
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: Pass on. The Ark ordinarily traveled at the head of the people, as explained above (3:2), whereas now the people were commanded to proceed before the Ark, as explained above (verse 4). He therefore said, “Pass on” before the Ark. Until this point, the advance guard—the Reubenites and Gadites—had marched before the children of Israel, as explained above (4:12). Now the order was reversed, with the most important element coming last: the Ark marched at the rear, the advance guard before it, and the entire people before them. Thus it says, “The advance guard shall pass before the Ark of Hashem,” occupying an intermediate position between the people and the Ark. It might have been possible for the people to remain where they were, while the advance guard moved backward to take its place behind them, and the Ark then moved behind the advance guard. But this would have been disrespectful to the Ark. Joshua therefore commanded the Ark and the advance guard before it to remain in place while the people first passed them and moved to the front. The advance guard then passed and stood between the people and the Ark, leaving the Ark at the rear. The purpose of this order was to demonstrate that victory would come through the Ark. The advance guard therefore needed to remain close to it, just as the Cherethites and Pelethites encamp around the commander of an army. This also fulfilled the original condition, as it says, “Every armed man among you shall cross over before Hashem for battle” (Numbers 32:21). This is explained more fully above (1:13): When Moses originally stipulated the condition with them, he required them to march as advance troops before Hashem, because he thought that the entire war would be conducted miraculously. In that event, they would not march before the children of Israel, but before the Ark, which would itself fight and conquer. Afterward, Moses saw that the war would follow a more natural course of military conquest, and they therefore needed to march before the children of Israel, who would themselves fight and conquer. But in the battle of Jericho, where the conquest was miraculous, the words “Every armed man among you shall cross over before Hashem” were fulfilled: They did not march before the children of Israel, but before the Ark.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(8) The statement, “And it came to pass when Joshua had spoken,” is unclear, for the sentence lacks a predicate telling us what then occurred. The commentators’ explanation is strained. Furthermore, why does Scripture repeat “passed on and sounded” and “going on and sounding”?
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 7_Verse, 1_Comment: And it came to pass when Joshua spoke, etc., that they passed on and sounded the shofars. Do not think that while the priests and the Ark stood and waited for all the people and the advance guard to pass before the Ark, as explained above (verse 7), the priests did not sound the shofars because they had been commanded to sound them only while circling the city. Scripture therefore explains that when Joshua spoke to the people—when he gave them the command stated in verse 7, “Pass on and march around the city”—the seven priests carrying the seven shofars were already standing before Hashem. At that time, they passed on and sounded the shofars: The people passed before the Ark, while the priests sounded the shofars throughout the entire time that the people were passing. Once the people had passed, the resulting order was that the Ark of the Covenant of Hashem proceeded behind them—that is, behind the people.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And the advance guard marched before the priests. It occupied an intermediate position between the people and the Ark, as explained above (verse 7). Do not think that all the priests were stationed beside the Ark; only the seven priests sounding the shofars were there, while the remaining priests marched together with the tribe of Levi among the people.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 8_Verse, 1_Comment: And the rear guard. This was the tribe of Dan, which marched behind the Ark, while all the other tribes marched before it, ahead of the advance guard.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 8_Verse, 2_Comment: Going on and sounding. Even while they marched, they did not cease sounding the shofars. In the preceding verse, Scripture spoke of their sounding them while standing in place, until the people had passed.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: You shall not raise a teruah. This means a shout of rejoicing. Nor shall you even make your voices heard by crying aloud, nor shall any word come from your mouths, even in a whisper.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 9_Verse, 1_Comment: Until the day. That is, until the seventh day.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And they came into the camp. They returned to Gilgal, where the camp was situated, as stated below (9:6; 10:6) and elsewhere.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(12–13) Why did Joshua rise early on this day but not on the first day? Why does Scripture relate again that the priests carried the Ark and that seven priests carried seven shofars? It should have said briefly that everything was done as on the first day. And why does it repeat “they went on and sounded” and “going on and sounding”?
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 11_Verse, 1_Comment: And Joshua rose early. On the first day, they did not need to rise early because they were already within the territory of Jericho, as explained above (5:13; 6:1).
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 11_Verse, 2_Comment: And the priests carried. On this occasion, the priests carried the Ark directly from Gilgal to Jericho. This had not occurred on the first day, when the Levites carried it as far as Jericho, since the Divine communication came to Joshua only when he was already at Jericho, as explained above (verse 6).
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: And the seven priests. In this respect as well, this day differed from the first. On the first day, the priests had not carried the Ark from Gilgal to Jericho, nor had they proceeded in this formation, with the advance guard marching before the priests. Now, however, this order began immediately when they departed from the camp. There was also a difference in that the priests went on, sounding the shofars: They began sounding them as soon as they set out from Gilgal and did not stop throughout their journey. Therefore, Scripture says again, going on and sounding the shofars.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(15) Why does this verse contain an obvious repetition?
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 14_Verse, 1_Comment: In this prescribed manner, etc. The fact that all the actions performed in this matter were assigned the number seven—seven priests, seven shofars, seven days, and seven circuits—was intended to emphasize the seventh number, which is sacred in days, months, years, Sabbatical cycles, and everything else, as is well known. Here, the circuits contained two sets of seven. 1] A sevenfold cycle of days: They encircled the city for seven days, once each day. This cycle was completed by the first circuit on the seventh day. Thus it says, “They encircled the city in this prescribed manner”—meaning one circuit—which, together with the circuits performed on the preceding weekdays, made seven. That same circuit was then also counted as the first of the following set of seven circuits performed exclusively on that day, because it was the seventh and sacred day. Therefore, Scripture adds, Only on that day did they encircle the city seven times.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(16–20) The words “The priests sounded the shofars, and Joshua said, ‘Raise a teruah’” imply that the priests sounded a great blast. Why, then, does Scripture say again afterward (verse 20), “The people raised a teruah, and they sounded the shofars,” and then state a third time, “And it came to pass when the people heard the sound of the shofar that they raised a teruah”?
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 15_Verse, 1_Comment: And it came to pass that the priests sounded the shofars. This does not mean that they had already sounded the prolonged blast, for then the people would have been obligated to raise a teruah immediately, as explained above (verse 5). Rather, the priests were still sounding the shofars as they had until then and had not yet sounded the prolonged blast upon the ram’s horn. Joshua wished to signal the priests to sound the prolonged blast, which would mark the conclusion of the shofar blasts and the victory, at which point the people were required to raise a teruah. First, however, he needed to instruct them how to treat the city and its spoil. Once the wall fell, each man would advance directly before him, and there would be no opportunity then to issue commands and warnings. He therefore began by telling them, Raise a teruah—meaning: The time has come for you to raise the teruah as a sign that Hashem has given you the city.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: And it shall be. Since the conquest would be accomplished miraculously by Hashem, it was fitting that the city’s spoils should be consecrated to Hashem, Who conquered it.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 16_Verse, 1_Comment: Only Rahab the prostitute. She was excluded from the people and the spoil because she had hidden the messengers. (Here Scripture does not say that this was because they had sworn to her, for the people had not taken that oath, and the spies’ oath could not bind the entire nation. Only to the spies themselves did Joshua say (verse 22), “As you swore to her,” because they were personally bound by their oath.) Rahab herself deserved to be saved on her own account, since she had converted before the spies and accepted faith in Hashem, as explained above. This occurred before they crossed the Jordan, when, according to all opinions, they were obligated to accept her, as explained above (2:12). Nevertheless, her property would ordinarily have had to be destroyed because it was included in the ban upon Jericho, and the same would have applied to her family. Scripture therefore says that because she hid the messengers, she and all who are with her shall live. This includes even her property—her ox, her donkey, and everything belonging to her. Therefore Joshua continued, But as for you, guard yourselves from the devoted property. Although the ban did not apply to Rahab’s possessions, it did apply to everything else, and you are not included in her exemption.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: But as for you, guard. Guard both yourselves and others; this is why Scripture does not use the reflexive form, “Take care.” He explains that you must guard yourselves lest you take any of the devoted property, and you must also restrain others, because the resulting harm would affect the entire community. Thus he says, And you would make the camp of Israel subject to the ban.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: And all the silver. Objects unfit for the treasury of Hashem were to be destroyed, whereas all the silver and gold, which were suitable for consecration, were to be brought into the treasury of Hashem.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: And the people raised a teruah, and the priests sounded the shofars. At Joshua’s command, the people raised a teruah, while the priests sounded the prolonged blast, the two following one another immediately, as explained above (verse 5). He explains how this occurred: The moment the people heard the prolonged sound of the shofar, they immediately raised their teruah, so that the two sounds blended together.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 19_Verse, 1_Comment: And the people went up, each man directly before him. For the wall fell all around the city. Nevertheless, Rahab’s house did not fall, because the part containing her house stood outside the wall, as explained above (2:15), and was not included in the section that collapsed.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: And they utterly destroyed. Scripture first relates what they did to every creature possessing the breath of life: They utterly destroyed both people and animals, except for Rahab.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(22–25) Joshua told the spies to spare Rahab because of their oath, whereas earlier (verse 17) he said it was because she had hidden the messengers. Then Scripture states for a third time (verse 25) that Joshua spared her because she had hidden the messengers. Why repeat what had already been said?
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 21_Verse, 1_Comment: Go into the house of the prostitute. The obligation rests upon you because you swore to her; you must also act in accordance with every detail and condition of the oath.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: The young men. They entered with the swiftness of young men and fulfilled their oath.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: And the city. Scripture now relates what they did with everything else: They burned the city and all its possessions, while placing the metals in the treasury of the house of Hashem.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: But Rahab. Since Joshua was not personally bound by the spies’ oath, Scripture relates that he nevertheless spared her. More than this, she dwelt in the midst of Israel: They provided her with a home and sustenance and accepted her into the religion of Israel because she had hidden the messengers.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: Whoever arises and rebuilds it. Rambam explains that the city was to remain as a memorial to the miracle, so that everyone who saw its ruined wall would remember the miracle. Thus our Sages said, “One who sees the wall of Jericho swallowed into the ground must recite a blessing” (Berakhot 54a).
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 25_Verse, 1_Comment: This city. Our Sages explained (Sanhedrin 113a): Neither may Jericho be rebuilt under the name of another city, nor may another city be built under the name of Jericho. The prohibition applied both because it was this city and because its name was Jericho.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 25_Verse, 2_Comment: At the cost of his firstborn. Because he seeks to rebuild ruins for himself as a memorial to his name—as it says, “Their inward thought is that their houses will endure forever,” etc., “they call their lands by their own names” (Psalms 49:12)—neither name nor remnant, offspring nor descendant, will remain to him.
text.1_, 5_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: And Hashem was with him. For the Heavenly Court concurred with Joshua’s curse, as was demonstrated in the case of Hiel the Bethelite (I Kings 16:34).
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: And they acted unfaithfully. Scripture informs us of two principles. 1] All Israel is bound together like a single body, so that each individual relates to the community as one limb relates to the entire organism. Just as disease or injury in one limb produces illness or defect in the whole body, so, because Achan took from the devoted property, it was regarded as though the entire people had acted unfaithfully. Thus it says, “The children of Israel acted unfaithfully,” followed by, “And Achan took.” 2] There is a distinction between punishment actively inflicted by Hashem and harm that comes through the withdrawal of His Providence. When Hashem actively administers punishment, He does not punish the innocent because of the sinner, as occurred afterward when Achan alone was stoned. This is not so, however, with harm arising incidentally because Hashem withdraws His Providence. Such harm affects the entire community: When sinners are among them, Hashem hides His face from them all, as it says below, “Did not Achan act unfaithfully concerning the devoted property, and wrath fell upon the entire congregation of Israel?” (22:20). They then all become exposed to chance and misfortune. Consequently, an innocent person who happens to be in a dangerous place may sometimes be struck, while the sinner, who is not present there, remains unharmed, as the same verse says, “And he was not the only man who perished because of his iniquity.” Thus, the anger of Hashem burned against the children of Israel means that He withdrew His Providence from them. Rabbi Isaac Abravanel likewise explains it this way.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(2–3) Why does Scripture elaborate by identifying the places near Ai? The words “He said to them, ‘Go up and spy’” appear superfluous, since we already know that spies are sent to spy. Joshua told them to spy out the land, but they spied out only Ai. The word “the men” is also superfluous. Why does he repeat, “Let not all the people go up,” and, “Do not weary all the people by sending them there”?
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: And he sent. Scripture relates how the hand of chance immediately gained power over them and caused their counsel to fail. Joshua sent spies from Jericho to Ai, which is beside Beth-aven. Scripture identifies the city’s surroundings to demonstrate that all Israel really should have gone there. Although Ai was a small city, it was close to Beth-aven and Bethel, and the inhabitants of Bethel and Beth-aven could easily come to its assistance. This is what actually happened during the second attack, as it says, “Not a man remained in Ai or Bethel who did not go out after the children of Israel” (8:17). Joshua had told them, Go up and spy out the land. He did not send them to spy out Ai alone, but the land—that is, the entire region, including Ai and the surrounding places. Had they carried out his command properly, they would have seen that several cities were situated nearby and would not have said, “Let not all the people go up.” But they altered his command: And the men went up—meaning on their own initiative—and spied out Ai alone, rather than the entire region. Therefore: (3) They returned and said, “Let not all the people go up.” They repeated their recommendation for two reasons: 1] As their report concerning the mission, they stated that the entire people did not need to go up. 2] As practical advice, they argued that since the entire people were unnecessary, it was improper to weary them for no purpose.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And they went up—and they fled. They did not even form ranks for battle; rather, they immediately began to flee. Although the people of Bethel did not assist Ai on this occasion, the Israelites fled before the men of Ai alone.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: About thirty-six. The prefix kaf, meaning “about,” is used here in its literal sense. Our Sages, however, interpreted it as referring to Jair son of Manasseh, who was equivalent in worth to the majority of the Sanhedrin (Bava Batra 121b). That is, they struck down thirty-six men, and among them was one man whose worth was equivalent to that of about thirty-six fallen men.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 4_Verse, 1_Comment: And they pursued them. Their hearts were emboldened to pursue them as far as Shebarim, and the hearts of the people of Israel melted.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(7–9) This prayer appears disorderly. What did Joshua mean by saying, “If only we had been content”? And what is the meaning of “Please, my Hashem, what can I say after,” which the commentators struggled to explain?
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: And he tore his garments. Because of those who had been killed.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 5_Verse, 2_Comment: And he fell upon his face. In order to pray.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 5_Verse, 3_Comment: And they put dust upon their heads. As if to say: Behold, we are regarded as dust.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 5_Verse, 4_Comment: Alas, Hashem God. After Joshua saw that God had not gone forth with their armies but had abandoned them to wage war according to nature and chance, he argued from two perspectives. First, regarding the past: A people will go to possess lands that do not belong to it under one of two circumstances. Either they know with certainty that they will triumph because they are powerful, and they therefore go forth to conquer—even though they already possess an inhabited land—in order to enlarge their kingdom and extend their borders; or they have no land in which to dwell, and therefore risk battle, whether to conquer or be conquered. Accordingly, Joshua asked, Why did You bring this people across, etc., only to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites? Since You intended to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites—that is, to abandon us to chance and allow the battle to follow its natural course, in which the Amorites might also prevail and destroy us—why did You bring us across to this place and expose us to the dangers of war? Did we not already possess an inhabited land? If only we had been content—that is, we would have been satisfied to remain beyond the Jordan, and nothing compelled us to risk our lives in battle, since we already possessed a place in which to dwell there.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Please, my Hashem. He now presents his second argument, concerning the future. Even if You thought that we could triumph through natural means because we are stronger than the nations of the land—and that our defeat at Ai occurred only because merely three thousand men went out, while the sword devours one as well as another, so what significance is there in the loss of thirty-six men, since such is the way of war?—that reasoning was valid only until now. Our terror had fallen upon the inhabitants of the land, and no man retained the courage to array himself against us in battle; we could therefore have defeated them easily even through natural warfare. But this is no longer so. What can I now say after Israel has turned its back? Their fear of us has now departed, and their hearts will be emboldened to unite against us. Therefore, from this point onward:
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: The Canaanites will hear, etc., and surround us—all of them united together as one.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 8_Verse, 1_Comment: And they will cut off our name. That is, they will destroy the reputation for might that we have acquired until now. But if our name is cut off, Your great name will be profaned, for through the renown we attained, Your name became known as our mighty stronghold.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Arise, go. Why do you offer arguments? Since a cause has brought about the withdrawal of Divine Providence, you must remove that cause. And what is it?
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Israel has sinned. He explains that the sin was twofold. 1] The nature of the sin itself: They also transgressed My covenant—this refers to desecrating the Sabbath, for they carried objects from the public domain into the private domain. The conquest of Jericho occurred on the Sabbath, and the Sabbath is called a covenant, as it says, “To observe the Sabbath throughout their generations as an everlasting covenant” (Exodus 31:16).
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 10_Verse, 1_Comment: And they also took from the devoted property. They transgressed both the Sabbath and the ban upon property devoted to Heaven. 2] The manner of the sin: They also stole—they did not take it openly, but through theft and concealment. In doing so, they also denied Divine Providence, treating the Eye above as though it did not see. 3] The purpose of the sin: “Men do not despise a thief if he steals to satisfy himself when he is hungry,” but Achan had no need to steal, for they also placed it among their possessions—he buried it in the ground, demonstrating that he had no immediate need for it.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(12–13) Why does He repeat, “They will be unable to stand,” etc., “because they have become subject to the ban,” and, “I will no longer be with you unless you destroy the devoted property”? And why did Joshua say only, “You will be unable to stand until you remove the devoted property,” without also saying that Hashem would not be among them until they destroyed it?
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 11_Verse, 1_Comment: And they will not. Therefore, the children of Israel will be unable to stand before their enemies. He explains that this will result from two causes. They will not stand through natural strength, for they will turn their backs, because they have become subject to the ban. The intrinsic effect of devoted property is to place a curse upon their strength and weaken them even on the natural level. Nor will they stand through Divine Providence, for I will no longer be with you unless you destroy the devoted property. He further establishes two different conditions. For them to stand before their enemies—that is, for their natural strength to return—it is sufficient that the devoted property no longer remain among them, meaning that they burn what was stolen from it. Thus the following verse says, “You will be unable to stand before your enemies until you remove the devoted property.” But for Hashem to be with them, they must destroy the devoted thing from their midst—meaning that they must destroy the man who violated the ban. It is not enough for the stolen property itself to cease to exist; the person who transgressed the ban must be removed from the face of the earth.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: You will be unable to stand until you remove the devoted property. He did not mention the second condition—that Hashem would not be among them until they destroyed the devoted thing, meaning the person who had violated the ban, as explained in the preceding verse. He did not want them to know that the offender would be liable to death, for then the sinner would be unwilling to confess. He therefore informed them only of the first condition described above.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: He shall be burned with fire. Because he violated the ban upon property that was itself destined to be burned, his punishment was likewise burning.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 14_Verse, 1_Comment: For he has transgressed. That is, he sinned against God by violating His covenant, and against Israel by committing a disgraceful act among Israel, through which they were punished. Scripture explains that because he violated the ban, he deserved burning. Nevertheless, he was stoned because he had desecrated the Sabbath and was therefore liable to stoning. This accords with the law that one liable to two forms of judicial execution receives the more severe one. For this reason, they also stoned his ox and donkey, so that their manner of death would not be less severe than that of their owner.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(17) Scripture should have said, “He brought forward the tribe of Judah by its families,” as it does in all the other cases. Why does it say, “He selected the family of the Zerahites,” in the active form, whereas in all the other cases it says, “was selected,” using the passive form?
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 16_Verse, 1_Comment: And he brought forward the family of Judah. Scripture does not say here, “He brought forward the tribe of Judah by its families,” as it does in the other cases. Likewise, in all the other cases it says, “was selected,” in the passive form, whereas here it says, “he selected,” in the active form. This is because all the preceding selections were made through the Ark. That is, Joshua brought forward Reuben, Simeon, and Levi, and Judah was selected by the Ark. He then did not bring forward the remaining tribes that followed Judah. Thus it says, “He brought Israel forward by its tribes”—meaning one tribe after another—for he did not finish bringing them all forward. The families were different: The family of the Zerahites came last, and Joshua brought forward all the other families of Judah, but the Ark did not select them. Since the family of the Zerahites alone remained at the end, there was no need to bring it before the Ark; the lot necessarily fell upon it, and Joshua himself selected it.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: Please give glory to Hashem. Do not deny the lot, which was directed by Hashem, for doing so would profane His blessed glory.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 18_Verse, 1_Comment: And confess to Him. Confess your other transgressions as well. He then explains, corresponding to “Give glory to Hashem”:
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 18_Verse, 2_Comment: Tell me what you have done. Corresponding to “And confess to Him,” he says, Do not conceal from me the other transgressions you have committed.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: Indeed, I have sinned. By taking from this devoted property.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 19_Verse, 1_Comment: And such and such have I done. He had likewise taken from other devoted property in the days of Moses. He then sought to justify himself on several grounds: 1] He had already become accustomed to this transgression, so that it came to seem permissible to him. Thus he said, And such and such have I done.
text.1_, 6_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: 2] And I saw among the spoil. He thought that since it was spoil, he was permitted to take it. Thus our Sages said (Tanchuma, Masei 5) that he relied upon the Torah’s words, “And you shall consume the spoil of your enemies” (Deuteronomy 20:14). 3] It was a Babylonian mantle belonging to the king of Babylon, who came from another country. He thought that Joshua had devoted only the property of Jericho to destruction, not the property of someone from another country. 4] It was beautiful, and his inclination enticed him to covet it. 5] There were two hundred shekels of silver and a bar of gold. He thought that metals were not included in the ban, since they were not destined to be burned but were to enter the treasury of Hashem, and that he had violated only the prohibition against misappropriating sacred property. 6] Behold, they are hidden in my tent. He had neither used nor benefited from them and therefore thought that he had not committed misappropriation, for in the case of gold, which is not diminished through use, one does not become liable for misappropriation until deriving benefit worth a perutah, as explained by Rambam (Laws of Misappropriation 6). Here he neither benefited from nor diminished them. Thus he says, “And the silver is beneath it”—covered beneath the mantle and left undiminished. From this statement we also see how Joshua justified punishing him without witnesses, for all the identifying signs were present: 1] The nature of the stolen property, which consisted of three kinds of objects. 2] Their weights—the specified weights of the gold and silver. 3] Their location—hidden in his tent. 4] Their arrangement—the silver beneath the mantle. The expression be’oholi, “in my tent,” combines a possessive suffix with the definite article. This indicates that Achan had a separate tent distinct from those of his household and that it contained two chambers, one larger and principal. The possessive suffix identifies it as his tent rather than that of his family, while the definite article identifies his well-known principal tent.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And you shall do. You shall burn the city and kill all its inhabitants.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: Only its spoil. Unlike the spoil of Jericho, which was placed in the treasury of Hashem.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 1_Verse, 2_Comment: And its livestock. At Jericho, the livestock was devoted to destruction; now, however, you may take it as spoil for yourselves. For here the conquest would not be entirely miraculous, as was the fall of Jericho’s wall, on account of which its spoil was consecrated. Rather, the city would be conquered through military strategy. Therefore, set an ambush for the city.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(3) Why did Joshua send this ambush two days before the second ambush?
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 2_Verse, 1_Comment: And Joshua arose. He acted as Hashem had commanded him: 1] He himself went at their head. 2] All the people of war went with him. And he selected. This was to fulfill the command, “Set an ambush for the city.”
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 2_Verse, 2_Comment: And he sent them out at night. This occurred two days before the conquest, as the reason will be explained in verse 9.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: See that you lie in ambush against the city. There are several kinds of ambushes, as can be seen from the account of Abimelech (Judges 9:43). 1] An ambush directed against the inhabitants of a city, intended to fall upon them suddenly when they emerge from the city gate. Such an ambush must be positioned in front of the city rather than behind it—that is, on the side where the gate is located—so that it is ready for those coming through the gate. 2] An ambush in the countryside, as it says, “The men of Shechem stationed ambushers against him upon the mountaintops, and they robbed everyone who passed them along the road” (ibid. 9:25). Such an ambush must be positioned far from the city, lest those who were robbed return and warn its inhabitants, who would then guard themselves against the ambushers. 3] An ambush directed against both groups together, as in Judges 9:43–44, where Abimelech divided his people into three companies. Two companies lay in ambush for those going out into the countryside, while one company stood at the entrance to the city gate to prevent them from returning to the city. In this kind of operation, some of the ambushers may be stationed behind the city if the field where the people gather lies on that side. Likewise, if the gathering place is distant from the city, they will lie in ambush there. But in this case, not all the forces are prepared to ambush: Only those in the field actually lie in ambush, while those near the city merely hold a strategic position to prevent the fugitives from escaping. In all three arrangements, the ambush is directed not against the city itself but against its inhabitants. Joshua therefore said, See that you lie in ambush against the city—against the city itself, not its inhabitants, unlike all three arrangements mentioned above. Therefore: 1] Lie in ambush behind the city, unlike the first type. 2] Do not go very far from the city, unlike the second type. 3] And all of you shall be ready, unlike the third type.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And I. I will confront those who come out to the battlefield.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 4_Verse, 1_Comment: As at the first. That is, since they came out on the first occasion, they would certainly come out now.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(6–8) What is the significance of the words, “For they will say, ‘They are fleeing’”? Why does he repeat, “And we will flee before them”? And what is the meaning of, “See, I have commanded you”?
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: For they will say. That is, they certainly will not realize that our flight is a stratagem. They will assume that because we fled from them on the first occasion, our hearts melted before them, and therefore we are fleeing from them a second time. Joshua arranged his words in parallel clauses: “Until we have drawn them away from the city” corresponds to “And we will flee before them,” while “For they will say, ‘They are fleeing before us’” corresponds to “And they will come out after us.”
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 5_Verse, 2_Comment: And we will flee. We will continue fleeing even after they have been drawn away from the city, until we draw them into the wilderness. This will give the ambush sufficient time to set the city on fire and block the southern route before them, as will be explained.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And you shall arise. While we are fleeing, you shall arise when you see the signal of the javelin.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: From the ambush. That is, from the place of ambush.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: See, I have commanded you. That is, do not say: Since Hashem permitted you to take its spoil, as He said, “Only its spoil and its livestock you may take as plunder for yourselves,” you should first secure the spoil before burning the city. Therefore, Joshua said, “See that you follow what I have commanded you,” thereby teaching them the proper meaning of Hashem’s command.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(9) How could they remain west of the city without encountering the men of Bethel, who came from the west to assist Ai? Moreover, Scripture says (verse 14) that they lay in ambush behind the city, which would mean to its south, since the front of the city faced north, as stated in verse 11.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 8_Verse, 1_Comment: And he sent them. Joshua sent this ambush two days before the battle because the fighting force would encamp north of Ai, whereas the ambush would be stationed at a distance from Ai on its southern side, as will be explained. To reach that location without anyone noticing their movements, they had to take a long circuitous route, traveling several parasangs from the city through fields and wilderness so that they would not be seen.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 8_Verse, 2_Comment: And he lodged there. So that he would be prepared for the following day.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 8_Verse, 3_Comment: Between Bethel and Ai. It is impossible to say that they were stationed directly west of the city, in the area between Bethel and Ai, for if so, how could the men of Bethel, who came to assist Ai, have failed to see them, as stated in verse 17? Moreover, this ambush was stationed behind the city, as stated in verses 4 and 14, which means on its southern side. Since the gate of Ai was on the north, where Israel’s camp was situated, as stated in verse 11, the rear of the city was necessarily to the south. The ambush must therefore have been positioned southwest of the city. Because its position extended southward, it was behind the city; and because it also extended westward, it was west of the city. The men of Bethel consequently did not encounter them when traveling directly toward Ai, for the ambush lay off to their side.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And he mustered. Joshua himself served on that occasion as the military commander who mustered and organized the people.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 9_Verse, 1_Comment: And he went up. This fulfilled the two conditions Hashem had given him: 1] He himself went at their head.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(11–12) What was the second ambush that Joshua stationed there? The plain meaning of the verse indicates that it too was west of the city, but the first ambush was already stationed there, and we do not know what task the second was meant to perform. The words “And they stationed the people,” etc., are also unexplained. Why is this ambush called “its rear guard,” and why does the possessive form “its rear” appear to refer to the camp? Why did Joshua go into the valley?
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 10_Verse, 1_Comment: 2] And all the people went up. And they came opposite the city. The city gate was on the northern side, and therefore they encamped north of Ai.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 10_Verse, 2_Comment: And the valley. A valley separated them from the city.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And he took about five thousand men. There was a great difference between this ambush and the first. The first ambush was stationed southwest of the city, at some distance from it—although not exceedingly far, as Joshua had said, “Do not go very far”—and was concealed from the city’s inhabitants, as explained above (verse 9). This ambush, however, was stationed beside the main camp, which stood north of the city, but extended westward. Thus, the camp on the north, together with the ambush extending from its side toward the west, formed the shape of a reversed letter dalet. For this reason, the following verse calls this ambush “its flanking force.” A flanking force surrounds the enemy, and the purpose of this unit was to encircle the enemy from two sides, in accordance with ordinary military strategy. This ambush was not concealed at all, for the city’s inhabitants could see it, since it stood beside the camp close to the city. Thus it says:
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: And they positioned the people. That is, they prepared the forces that would seize the city: the camp situated to the north and its flanking force—the five thousand men whom they stationed to encircle the enemy. These men stood beside the camp, west of the city, at its northwestern corner. The army was therefore arranged in two lines: one line north of the city, and another line of five thousand men extending from it along the western side, in this formation [a diagram appears in the original]. All this was plainly visible to the men of Ai. You will see below the great stratagem Joshua accomplished through this arrangement.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 12_Verse, 1_Comment: And Joshua went. Although they had encamped before the valley during the day, Joshua and his men began advancing during the night into the valley between the camp and Ai, so that the men of Ai would see them approaching the city. Thus it says:
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(14) Why did the king of Ai not see them until the following day? What is the meaning of “at the appointed time”? And why did he go toward the Arabah rather than toward the city gate or the valley?
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 13_Verse, 1_Comment: And it came to pass when he saw. When the king of Ai saw that they had approached and were advancing through the valley:
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 13_Verse, 2_Comment: They hurried, arose early, and went out to meet Israel. They did not wait for the Israelites to ascend from the valley and approach the city gate, as they had on the first occasion. Since they had defeated them on the descent the first time—that is, in this very valley—they thought they would defeat them there again.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 13_Verse, 3_Comment: At the appointed time. Joshua had established a specific time with the ambush he had sent two days earlier: On the third day, at a designated hour, they were to attack the city, so that they would be prepared at that time. The battle commenced at this appointed time.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 13_Verse, 4_Comment: Before the Arabah. This refers to the plains of Jericho, which lay to the east. Since the Israelite camp was arranged like the letter gimel along the northern and western sides, the men of Ai could not approach from those directions, lest they become surrounded on two sides. They were therefore compelled to turn toward the opposite corner, on the eastern side. Joshua understood that they would necessarily take their position there, where he would trap them through his strategy, as will be explained.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 13_Verse, 5_Comment: But he did not know that an ambush lay behind the city. Although he saw the ambush positioned before the city and guarded against it by turning eastward, he did not know about the first ambush of thirty thousand men stationed behind the city.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And they acted as though they had been struck. They made themselves appear as if they had suffered defeat. It may be a reflexive form, like “Do not defile yourselves through any of these” (Leviticus 18:24), according to Ibn Ezra, and it denotes a feigned action, like “one who pretends to be rich” or “one who pretends to be poor.”
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 14_Verse, 1_Comment: And they fled by way of the wilderness. This was the wilderness of Beth-aven mentioned below (18:12), which lay between Jericho and Bethel, opposite Ai on its northern side, for Ai was near Beth-aven, as stated above (7:2). Thus, the Israelite camp withdrew directly northward, once again forming the shape of a reversed letter dalet.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And they were summoned. Then even the people who had remained behind to guard the city pursued the Israelites, together with the men of Bethel, leaving the city open.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: With the javelin. As a signal to the ambush stationed southwest of the city, from which position they captured it.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(20–22) After Scripture says, “The people who had been fleeing turned against their pursuers,” why does it repeat, “And Joshua,” etc., “and all Israel,” etc., “turned back,” etc.? Furthermore, how were the men of Ai trapped in the midst of Israel? They were surrounded only from the north and south and could still have escaped eastward or westward.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 19_Verse, 1_Comment: And they turned, etc., and they had no direction in which to flee, etc. At first, when Joshua extended his hand with the javelin, the fleeing Israelites stopped and turned to face the enemy. The enemy became terrified upon seeing the city’s smoke behind them and the Israelite camp before them. They stood bewildered, not knowing what to do. After some time, when Joshua estimated that the ambush had had sufficient time to leave the city and block the enemy’s escape so that not a single fugitive could get away, they turned back and began striking the men of Ai.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: And these. Then the ambush came out to confront them, for they sought to flee back toward the city.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 21_Verse, 1_Comment: And they were in the midst of Israel. They were now surrounded on all four sides. Joshua’s camp enclosed them from the north and west in the shape of the letter gimel, while the ambush advanced against them from the south. The open eastern side faced Jericho, which was already under Israelite control. This demonstrates Joshua’s military wisdom, for a fundamental principle of military strategy is to surround the enemy on every side.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 29_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(30–32) Our Sages expressed three opinions concerning this commandment, and all are difficult to reconcile with the plain meaning of the verses. The Torah commands (in the portion of Ki Tavo) that on the day Israel crossed the Jordan, they were to erect stones, coat them with plaster, build an altar from them, and write the words of the Torah upon them. In the Book of Joshua, chapter 4 states that Joshua erected the stones at Gilgal, whereas here it says that he built the altar on Mount Ebal. According to the first opinion—the anonymous Mishnah in Sotah 32a—on the very day they crossed the Jordan, they traveled to Mount Ebal, built the altar, wrote the Torah upon the stones, removed the plaster, returned that same day, and lodged at Gilgal. Rabbi Isaac Abravanel raised numerous objections to this view: 1] If so, extraordinary miracles were required for them to travel sixty mil there and back in a single day while also writing all the words of the Torah and building the altar. Why does Scripture not mention these miracles? 2] Why is this account not recorded in its chronological place? The second opinion appears in the Jerusalem Talmud (Sotah 7:3). Rabbi Elazar maintains that two mounds stood near Gilgal, one of which they called Mount Gerizim and the other Mount Ebal.
