But this too is astonishing: Why did Scripture not record this event in its proper place, particularly when its present placement might lead us to think that Joshua acted contrary to the Torah, which commanded that the altar be built and the Torah written immediately on the day they crossed the Jordan? The third opinion appears in Sanhedrin 44a: Rav Shila said that Hashem told Joshua, “‘Arise, go’—you brought this upon yourself. I said, ‘And it shall be on the day that you cross the Jordan, you shall erect large stones for yourself,’ but you traveled sixty mil away.” After Rav Shila departed, Rav appointed an expositor and taught: “‘As Hashem commanded Moses, so Joshua did.’” According to Rav Shila, this event occurred several days after the crossing of the Jordan, which resolves all the other difficulties. One question remains, however: How could Joshua have transgressed Moses’ command? Moreover, how did Rav make the crooked straight merely by expounding, “As Hashem commanded Moses, so Joshua did,” when Joshua seemingly did not act accordingly? Rav should have explained that a miracle occurred, following the first opinion, or that there were two nearby mounds, following the second.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 29_Verse, 1_Comment: Then Joshua built. According to the plain meaning, Joshua performed this act after the battle of Ai, in accordance with the sequence of the verses. The Torah says: “And it shall be on the day that you cross the Jordan,” etc., “you shall erect for yourself large stones and coat them with plaster. You shall write upon them all the words of this Torah when you have crossed,” etc.; “And it shall be when you have crossed the Jordan, you shall erect these stones, concerning which I command you today, on Mount Ebal, and you shall coat them with plaster. There you shall build an altar to Hashem your God, an altar of stones,” etc.; “You shall offer burnt offerings upon it,” etc.; “And you shall write upon the stones all the words of this Torah” (Deuteronomy 27:2–8). We must understand why the command to erect the stones, coat them with plaster, and write the words of the Torah upon them is repeated twice. Why does Scripture first say, “On the day that you cross,” but afterward, “When you have crossed”? Why does it initially say merely, “You shall erect for yourself,” without specifying that the stones were to be erected on Mount Ebal, and only afterward say that they were to be erected there? And why does it say, “You shall write upon them all the words of this Torah when you have crossed,” when the words “when you have crossed” appear superfluous? From this it is clear that these are two commands applying at two different times. First it says, “And it shall be on the day that you cross the Jordan, you shall erect for yourself large stones.” This was the first command, which they were required to fulfill on the very day they crossed the Jordan, without delay. Joshua did exactly this, erecting large stones at Gilgal on that same day, as related above (4:8, 20). These served as a sign and memorial of the miracle performed for them at the Jordan. The Torah then told them, “You shall coat them,” etc., “and write,” etc., “when you have crossed.” That is, afterward, once you have crossed—not “on the day you cross,” but sometime after crossing—you shall perform another commandment with these stones: You shall coat them with plaster and write the words of the Torah upon them. Since this second command was mentioned initially only in passing, Scripture stated it briefly. It then explained in detail how this second commandment was to be performed. Thus it says: What I have told you—“You shall write,” etc., “when you have crossed”—you shall perform in the following manner: When you have crossed the Jordan—meaning several days afterward, for here it does not say “on the day you cross”—you shall erect these stones on Mount Ebal. You shall take them from the lodging place where you first erected them and set them up on Mount Ebal. There you shall fulfill the second commandment with all its details: coating the stones with plaster, building an altar from them, writing the words of the Torah upon them, and making the writing exceedingly clear. According to this explanation, Joshua omitted nothing from the commandments of his teacher. The initial words, “On the day that you cross,” refer only to erecting the stones. The subsequent commands, “You shall coat them” and “you shall write,” mean that the stones should be suitable for writing the Torah upon them “when you have crossed”—that is, at a later time. Our interpretation accords with the opinion of Rav Shila in Sanhedrin 44a, who maintains that this event occurred after the battle of Ai, and with the opinion of Rav (there), who expounded that Joshua did not deviate from Moses’ instructions. Rav intended precisely what we have written, contrary to the explanation of Tosafot (s.v. ve’atem) there.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 30_Verse, 0_Comment: As Moses commanded. That is, Joshua coated the stones with plaster, and the altar was made from the stones he had erected at the lodging place, just as Moses commanded. It means that Moses commanded this in the Book of Deuteronomy, which is attributed to him.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 30_Verse, 1_Comment: As written in the Book of the Torah of Moses. This refers to what follows—that they were whole stones—which is likewise stated in the Book of the Torah of Moses, meaning in the book of Ve’eleh Shemot, at the end of the portion of Yitro (Exodus 20:22).
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 32_Verse, 0_Comment: To bless the people. According to Ibn Ezra’s interpretation in his commentary on the Torah, the six tribes upon Mount Gerizim recited the blessings, while the six upon Mount Ebal recited the curses; the Levites standing below recited only the declarations beginning with “Cursed” that are written there. Thus it says, “These shall stand to bless,” etc., “and these shall stand for the curse,” etc., “and the Levites shall proclaim” (Deuteronomy 27:12–14). Scripture therefore says that Israel stood opposite the priests and Levites, for the Levites began with “Cursed.” There was no need to relate that here, since it was already known that they acted according to the Torah. The sense of the verse is: Israel was first to bless the people. Israel began by reciting the blessing first, unlike the Levites, who began with the curse. The word “Israel” refers to those pronouncing the blessing, and the sense is: Those who first blessed the people were Israel. According to the commentators’ interpretation, the definite article in “the people” is out of place here, and the expression “the people Israel” would likewise be unusual. The words “and half of it,” with the possessive suffix, refer to the particular half already designated in the Torah to recite the curses. Without the suffix, “half” would denote merely any unspecified half.
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 33_Verse, 0_Comment: And afterward he read. Joshua himself read the blessings and curses contained in the passage there (Deuteronomy 28): “And it shall be, if you diligently obey,” etc., and “And it shall be, if you do not obey.”
text.1_, 7_Chapter, 34_Verse, 0_Comment: There was not a word. This includes all the positive and negative commandments.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: But the inhabitants of Gibeon. They too heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and Ai: He had not offered them peace and had spared no living soul. They therefore assumed that Israel would not accept them either. According to Rambam (Laws of Kings 6:4), Israel was commanded to offer peace even in an obligatory war against the seven Canaanite nations. Acceptance of that peace depended upon their agreeing to three things: tribute, servitude, and the seven Noahide commandments. Once they accepted these conditions, Israel was obligated to make peace with them, as it says, “And it shall be, if it answers you peacefully, then all the people found within it shall pay tribute to you and serve you” (Deuteronomy 20:11). Nevertheless, Israel was forbidden to make a covenant of friendship with them, as it says, “You shall not make a covenant with them” (ibid. 7:2). The people therefore complained against the leaders for accepting the inhabitants of Gibeon, because the leaders had made a covenant with them. Joshua did not offer peace to Jericho and Ai because, before crossing the Jordan, he had sent three proclamations, including: “Whoever wishes to make peace may do so”—meaning by accepting tribute, servitude, and the seven commandments. He had thereby issued a general offer of peace to all the inhabitants of the country. Rambam’s proof is the verse, “There was no city that made peace with the children of Israel except the Hivites,” followed by, “For it was from Hashem to harden their hearts so that they would meet Israel in battle” (Joshua 11:19–20). This shows that had they wished to make peace, Israel would have been obligated to accept them. (Although Rashi in his Torah commentary and Raavad in his glosses disagree with Rambam, the verses here are explained well according to Rambam’s opinion. Radak likewise agrees with Rambam.) Accordingly, Scripture needed to explain why the inhabitants of Gibeon resorted to deception: They had heard what Joshua did to Jericho and Ai and mistakenly concluded that Israel would not accept them in peace.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: They too acted. Just as all the other kings took action to save themselves, the Gibeonites acted through deception.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 3_Verse, 1_Comment: And they presented themselves as envoys. There is a distinction between an envoy and an ordinary messenger. An envoy is sent on a mission with the purpose of bringing an answer back to the one who sent him, as I explained in my commentary on Isaiah, chapter 18. They presented themselves as representatives of their country who were required to return with an answer to those who had sent them.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 3_Verse, 2_Comment: And they took worn-out sacks. So that it would appear that they had come from a distant land.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And they said to him and to every man of Israel, etc. A covenant between one people and another may take three forms. 1] Neighboring peoples may make a covenant that neither will cross the other’s border to harm it through offenses arising between neighbors. Such a covenant is made between the peoples themselves, so that no person harms another and no neighbor harms his neighbor. 2] Peoples that are not neighbors may make a covenant to assist one another against an oppressive enemy with armies, troops, chariots, and horses, or to permit each other to trade freely within the other’s territory, like the covenant between Hiram and Solomon. Such a covenant is made not by the peoples themselves but by their kings, since it concerns matters affecting the community as a whole. Nor can such a covenant exist between two countries separated from one end of the earth to the other, for they could neither assist each other in time of distress nor trade within each other’s lands. 3] A covenant may concern religion and faith, whereby one people accepts the religion and beliefs of another and makes a covenant with them to enter the tradition of their religious faith. Such a covenant is likewise made with the people themselves rather than merely between kings. It can also be made between exceedingly distant countries, since it concerns spiritual matters, which are not separated by the length of the journey or by distant islands. These envoys initially approached the people as a whole, as it says, “They said to him and to every man of Israel,” and declared, We have come from a distant land; now make a covenant with us—which would be the first kind of covenant. The Israelites therefore did not believe them, for a covenant made directly between peoples is inconceivable when they live in distant lands and have no possibility of harming one another as neighbors; a covenant between distant peoples would ordinarily be made only between their kings. Therefore:
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And the men of Israel said. The people’s response was well reasoned: “Perhaps you dwell among us.” I have explained that the word ulai, “perhaps,” is used when the proposition is likely to be true and inclines more toward affirmation than denial. That is, reason suggests that you do dwell among us; otherwise, why would you seek to make a covenant with the entire nation? If so, how can I make a covenant with you? We have been expressly forbidden, “You shall not make a covenant with them.”
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: And they said to Joshua. When they realized that they had become ensnared by their own words, they turned to Joshua alone and said, We are your servants. That is, we have come to you alone to make a covenant between you and the king of our land—the second kind of covenant. Such a covenant between kings is possible even between distant countries, since they can assist one another in times of distress.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 7_Verse, 1_Comment: And Joshua said to them. Even according to this claim, their country could not have been exceedingly distant from the borders of his land, for otherwise they could not come to one another’s assistance. He therefore asked them, Who are you, and from where do you come? Sometimes a people is known because it is famous, and concerning this he asked, “Who are you?” At other times, the people itself is not famous, but the name of its country is known, and concerning this he asked, “From where do you come?” His meaning was: Since you are emissaries of your king, I must necessarily know the name of either your people or your country before making a covenant with him, so that I know that I have made a covenant with the king of a particular people or country. They were now caught a second time, for they could not invent a fictitious name; if they did, the covenant would not apply to the king of Gibeon.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And they said to him. They therefore devised a new stratagem, claiming that they had come to establish the third kind of covenant. They said: We cannot tell you the name of our people or country, because your servants have come from a very distant land—so exceedingly remote that you would not know who they are. If you ask why people from such a distant land would need a covenant with you, know that the covenant we seek, and the reason for our coming, is for the sake of the name of Hashem your God. We wish to establish a covenant of religion and faith by accepting His Divinity and His Torah, for we have heard that He created the world, continually sustains it, and governs it; we have also heard what He did in Egypt, overriding nature according to His will, and what He did in the wars against Sihon and Og. They did not mention the splitting of the Jordan, since they claimed to have come from a distant land.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And our elders and all the inhabitants of our land said to us. We have been sent for this purpose both by the people as a whole and by the elders who govern them. They told us, Go to meet them and say to them—meaning to the entire people, since this is a religious covenant—We are your servants in this respect, for you will receive us into your religion, faith, and Torah; and on this basis, make a covenant with us.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: This. After they succeeded in removing suspicion and dispelling Israel’s doubts about them, they added affirmative evidence that they had come from a distant land. They said: This bread of ours bears witness to the matter. Do not think that it was already dry when we departed, for we took it hot as provisions, and this was on the day we departed to come to you. Our wineskins and garments likewise bear witness.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And the men took. They accepted the evidence of their dried provisions as proof that their account was true, and on the basis of this evidence they believed them. Although they could have determined the truth through the Urim and Thummim, they did not inquire of Hashem.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And Joshua made. Although Israel would have been obligated to accept them even had they known that they belonged to the seven Canaanite nations, since they had accepted the seven Noahide commandments, they nevertheless did not act according to the law in two respects: 1] The Gibeonites should also have accepted tribute and servitude, as explained above (verse 3), but they did not do so explicitly, and Joshua made peace with them unconditionally. 2] Israel made a covenant with them, which is forbidden by a negative commandment. Nevertheless, Joshua took care to make a covenant with them only to let them live—that is, not to kill them. It was concerning this covenant that the leaders of the congregation swore to them. They accepted no other obligations, such as promising not to subject them to servitude; they swore only to preserve their lives.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(16) Why the repetition: “They were near him” and “they dwelt in his midst”?
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 15_Verse, 1_Comment: And it came to pass, etc., after they had made the covenant. At that point, it was no longer possible to withdraw from it.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 15_Verse, 2_Comment: And they dwelt in his midst. They were unlike the Girgashites, who had initially lived nearby but withdrew and departed for Africa. That is, because the Gibeonites were nearby, Israel was forbidden to make a covenant with them; and because they dwelt in Israel’s midst, they were required to accept tribute and servitude.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(18–22) Since the congregation’s complaint concerned the oath taken by the leaders, what answer did the leaders provide by saying, “We have sworn to them,” etc.? That was precisely the subject of the complaint. The statement, “This we shall do to them, and let them live,” is an obvious repetition. Why does Scripture twice say, “The leaders said,” and then repeat for a third time, “Let them live”? The phrase “as the leaders had spoken concerning them” also appears unnecessary. Finally, how could they alter their oath by appointing the Gibeonites as woodcutters?
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 17_Verse, 1_Comment: But they did not strike them. That is, Israel came to their cities and wished to kill them. Since the Gibeonites had not explicitly accepted tribute and servitude, Israel remained bound by the prohibition, “You shall not allow any soul to live.” The leaders’ oath did not bind all Israel, especially since it had been taken in error and would have nullified a commandment of the Torah. Nevertheless, they did not strike them, because the leaders of the congregation had sworn to them by Hashem, the God of Israel. The leaders would not permit the people to kill them, because this would cause a desecration of God’s name. Therefore, the entire congregation complained against the leaders.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: And all the leaders said. They said: It is impossible for you to kill them, because we have sworn to them, and the oath was taken in the name of Hashem; violating it would therefore desecrate His name. Moreover, the people were obligated to honor the commitments undertaken by the leaders of the congregation.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: This we shall do to them. Nevertheless, since the oath obligated them only to preserve the Gibeonites’ lives and did not prohibit imposing tribute and servitude upon them, we can fulfill the oath while still acting according to the Torah’s command. We will keep the oath and let them live, for this alone is what we swore to do; and thus there will be no wrath upon us because of the oath that we swore to them—Hashem will not be angry with us for violating it. Their meaning is explained in the following verse:
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: And the leaders said concerning them. They now explained how they would fulfill both their oath and the Torah’s commandment:
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 20_Verse, 1_Comment: Let them live. In this way, we will fulfill the oath.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 20_Verse, 2_Comment: And they became woodcutters. In this way, we will fulfill the Torah’s commandment. Their oath to preserve the Gibeonites’ lives meant only that they would not kill them, not that they would refrain from imposing tribute and servitude upon them. Nor should you think that this would nevertheless make us violators of a covenant: Since we made a covenant of friendship with them, how could we subjugate them as servants? Concerning this, Scripture says, As the leaders had spoken to them. The leaders had initially said to them, “Perhaps you dwell in our midst; how, then, can I make a covenant with you?” Although the verse there says, “The men of Israel said,” it was certainly their leaders who spoke. They had thus already explained that Israel could not make a covenant with Canaanites dwelling in their midst. The Gibeonites lied, and consequently their covenant was founded upon falsehood; only the oath to preserve their lives remained binding. Scripture says, “They became woodcutters,” in the past tense, meaning that they voluntarily became woodcutters. This was implicit in what the leaders had originally told them: “Perhaps you dwell in our midst,” which made clear that if this were so, they would be obligated to accept tribute and servitude.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: And Joshua summoned them. He wished to inform them that they had violated the covenant at its very inception by deceiving Israel, since Israel had made known to them that they would not make a covenant with those who lived nearby. Thus he said, Why did you deceive us?
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: And now you are cursed. One who is cursed cannot enter into a covenant with one who is blessed. The oath obligated us only to preserve your lives, but I now impose the condition that you accept tribute and servitude.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 22_Verse, 1_Comment: And you shall never cease to be servants. This constitutes the servitude.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 22_Verse, 2_Comment: And woodcutters, etc., for the house of my God. This constitutes the tribute. The leaders had said that they would be woodcutters for the entire congregation, thereby combining servitude and tribute. Joshua, however, imposed servitude upon them separately; he therefore did not require them to serve as woodcutters for the entire congregation, but only for the house of God. This service would constitute their tribute.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: And they answered Joshua. They had not devised this deception in order to exempt themselves from tribute and servitude, but only to save their lives, as they said, We were afraid, etc., and therefore we did this thing. They had believed that the command was to destroy all the inhabitants of the land and not to accept them under any circumstances.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: And now, etc. Behold, we are prepared to do whatever is right in your eyes.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment:
The Questions
(26) Why does Scripture say that Joshua saved them from the hand of the children of Israel? It already stated (verse 18) that Israel did not strike them because of the leaders’ oath. Furthermore, the statement in verse 27 that Joshua made them woodcutters for both the congregation and the altar appears to contradict verse 23, where he assigned them as woodcutters only for the altar.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 25_Verse, 1_Comment: And he delivered them from the hand, etc. Had the Gibeonites not accepted tribute and servitude, the people would have killed them, for they believed that the leaders’ oath did not bind them in this matter, as explained above (verses 17–18).
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: And he appointed them. Since the house of Hashem was not yet established in its proper place, Joshua appointed them on that day to serve, until the Temple was established, as woodcutters for the congregation while the people were engaged in war during the seven years of conquest and the seven years of dividing the land. Afterward, they would serve as woodcutters for the altar of Hashem. This arrangement continued until the very day on which the book was written.
text.1_, 8_Chapter, 26_Verse, 1_Comment: At the place that He would choose. When He would choose a place for His dwelling.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: And it came to pass when he heard. Above, at the beginning of chapter 9, Scripture relates that all the kings assembled to wage war against Israel. Hashem frustrated their plans and cast confusion among them, so that they did not all come together at once. The inhabitants of Gibeon—whose king had also participated in the council of those kings, for the Hivites are mentioned there—decided to make peace with Israel. This aroused the anger of the five kings named here, and they went up to wage war against Gibeon. They then fell into Joshua’s hands while separated from the larger alliance described at the beginning of the preceding chapter.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 0_Verse, 1_Comment: For he had captured. 1] He heard that Joshua had captured Ai through cunning and military stratagems. This emboldened him to gather his allies and wage war, since Israel’s strength appeared to depend only upon cunning and strategy. 2] He heard that as Joshua had done to Jericho, so he had done to Ai. Had Joshua devoted only Jericho to destruction, this could have been understood as the customary practice of conquerors, who destroy the first city in order to instill fear. But since he also destroyed Ai, it was evident that he intended to destroy them all. This stirred them not to remain silent. 3] And that the inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace. This brought discouragement into everyone’s heart, for they would say: If Gibeon is afraid to fight, how can we withstand Israel? 4] And they were in their midst. Once Israel had accepted the Gibeonites, many others might likewise make peace with them and submit to tribute so that Israel would spare their lives. Moreover, because the Gibeonites now dwelt among Israel, Israel had acquired inhabited cities that could provide provisions, food, shelter, and refuge.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And they were greatly afraid. For everyone would take Gibeon’s conduct as an example.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: For Gibeon was a great city. That is: 1] It was great in quality, possessing importance and authority like one of the royal cities. 2] It was great in size, being larger than Ai. 3] It was great in military strength, for all its men were mighty warriors.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And let us strike it. Since all the kings had assembled and agreed to wage war, the Gibeonites had violated the law of the country and harmed the entire confederation by giving assistance to its enemies.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Save us and help us. The distinction between salvation and assistance is clear: One who saves accomplishes everything himself, whereas one who assists contributes only part of the effort, leaving the person receiving assistance as the principal actor. Therefore, they said, “Save us—or at least help us to some extent, and we ourselves will fight.” (For they have gathered together. In verse 5, however, Scripture says, “They assembled,” because assembling follows gathering, as I explained in my commentary on Isaiah, chapter 11. The kings had already gathered together above, in chapter 9; here they needed only to assemble for action against Israel. The Gibeonites, however, spoke from the perspective of those being attacked. Since this was the beginning of the kings’ concerted action against them, they said, “For they have gathered together.”)
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: For I have delivered them into your hand. This had already been done, for their very coming was brought about by Me in order to deliver them into your hand. (Not a man shall stand. There is a distinction between “No man shall take his stand before you,” which always refers to his initially positioning himself for battle, and “not a man shall stand,” which means that even though they took their stand—for here they did position themselves for battle—they did not remain standing, but collapsed and fell.)
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: He went up from Gilgal all night. Consequently, he came upon them suddenly.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And Hashem cast, etc., as far as Azekah. That hailstones should fall upon a particular place and kill people and animals is a natural occurrence. Here, however, it was miraculous: they fled as far as Azekah with Israel pursuing them, yet the hailstones did not strike the pursuing Israelites, who continually reached the places where the enemy had stood. Rather, the stones pursued the enemy from above and departed from each place as soon as Israel arrived there.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(12–14) Why does Scripture say, “On the day that Hashem delivered,” etc.? This appears superfluous, since it already says “Then Joshua spoke,” meaning at that very time. Why does it repeat itself, saying both “the sun was still” and “the sun stood”? And why does it insert between them, “until the nation had avenged itself upon its enemies”? It should have said, “The sun and the moon stood in the midst of heaven until the nation had avenged itself upon its enemies.” What is the book called the Book of Jashar? Why did the sun stand still for precisely twenty-four hours? What does Scripture mean by saying, “There was no day like that day,” etc.? The Sages said (Avodah Zarah 25a) that the sun also stood still for Moses, and Hashem had already heard the prayers of the prophets and performed signs and wonders through them in every generation. And why does it conclude, “For Hashem fought for Israel,” implying that this was what distinguished that day from all preceding and subsequent days? Hashem had fought for Israel both before and afterward whenever they were worthy. Moreover, it is astonishing: What need was there for this miracle, and what purpose did it serve? They had already conquered and defeated the Amorites, so why did Joshua request this miracle without necessity?
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 11_Verse, 1_Comment: Then Joshua spoke. In the portion of Ki Tissa (Exodus 34:9), Moses prayed: “If I have found favor in Your sight, O Hashem, let Hashem, I pray, go in our midst,” etc. That is, he asked that Hashem’s Providence over them be revealed and remain directly attached to them, without an intermediary, so that their warfare would not be conducted naturally through an angel, but miraculously. Hashem answered him (ibid., 10): “Behold, I make a covenant: before all your people I will perform wonders such as have not been created in all the earth or among any of the nations; and all the people among whom you dwell shall see the work of Hashem, for it is awesome.” He informed Moses that He would grant his request and distinguish Israel in three respects: First, the wonders He would perform for them would be manifest and known to the entire people, as it says, “Before all your people I will perform wonders.” Second, they would be wonders without precedent, as it says, “Wonders such as have not been created.” Third, they would not merely occur before all Israel—that is, in the presence of the entire nation—but would afterward become renowned throughout the earth and among all the nations, so that everyone would know the work of Hashem. It then says (ibid., 11–12): “Observe that which I command you this day. Behold, I drive out before you the Amorite,” etc.; “Take heed lest you make a covenant,” etc. From this we learn that these wonders would be performed during the conquest of the seven nations, the first of which mentioned is the Amorite. It further says (ibid., 27): “Hashem said to Moses: Write these words for yourself, for in accordance with these words I have made a covenant with you and with Israel.” This means that Hashem commanded him to record this passage because the covenant with him was made in accordance with these words. That is, the promise, “Behold, I make a covenant: before all your people I will perform wonders,” was conditional upon these words; if Israel did not fulfill them, He would not perform the promised wonders. Moses recorded this in a book, which Scripture here calls the Book of Jashar, because through it He guided them to walk in the light of Hashem. With this, consider and understand these verses: When Joshua saw that Hashem was fighting for Israel against the Amorites, he desired that Hashem fulfill the covenant He had made with Moses and which was recorded in the Book of Jashar—to perform for them a manifest and renowned miracle. Therefore, Scripture says, “Then Joshua spoke to Hashem”: he spoke of and invoked the covenant that Hashem had made.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 11_Verse, 2_Comment: On the day that Hashem delivered the Amorite before the children of Israel. The Amorite was the first of the nations enumerated there in the Book of Jashar. Corresponding to the first condition—“Before all your people I will perform wonders”—Scripture says, “And he said in the sight of Israel”: Joshua proclaimed this aloud so that all Israel would hear. Corresponding to the other two conditions, he said, “Sun, stand still at Gibeon.” This would fulfill “wonders such as have not been created,” for no such miracle had yet been performed among the heavenly bodies; and it would also fulfill “throughout the earth and among all the nations,” because this miracle would become known from the rising of the sun to its setting. Now, Joshua asked only that the sun and moon themselves be halted, not that the entire daily celestial sphere cease revolving. The latter would not have been so great a wonder. It was a greater wonder for the sphere that moves everything not to depart from its regular course, with all the stars continuing to revolve in their orbits, while only the two great luminaries became still and ceased moving. The first would be comparable to stopping a millwheel by damming the flowing water that turns its wheels, which is a relatively minor feat. The second, however, resembles a mighty man grasping the millwheels with his hands while the water continues driving them, exerting his strength against the force moving them and arresting their motion—a display of tremendous power and strength. This is what Joshua accomplished: he arrested the movement of the sun and moon even while the daily sphere continued moving and drawing the mighty celestial bodies along through its power and strength. The sun then stood opposite Gibeon and the moon opposite the Valley of Aijalon, and he commanded them to cease their movement. In their figurative language, the Sages said (Tanchuma, Acharei Mot 9; see Shocher Tov on Psalms 19) that “stand still” means: Cease singing. They also interpreted “Then Joshua spoke to Hashem” to mean that Joshua sang in place of the two luminaries. For the creatures’ operation according to their nature constitutes their song: through their natural activity they proclaim the glory of God, Who implanted that nature within them and established it as an unchanging law. The cessation of their natural activity is therefore their silence from this song. Yet because this cessation was not accidental but deliberate, brought about through Joshua and Israel—His servants who perform His will—to demonstrate that through them God overturns the celestial order by His Providence, it constituted a song even more wondrous than the song of nature. This was the song that Joshua sang.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: [And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped.] This is a parenthetical statement. Therefore, the word amad (“stopped”) is vocalized with a kamatz, indicating a pause and teaching that this is a parenthetical statement, as is known from the rules of language. The verse should be understood as follows: “Joshua said: ‘Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon, until the nation has avenged itself upon its enemies.’ Is this not written in the Book of Jashar?” All of this was spoken by Joshua. The words “And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped” are those of the author of the book, reporting that Joshua’s words were fulfilled. Moreover, the miracle did not wait until Joshua had finished speaking: when he said, “Sun, stand still at Gibeon,” the sun became still at that very moment; and when he said, “And moon, in the Valley of Aijalon,” the moon became still at that very moment. This, then, is the meaning of his words: Joshua said, “Sun, stand still at Gibeon” until the nation has avenged itself upon its enemies—that the sun and moon should remain still until the vengeance was complete. He then gave the reason for his request: “Is this not written in the Book of Jashar?” That is, is it not written in the Book of Jashar, where Hashem made the covenant, “Before all your people I will perform wonders,” promising to perform such a manifest miracle during the war against the Amorite? Therefore, I ask: “Sun, stand still at Gibeon.”
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 12_Verse, 1_Comment: And the sun stood. Scripture initially said, “And the sun became still,” for stillness means the cessation of motion. This related that the very moment these words left Joshua’s mouth, even before he had finished speaking, the sun ceased moving. It now proceeds to state where the sun stood and how long it remained there: “And the sun stood”—that is, it remained standing in the midst of heaven, at the zenith of that horizon, and this continued for approximately a whole day, twenty-four hours. Although the completion of the vengeance did not require so much time, the sun nevertheless “did not hasten to set” of its own accord. For since only the sun and moon ceased moving while all the host of heaven continued revolving in their usual courses, had the sun remained still for less than twenty-four hours, great confusion and disorder would have arisen in the celestial system. Each star has its own particular position relative to the sun, at a distinct point, and never alters this position or its distance from the sun. If, for example, the sun had hastened to set after twelve hours, it would have approached the stars that had stood as far from it as east is from west and withdrawn by that same measure from the stars that had been near it. This alteration would then have remained forever, producing a permanent change in the order of creation, which is impossible. The sun therefore necessarily remained standing until the stars returned to the point at which they had stood the previous day when the sun became still; it then resumed its motion according to the fixed order of their courses. It also necessarily follows that the sun and moon ceased only their daily movement from east to west, while their annual movement from west to east did not cease. Had that movement also stopped, the sun would necessarily have had to remain standing for an entire year, until the celestial system—which continued moving that day and thus altered its order and position relative to the sun and moon—returned to its original position. Since the sun, despite ceasing its east-to-west motion, nevertheless moved one degree westward through its annual course, it had to remain standing slightly longer than twenty-four hours, until the stars reached the position to which it had shifted westward, as is known to those versed in astronomy. Scripture therefore says, “approximately a whole day,” employing the comparative prefix kaf.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And there was not. That is, this miracle contained something unprecedented, the like of which had never occurred. First, with respect to the one who brought about the miracle: all miracles were performed either by the will of Hashem, or, if they were performed through a prophet, the prophet had to offer prayer and supplication. Never did a prophet perform a miracle by issuing a decree, as Joshua did when he decreed that the sun and moon should become still, and they did so. Thus, Scripture says that there was no day like that day, etc., when Hashem listened to the voice of a man. There was no prayer or supplication here, only a voice: Joshua issued a command with his voice to the sun, and Hashem listened. Second, it was unprecedented in the purpose for which the miracle was performed. Whenever a miracle occurred by the will of Hashem, its purpose was sometimes to magnify His great name and sometimes to exalt Israel. But whenever a miracle came about through a prophet’s prayer, it was either for the honor of Hashem or to save Israel from an oppressor. Never had a prophet requested a sign or wonder whose sole purpose was to make known that Hashem fought for Israel, for whenever deliverance was readily attainable by natural means, he did not request a miracle. Here, Israel had already been saved through natural means, or through a miracle close to nature, and Joshua’s decree that the sun stand still was intended solely to make known that Hashem fought for Israel. No such miracle brought about through a prophet had occurred before or afterward. The meaning of the verse is therefore that there was no day like that day, when Hashem listened to a man’s voice—to the command that a man issued aloud, seeking to announce and publicize that Hashem fought for Israel—and Hashem heeded his voice and decree for that purpose. Such a thing had never occurred.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(15–21) Here it says that he returned to Gilgal, whereas verse 21 indicates that the camp remained at Makkedah and that from there they fought their surrounding enemies, without immediately returning to Gilgal.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 14_Verse, 1_Comment: And he returned. At that time they did not find the kings among the slain, and assumed that they had escaped to their cities, where they would gather an army once again. Israel would therefore have to march against those cities, so Joshua intended to return to Gilgal and renew the war after the troops had rested for a while. I have already explained in Ayelet HaShachar (Principle 10) that certain verbs indicate that the subject intended to perform an action even though he did not actually perform it.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And they fled. But through Hashem’s Providence, the kings who fled did not return to their cities; instead, they hid in a cave at Makkedah, near Joshua’s camp, and the matter became known to Joshua.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: Have been found. For until then they had searched for them but had not found them, as explained above (verse 15).
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said. From this Joshua perceived that it was through the Providence of the blessed God that they should finish the war now that the enemy’s kings had fallen, before the people could appoint other kings, as the inhabitants of Hebron later did (below, verse 37). He therefore abandoned his earlier intention (above, verse 15) to return to Gilgal, and commanded that stones be rolled over the cave’s entrance and that the troops not remain there, but continue the pursuit.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 17_Verse, 1_Comment: And strike their rear guard. That is, cut down even the tail end of the army—the surviving fugitives—for it has already become evident that Hashem has delivered them into your hand.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: And it came to pass. After they had struck them all down—and only a few survivors escaped into the fortified cities—all the people returned safely to the camp at Makkedah.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 19_Verse, 1_Comment: None sharpened—against even one man of the children of Israel, no one sharpened his tongue. (24–25) Place your feet. This served as a sign that all their enemies would likewise fall beneath their feet, thereby strengthening and encouraging them, as it says, “Be strong and courageous.” The letter heh in ha-halekho functions in place of asher (“who”), as in “whom Samuel had dedicated” (I Chronicles 26:28), while the final aleph is additional, as in (Isaiah 28:12), “but they would not listen.”
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(28) Why did they not attack Makkedah immediately, before they found the kings?
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 27_Verse, 1_Comment: And Makkedah. At first, when Joshua thought that the kings were still at large, he was afraid to attack Makkedah lest he be forced to fight on two fronts, for the cave in which the kings had hidden was outside Makkedah. Now, however, he captured Makkedah.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(29–36) Why does Scripture say, “He fought against Libnah,” whereas concerning Lachish it says, “He fought against it,” and afterward, “They fought against it”?
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 28_Verse, 1_Comment: And he fought against Libnah. With the verb “to fight,” there is a distinction according to whether it is followed by “with,” “against,” or “in.” When “fight” is followed by “with,” it indicates that both sides engage one another in battle. This occurred at Libnah, for Joshua was then pursuing the five kings and had not intended to attack Libnah. Rather, as Joshua passed by there—as Scripture says, “Joshua passed on to Libnah”—the inhabitants of Libnah came out against him and initiated battle, so the two sides fought one another. Concerning Lachish, Scripture says, “He fought in it,” meaning that he penetrated the city and fought within it. In all the other cases, it says, “He fought against it,” because they were fortified cities, and he fought against each one in order to capture its stronghold.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 36_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(37–39) Does it not say below (chapter 14) that Caleb captured Hebron, and in Judges that Othniel captured Debir, which is Kiriath-sepher?
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 36_Verse, 1_Comment: And they captured it. Below (chapter 14), it is stated that Caleb captured Hebron in the fifth year after Israel entered the land. Likewise, the subsequent statement that Joshua captured Debir appears to contradict Judges 1:13, which says that Othniel son of Kenaz captured it. We must therefore say that Joshua captured the city of Hebron, whereas Caleb conquered the city’s surrounding fields and villages; for it is stated there that only the city’s field and villages were given to Caleb, while Hebron itself was a Levitical city, as explained below (chapter 21). The same must be said regarding Debir. Alternatively, the account recorded below in chapter 14 actually belongs here: when Joshua came before Hebron, Caleb reminded him of Moses’ promise. Joshua then gave Hebron to Caleb, who fought against the city and cut down the Anakim. The conquest is attributed to Joshua because it was accomplished under his authority and command. Similarly, Othniel son of Kenaz struck Debir at that time, and its conquest is likewise attributed to Joshua for this reason. Scripture relied on the later account concerning the allotments to explain the precise circumstances of the conquest. As for the statement here that Joshua killed its king, although that king was already said to have been killed in the battle of Gibeon, Radak explains that in the meantime they had appointed another king. Alternatively, there may have been two kings there.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 38_Verse, 0_Comment: And as he had done to Libnah. The words “as he had done to Hebron” might lead one to think that he captured Debir’s king alive and hanged him, as he had done to the king of Hebron. Scripture therefore says that he did the same to Debir—that its destruction resembled Hebron’s—and to its king as he had done to Libnah, where the king was killed among the slain, as stated in verse 30: “as he had done to the king of Jericho.” This means that he was not captured alive.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 39_Verse, 0_Comment: All the land. The entire southern region.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 39_Verse, 1_Comment: The hill country and the Negev. That is, the dry and arid land. The opposite of “the hill country” is the lowland, and the opposite of “the Negev” is the slopes—that is, the slopes of the streams.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 40_Verse, 0_Comment: And he struck them. In this battle.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 40_Verse, 1_Comment: From Kadesh-barnea to Gaza. This is the southern territory extending from east to west, which constitutes the southern boundary of the land of Judah.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 40_Verse, 2_Comment: And all the land of Goshen. In the hill country, he conquered the land of Goshen, which was situated in Judah’s allotment in the hills (below, 15:51).
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 40_Verse, 3_Comment: As far as Gibeon. Which lay within Benjamin’s allotment.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 41_Verse, 0_Comment: And all the kings. Who ruled within this southern territory.
text.1_, 9_Chapter, 41_Verse, 1_Comment: Joshua captured them in a single campaign. This excludes the kings in the other regions of the land, whom he did not conquer in a single campaign, as stated in the following chapter.
text.1_, 10_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And to the kings who were in the north. For the southern region had already been conquered. The word mitzafon (“in the north”) is vocalized with a sheva, although it is not in the construct state; its regular vocalization would be with a kamatz.
text.1_, 10_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: The Canaanite. That is, on the eastern side of the northern region was the Canaanite in the east, and likewise in the west, as indicated by “and by the sea.” There were also peoples in the middle, as indicated by “the Amorite and the Hittite,” etc., and the Hivite, who dwelt beneath Mount Hermon in the valley.
text.1_, 10_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And they went out. They no longer dared to go out individually, as the earlier kings had done. They also possessed horses and chariots, which the earlier kings had not, for they intended to fight in open battle.
text.1_, 10_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And they assembled by appointment. They fixed a designated time for the kings to gather, and they encamped by the waters of Merom.
text.1_, 10_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Do not fear. As it is written, “When you see horses and chariots,” etc., “you shall not fear them” (Deuteronomy 20:1).
text.1_, 10_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: You shall hamstring. So that Israel would not place their trust in horses in battle. The king had already been commanded not to acquire many horses for himself (Deuteronomy 17:16).
text.1_, 10_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: None was left. I have explained that nish’ar (“remained”) denotes what is left intentionally, whereas notar (“was left over”) denotes what remains unintentionally. Therefore, above (verse 8) and below (verse 14), Scripture uses “they left none remaining,” meaning intentionally, since some escaped without Israel’s knowledge. Here, however, where not a single person escaped even without their knowledge, Scripture states the greater point: none was left at all.
text.1_, 10_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And all the cities. This did not occur during this particular campaign, but throughout the seven years of conquest, as will be explained in verse 18.
text.1_, 10_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: As He commanded—so Moses commanded. Moses transmitted everything to Joshua, as stated (at the beginning of Pirkei Avot): “and transmitted it to Joshua.” Moreover, although the conquest would have been more miraculous had it been accomplished through Moses than it was through Joshua, nothing was changed regarding the commandments governing the conquest and the division of the land.
text.1_, 10_Chapter, 14_Verse, 1_Comment: He omitted nothing. Even regarding matters that Moses had not explicitly commanded him, Joshua independently discerned what Hashem had commanded Moses (as the Sages explained in Midrash Rabbah).
text.1_, 10_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: For many days. This explains that the statement in verse 12, “And all the cities of those kings,” etc., did not refer to a single campaign, as with the five preceding kings; rather, the conquest continued for many days.
text.1_, 10_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: There was not. Scripture explains that this was from Hashem. Had Joshua proceeded immediately after defeating the combined armies to wage war against the individual cities, they would have sought peace, and Israel would have been obligated to accept them if they agreed to tribute, servitude, and the seven Noahide commandments, as explained above (chapter 9). But because he waged war for many days, their hearts were thereby hardened and they did not make peace. Thus, no city made peace, and consequently Israel captured them all through warfare. Scripture says, “made peace with the children of Israel,” using the preposition el rather than the expected direct-object marker et. This means that they did not wage war against Israel, as in, “and the beasts of the field shall be at peace with you” (Job 5:23). By contrast, “made peace with” using et indicates that warfare had previously taken place.
text.1_, 10_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: For. Scripture now explains why Hashem arranged matters so that they would not make peace. There were two reasons. First, the measure of their sin had become full, and Hashem wished to punish them. Thus, it says, “in order to utterly destroy them,” and this was “so that they would receive no favor,” meaning that they were unworthy of mercy from Hashem. Second, it was so that Israel would fulfill the commandment, “You shall not let any soul live,” as Hashem had commanded, and so that they would not remain in the land and cause Israel to sin. Radak explains it likewise.
text.1_, 10_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: And Joshua came at that time. During the seven years of conquest. Although Caleb dispossessed the Anakim from Hebron, Joshua dispossessed them from the city itself, as explained above. Alternatively, as stated above (10:37), Caleb dispossessed the Anakim, but the deed is attributed to Joshua for the reason explained there.
text.1_, 10_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: None was left. I have already explained (above, verse 11) that nish’ar denotes what remains intentionally, whereas notar denotes what is left unintentionally. In the Land of Israel, therefore, none was left at all, even unintentionally. Only in Gaza were some intentionally left, because Israel did not fight against them at all; they remained in order to test Israel, as stated in Judges 3:3–4.
text.1_, 10_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: And Joshua took. During the seven years of conquest.
text.1_, 10_Chapter, 22_Verse, 1_Comment: And Joshua gave it as an inheritance. During the seven years in which the land was divided.
text.1_, 10_Chapter, 22_Verse, 2_Comment: And the land was at rest. After the conquest and the division of the land.
text.1_, 11_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Sihon. Scripture now describes Sihon’s territory separately, as stated in Numbers 21:24 and Deuteronomy 2:36.
text.1_, 11_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And the territory of Og. Scripture describes Og’s territory separately.
text.1_, 11_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Moses, servant of Hashem. That is, he did this at Hashem’s command, even though this territory was not part of the Land of Israel and they were commanded not to conquer lands outside it before conquering the Land of Israel, as stated in the Sifrei at the end of Eikev. Likewise, his giving it to the Reubenites was done as a servant of Hashem and at His command.
text.1_, 11_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And these. Scripture now details Joshua’s conquests.
text.1_, 11_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: Whom he defeated. For Scripture does not enumerate the entire land here, but only the portion that Joshua conquered during his lifetime; much land still remained to be possessed, as stated in the following chapter.
text.1_, 11_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: The king of Jericho, one. Among the kings enumerated here were many whose lands Joshua did not conquer during his lifetime, although the kings themselves were killed by Joshua in battle. These were the king of Jerusalem (Judges 1:21), the king of Gezer (below, 16:10; Judges 1:29); Bethel was not conquered during his lifetime (Judges 1:22), nor was Aphek (ibid., 31), or Taanach, Megiddo, and Dor (ibid., 27). Some of the kings enumerated here are explicitly mentioned in the book: the kings of Jericho and Ai (chapter 8); Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, Debir, Eglon, Gezer, Libnah, and Makkedah—all of whom he defeated in a single campaign (chapter 10); and the kings of Hazor, Madon, Shimron, and Achshaph (chapter 11). The king of Bethel, although his death is not explicitly recorded, was undoubtedly killed when he went to aid Ai. Thus, we have found seventeen kings; the remaining fourteen are included in the statement (11:12), “Joshua captured all their kings and struck them down.”
text.1_, 12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: All the regions. In this verse, Scripture enumerates what remained unconquered along the southern border, from east to west.
text.1_, 12_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: And the Avvim. They too remained unconquered.
text.1_, 12_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: From the south. Scripture now enumerates the unconquered territories along the western side, proceeding from south to north.
text.1_, 12_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And the land. Scripture now enumerates the unconquered territories along the northern border, from east to west.
text.1_, 12_Chapter, 4_Verse, 1_Comment: As far as Lebo-hamath. Which lies in the northwest.
text.1_, 12_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Only divide it—as an inheritance. Above (12:7), Scripture says, “Joshua gave it to the tribes of Israel as a possession,” whereas here it says “as an inheritance.” There is a distinction between yerushah (“possession”) and nachalah (“inheritance”). Yerushah denotes a transfer of ownership, whereby something passes from one party’s domain into another’s; nachalah denotes property that one bequeaths to his descendants. Therefore, above, where Scripture enumerated what Joshua had conquered, it says that he gave it as a yerushah, because it was then transferred from the Canaanites’ possession into Israel’s. There it could not have said that he apportioned it as a nachalah, because he had not yet cast lots to determine who would inherit and bequeath each portion. Here, however, since the land had not yet been conquered, it could not be called a yerushah; rather, Scripture says, “divide it as a nachalah,” so that each person would know his inheritance.
text.1_, 12_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: And I will dispossess them. So that the land will pass from the Canaanites’ possession into Israel’s possession.
text.1_, 12_Chapter, 5_Verse, 2_Comment: As I commanded you. For He had told him above (1:6), “You shall cause this people to inherit.” This did not include dispossessing them—that is, dispossessing the Canaanites—but only allotting to each Israelite his portion.
text.1_, 12_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: With him. That is, it was unnecessary to apportion the land to them anew. The word “with him” means together with the other half of Manasseh.
text.1_, 12_Chapter, 7_Verse, 1_Comment: For they had received their inheritance, which Moses gave—as Moses gave. That is, they received it according to the apportionment Moses had assigned them, and it was not apportioned differently by Joshua. Scripture explains the phrase “they received their inheritance, which Moses gave” by describing its territory from Aroer onward, through verse 15. It then explains “as Moses gave” by detailing the manner of its apportionment: “Moses gave to the tribe of Reuben” (verse 15), “to the tribe of Gad” (verse 24), and “to half the tribe of Manasseh” (verse 29).
text.1_, 12_Chapter, 32_Verse, 0_Comment: And to the tribe of Levi. This was already stated in verse 14, but there Scripture says, “The fire offerings of Hashem are his inheritance,” whereas here it says, “Hashem is his inheritance.” This may be understood in light of Deuteronomy 18:1–2: “The Levitical priests shall have no portion or inheritance with Israel; they shall eat the fire offerings of Hashem and His inheritance. He shall have no inheritance among his brethren; Hashem is his inheritance.” There too, the statement is repeated: first it says “portion or inheritance” and “they shall eat the fire offerings of Hashem,” and afterward it says only “inheritance” and “Hashem is his inheritance.” However, the passage speaks from two perspectives. First, the Levites were not to receive a portion in the land—that is, the tribe was not to receive a distinct territory by lot when the land was divided, as the other tribes did. Therefore, Scripture says “portion or inheritance,” and explains that in place of their share in the land, Israel would give them Hashem’s fire offerings, namely, the priestly and Levitical gifts. Thus it says, “a portion or inheritance with his brethren”: the word “with” denotes partnership, for they were not to participate in the division of the land. Scripture then says that although they were given cities in which to dwell together with their pasturelands, which constituted an inheritance that they transmitted to their children, they nevertheless were not to receive this inheritance “among their brethren.” That is, their cities were not to be selected and set aside during the original apportionment—for example, immediately when a tribe’s lot was drawn and its territory divided among its members, the Levitical cities within that tribe’s territory were not yet to be designated. This is conveyed by the expression “among his brethren.” Rather, only after the division of all the tribes had been completed did the children of Israel give the Levites cities from their own inheritances, as related below (chapter 21). Scripture explains the reason: “Hashem is his inheritance.” Each tribe’s contribution would therefore be like an offering to Hashem, a sacred portion raised from its own territory. Accordingly, Moses did not set aside the Levitical cities from the inheritances of Reuben and Gad during his lifetime; Joshua did so only after the entire division had been completed. Therefore, above (verse 14), after mentioning Moses’ conquest in general terms but before describing the specific apportionments of Reuben and Gad, Scripture states that he did not assign Levi a separate tribal portion—even though one might have reasoned that he could have given them territory east of the Jordan, which is not part of the Land of Israel—and it gives the first reason: “The fire offerings of Hashem are his inheritance.” Here, after detailing the specific apportionments, Scripture adds that even afterward Moses did not give the tribe of Levi an inheritance—that is, he did not set aside the Levitical cities during his lifetime—because “Hashem is his inheritance.”
text.1_, 13_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: And these are those who received their inheritance. The most correct view concerning the manner in which the land was divided is that of Raavad (cited in Shittah Mekubbetzet, Bava Batra 117b). He writes: “Know and understand that the Land of Israel was divided among the twelve tribes by lot and through the Urim and Thummim. This is the question they asked (ibid., 122a): ‘Was it divided among the tribes, or according to the number of individuals?’ They were asking about the division by lot, and the answer is derived from ‘whether numerous or few’ (Numbers 26:56): whether a tribe was numerous or small, its territory was determined by lot. For the families, however, they did not resort to a lottery,” etc. “Another difficulty remains: If the portions were unequal, how could they have been divided by lot? Before the lottery, how was it known to whom a larger portion should be given and to whom a smaller one? What would happen if the lot assigned a large portion to a small tribe? A lottery is possible only among portions that are equal—whether equal in area, monetary value, or quality of land. We answer that only the boundaries of the regions were written upon the lots. For example, just as one might designate the territory extending from a particular boundary as the province of Catalonia and that extending from another boundary as the province of Provence, so they wrote the regions upon the lots and placed them in the urn. Whichever region a tribe drew was the region in which it received its portion; within that region, it was given more or less according to its population. You may know that this is so from the fact that the lots of Judah and the children of Joseph were drawn before the remaining tribes’ territories were apportioned, and portions belonging to some of the other tribes were located within their territories. You thus learn that the lots determined only the regional boundaries.” These are his words. You see that his opinion accords with that of Abarbanel: the lottery determined only the general regions. Once it was known within which region a tribe would receive its portion, Joshua and the heads of the tribal fathers apportioned the land according to population. A tribe with more people received a larger portion, and this was determined not by lot but by the judgment of those who apportioned the land. See Raavad’s extensive discussion there. Shittah Mekubbetzet (Bava Batra 121a) also cites Raavad as raising an objection to his own view from the verse, “You shall inherit the land by lot according to your families” (Numbers 33:54), and as inclining to distinguish between two lotteries: the division among the members of each tribe was conducted through a second lottery without the Urim and Thummim. This conclusion, however, is not necessary, for “according to your families” may refer to what follows—“to the numerous you shall give more”—meaning that first, “you shall inherit the land by lot,” to determine the tribes’ regional boundaries, and afterward, “you shall inherit it according to your families; to the numerous you shall give more,” through an apportionment made by judgment. In my opinion, Rashi also follows this approach. Commenting on the verse, “Among these shall the land be divided as an inheritance according to the number of names; to the numerous you shall give a larger inheritance,” etc. (Numbers 26:53–54), Rashi explains: “A tribe with a large population was given a large portion. Although the portions were unequal, for everything was apportioned according to the tribe’s population, the portions were assigned only by lot; and the lot operated through Divine inspiration,” etc. “The Divine Spirit declared: If such-and-such a tribe is drawn, such-and-such a territory shall be drawn with it,” etc. Re’em, Abarbanel, and all who explained Rashi understood him to mean that the lottery assigned a larger portion to the tribe with the larger population. This, however, is not his meaning. When Rashi says, “A tribe with a large population was given a large portion,” he means that Joshua gave it a large portion, not that it received one by lot. Therefore, he continues, “Although the portions were unequal, for everything was apportioned according to the tribe’s population”—and consequently the division according to population could not have been accomplished by lot; for “to the numerous you shall give more” means that you, the person making the apportionment, shall give more—nevertheless, “the portions were assigned only by lot.” That is, the foundation of the division was established by lot, and this is the meaning of “Only by lot shall the land be divided” (ibid., 55). Rashi then explains that the lot declared: “If such-and-such a tribe is drawn, such-and-such a territory shall be drawn with it.” In other words, the lottery determined the regional boundaries, after which Joshua apportioned larger or smaller portions within that region according to the tribe’s population. The same applies to Rashi’s comment on “Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine like Reuben and Simeon; but your offspring whom you beget after them,” etc. (Genesis 48:5–6): “Although the land was divided according to the number of persons, as it is written, ‘To the numerous you shall give more,’ and each individual received an equal share, nevertheless, only these were designated as tribes.” This does not mean that the lottery divided the land according to the number of individuals—as Re’em understood, which would conflict with the ruling in Bava Batra that it was divided among the tribes. Nor does it mean that the lottery was conducted among the tribes and that each tribe received by lot a portion corresponding to the size of its population, as the other commentators understood. Rather, it means that although Joshua and the tribal heads apportioned the land according to population—and one might therefore ask what practical difference resulted from Ephraim and Manasseh being two tribes like Reuben and Simeon—Rashi answers that they were nevertheless designated as separate tribes so that each would receive its own lot in a distinct region. I have thus established this view upon firm pillars and foundations, and through it the plain meaning of the verses may readily be understood, as will be explained in each appropriate place. Ramban alone follows a different approach, against which the archers have bitterly directed their many arrows.
text.1_, 13_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: By lot. Here Scripture describes how the lottery was conducted; it does not discuss the apportionment according to the number of individuals.
text.1_, 13_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: As Hashem commanded. “Only by lot shall the land be divided.”
text.1_, 13_Chapter, 1_Verse, 2_Comment: For Moses had given. This explains why the land was apportioned to only nine tribes and a half.
text.1_, 13_Chapter, 1_Verse, 3_Comment: And to the Levites. This prevents the mistaken assumption that the Levites were included in the count of the twelve tribes.
text.1_, 13_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: For the children of Joseph were. They completed the count of twelve tribes.
text.1_, 13_Chapter, 3_Verse, 1_Comment: And they gave no portion. Even within the land, the Levites were not given a territorial portion, but only cities in which to dwell; therefore, they are not included in the count.
text.1_, 13_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: As He commanded. In all the other particulars as well, they apportioned the land in accordance with the Torah’s command: “To the numerous you shall give a larger inheritance,” and the like.
text.1_, 13_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Concerning me and concerning you. That is, Hashem first said (Numbers 14:22–24): “All the men who have seen My glory,” etc., “shall not see the land,” etc.; “But My servant Caleb, because he had a different spirit with him,” etc., “I will bring him into the land into which he came, and his descendants shall possess it.” This could have been understood merely to mean that Caleb would not die in the wilderness and that his descendants would inherit their portion together with the other tribes. Afterward, however, He said (ibid., 30): “You shall not enter the land,” etc., “except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun.” Accordingly, since He later stated explicitly that Caleb and Joshua would enter the land, why had He already promised Caleb twice, “I will bring him into the land”? It must therefore mean that He would bring Caleb into the particular land to which he had gone—Hebron—and that his descendants would inherit Hebron. Caleb therefore recalled what Hashem had said concerning both himself and Joshua, for from this he could prove that Hashem’s earlier statement concerning Caleb specifically referred to giving him Hebron.
text.1_, 13_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And I brought back word. Caleb presented four reasons why he deserved this reward. First, because he had been a faithful emissary and did not report according to what his eyes perceived, but according to the judgment of his discerning and perceptive heart, exercising his free choice to choose what was right. Thus, he says, “As it was in my heart.” Second, because others had attempted to entice him to sin, as he continues:
text.1_, 13_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: But my brethren made the people’s hearts melt. Yet Caleb withstood their enticements and did not fear the people. Thus, he says, “But I wholly followed” Hashem. The word hemasiv follows the Aramaic pattern of atyu chamra, “they brought wine”; according to Hebrew usage, its proper form would have been hemesiv, like natayu raglai, “my feet had almost turned aside” (Psalms 73:2). Its root is masas. Third, he deserved the reward because of the oath Moses had sworn, as he continues:
text.1_, 13_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And Moses swore. Fourth, because we see that Hashem’s Providence confirms this promise. First, behold:
text.1_, 13_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And now, behold, Hashem has kept me alive. Although forty-five years have passed and I am now eighty-five years old. Second, from the fact that:
text.1_, 13_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: I am still as strong today. His heart remained courageous, fearing no one; and his physical strength was likewise as my strength was then, so is my strength now. The expression “as my strength was then, so is my strength now” is like “for you are like Pharaoh” (Genesis 44:18). According to ordinary linguistic usage, however, the order should have been reversed: “As my strength is now, so was my strength then,” since the first term is always compared to the second. Rather, his strength at that earlier time had not become known until now, when he fought in the army and his might became evident. He therefore said that he estimated his strength then to have been exactly what it was now—neither less nor more. Therefore:
text.1_, 13_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And now, give me this hill country. For Hashem preserved my life and maintained my strength so that I myself might dispossess its inhabitants, as Hashem had said, “And his descendants shall possess it.”
text.1_, 13_Chapter, 11_Verse, 1_Comment: Perhaps Hashem will be with me. Grammatically, it should have said itti (“with me”) rather than oti. Alternatively, it may be understood like “But Hashem is with me like a mighty warrior” (Jeremiah 20:11), which I interpreted to mean, “Hashem is my sign”; or it may derive from the sense of firmness and strength.
text.1_, 13_Chapter, 11_Verse, 2_Comment: Therefore it became. That is, it did not come to him as part of the regular apportionment according to population, but was given to him as a reward.
text.1_, 13_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And the name of Hebron. Scripture states that giants were indeed there, for this reason it had been called Kiriath-arba.
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And it went out. Wherever Scripture says “and it went out,” the measuring line departed from a straight course and turned aside, either inward or outward. Wherever it says “and it turned,” the boundary turned along two directions, forming the shape of the letter dalet. Wherever it says “and it curved around,” the boundary surrounded a particular place on three sides and then returned to its original straight course. Here it says, “and it went out southward to the Ascent of Akrabbim,” whereas in the portion of Masei (Numbers 34:4) it says, “Your border shall turn southward toward the Ascent of Akrabbim.” This is because the Ascent of Akrabbim was not directly opposite the tongue of the sea but extended southward, so the measuring line proceeded diagonally from east to west toward the south. From this perspective, Scripture here says, “and it went out.” Yet because that location formed the corner or angle, with the boundary encompassing it along two directions, the expression “and it turned” is also appropriate.
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 2_Verse, 1_Comment: And it ascended southward to Kadesh-barnea. In the portion of Masei (Numbers 34:4), however, it says, “and its extremity shall be south of Kadesh-barnea.” The rule is that wherever Scripture says, “and its extremity shall be,” either the boundary itself terminates there or its deviation ends there: until that point the measuring line had deviated from its straight course, and there it returned to its original line. After Scripture says, “and it went out southward to the Ascent of Akrabbim,” the line was deviating, as implied by the expression “went out.” While following this deviation, it passed through Zin as far as Kadesh-barnea, where the deviation ended; therefore, it says, “and its extremity shall be.” The Torah consequently says there, “and it shall go out to Hazar-addar,” because from Kadesh the line turned inward, and at Hazar-addar it reached the straight boundary line again. Here Scripture abbreviates, relying upon what is stated in the Torah.
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And it went out to the Brook of Egypt. In the portion of Masei (Numbers 34:5), however, Scripture says, “and the border shall turn.” This accords with what was explained above. Since the boundary departed inward from its course and followed the brook as far as the sea, which lay farther inward, Scripture here says “and it went out,” viewed from the point at which it met the brook. There it says “and it turned,” viewed from the boundary’s curving course and its formation of a corner.
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Beth-hoglah. The city itself lay outside the boundary line and belonged to Benjamin (below, 18:21), whereas the slope of Beth-hoglah belonged to Judah (below, 18:19). Therefore, Scripture says there, “and it passed toward the slope of Beth-hoglah.”
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: North of Beth-arabah. Beth-arabah belonged to Judah and is the Beth-arabah enumerated below in verse 61. There was also another Beth-arabah belonging to Benjamin (below, 18:22). The one mentioned here corresponds to the places described there (18:18): “It passed toward the slope opposite the Arabah northward and descended to the Arabah.” Both are included here under the name Beth-arabah.
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And the boundary ascended to Debir. That is, from the Stone of Bohan it descended into the Valley of Achor, and from there it ascended to Debir. Debir belonged to Judah (below, verse 49); therefore, this landmark is not mentioned in the description of Benjamin’s border (18:19).
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: And the boundary turned northward toward Gilgal. This means that here the boundary line departed from its course and turned northward. The reference to Gilgal means “the district,” for Gilgal itself was situated before the Valley of Achor, between the Jordan and Jericho, as explained above (5:10; 7:26). In describing Benjamin’s border, Scripture says (below, 18:17), “and it went out toward the districts opposite the Ascent of Adummim,” without adding, “which is south of the brook.” Accordingly, “opposite the Ascent of Adummim” means that there were several districts extending from this boundary, and they belonged to Benjamin; but one of them—the district south of the brook—belonged to Judah. Scripture refers to that one here by saying, “toward Gilgal, which is opposite the Ascent of Adummim”—namely, the one south of the brook, which belonged to Judah. There, however, it refers to the other districts belonging to Benjamin, toward which Benjamin’s boundary line went out. This northward deviation of the boundary line continued as far as En-rogel, as Scripture says, “and its extremities were at En-rogel.” At that point the line began returning to its straight course, so En-rogel marked the end of the deviation.
