By the time it reached the Valley of Ben-hinnom, the line was again straight, opposite Debir and the Stone of Bohan. With this, you will understand the description of Benjamin’s border (ibid., 16–17): “It descended to En-rogel, curved around northward, went out to En-shemesh, went out toward the districts opposite the Ascent of Adummim, and descended to the Stone of Bohan.” The line proceeding from En-rogel to En-shemesh went outward; upon reaching En-shemesh, it curved around that place on three sides, which is the meaning of “curved around.” From there it went out toward the districts of the Ascent of Adummim, again deviating inward—an action also described by the term “went out”—and then descended to the Stone of Bohan, where it returned to the former straight line opposite the Valley of Ben-hinnom.
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: And the boundary ascended. This ascent continued as far as the spring of the waters of Nephtoah, from which point it began to descend. As the Sages said, “He considered building it at Ein Eitam, which is situated higher” (Zevachim 54b).
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 7_Verse, 1_Comment: It is Jerusalem. It was called the slope of the Jebusite because the Jebusites dwelt there. By saying “on the south,” Scripture indicates that Jerusalem belonged to Benjamin and was included within his inheritance (18:28).
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 7_Verse, 2_Comment: And the boundary ascended to the top of the mountain. This means the beginning of the mountain at the edge of its slope. In the description of Benjamin’s inheritance (18:16), Scripture calls this “the edge of the mountain.”
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 7_Verse, 3_Comment: West of the Valley of Hinnom. That is, the mountain lay west of the Valley of Ben-hinnom and north of the Valley of Rephaim.
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And the boundary curved around. I have already established that wherever Scripture says “and it curved around,” the boundary forms a curve encompassing three sides. Here the boundary line curved around and transferred a rounded strip from Benjamin’s portion into Judah’s portion, as the Sages said: “A strip extended from Judah’s portion into Benjamin’s portion, and the altar was built upon it” (Yoma 12a). This curve was completed at the spring of the waters of Nephtoah. Therefore, in the description of Benjamin’s border (18:16), the expression “and it curved around” is not used, because there the boundary line followed the convex side of the curve rather than its concave side.
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 8_Verse, 1_Comment: And the boundary curved around to Baalah. Kiriath-jearim belonged to Judah (verse 60) and bordered the entire width of Benjamin’s territory (18:14–15). Scripture specifies, “it is Kiriath-jearim,” because there was another Baalah in the Negev (verse 29), namely Balah, which was assigned to Simeon (19:3). Therefore, Kiriath-jearim is called “Baale-judah” in I Samuel 6:2. Accordingly, the boundary line went northward toward the cities of Mount Ephron, where it curved around Kiriath-jearim on three sides, bringing it within Judah’s territory. The entire city, however, projected outward beyond the boundary line toward Benjamin’s inheritance. South of Kiriath-jearim there was either a sea or a place bearing that name. After the boundary line went out and encircled Kiriath-jearim, it followed its curve around the city’s western and northern sides, returned along its eastern side, turned southward, and reached the sea. Thus, Scripture says:
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And it turned from Baalah toward the sea. For there the boundary turned in the shape of the letter dalet. This explains how, in the description of Benjamin’s inheritance (18:15), Scripture can say that the boundary went out from Baalah toward the sea, although there it proceeded from west to east: How could it have reached this sea? Rather, this sea lay southeast of Baalah. From the sea, the boundary turned toward Mount Seir, for the Judean mountain range meets Mount Seir on its southern side, and one part of it was called Mount Seir. It then passed westward and reached the northern side of Chesalon. This is not Chesil, mentioned in verse 30, which lay in the Negev and was assigned to Simeon.
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 9_Verse, 1_Comment: And it descended to Beth-shemesh. This was the Beth-shemesh belonging to Judah, for there was another Beth-shemesh in Issachar’s inheritance (below, 19:22) and another in Naphtali’s inheritance (ibid., 34). Likewise, we find that the Ark of Hashem was returned from Ekron to Beth-shemesh and from there to Kiriath-jearim (I Samuel 5:10; 6:12).
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 9_Verse, 2_Comment: And it passed on to Timnah. Which belonged to Judah (verse 57).
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And it went out. The boundary deviated northward a second time, toward the slope of Ekron, one of the Philistine cities, which belonged to Judah (verse 45).
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 10_Verse, 1_Comment: And it curved around—toward Shikkeron. Shikkeron lay outside the boundary, which curved around it on three sides and then returned to the point opposite the slope of Ekron. From there the line passed straight toward Mount Baalah, and from there it went out and deviated from its straight course toward Jabneel. This is not the Jabneel belonging to Naphtali (19:33).
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: According to the word of Hashem. Everywhere else Scripture says “by the word of Hashem”; only here, below (17:4) concerning the portion of Zelophehad’s daughters, and below (21:3) concerning the Levitical cities does it say “according to the word of Hashem.” This is because in all these cases the command had already been given through Moses and was not a new command, whereas a newly issued command is always described as being “by the word of Hashem.”
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And he dispossessed them. This occurred during Joshua’s lifetime. I explained in my commentary on Judges 1:11 why the book of Judges appears to place it after his death. Likewise, the account given here from verse 15 through verse 20 is repeated there, and I explained it in that context. (32) All the cities were twenty-nine. Yet when counted individually, they appear to total thirty-eight. The commentators write that the nine additional cities were taken by the children of Simeon from Judah’s portion and are listed in Simeon’s inheritance: Beer-sheba, Moladah, Hazar-shual, Ezem, Eltolad, Hormah, Ziklag, Ain, and Rimmon. I am not satisfied with this explanation. First, one obtains a total of thirty-eight only by interpreting “Hazor-hadattah and Kerioth-hezron, which is Hazor” as four separate cities. In truth, however, the words (verse 25) “Hezron, which is Hazor” indicate that it is one city, just as “Kiriath-sannah, which is Debir” (verse 49) and “Kiriath-baal, which is Kiriath-jearim” (verse 60) each refer to one city. Moreover, I do not understand why Scripture would say “Hezron, which is Hazor,” since Hazor was already enumerated in verse 23. Furthermore, Balah, listed in Simeon’s inheritance (19:3), is Baalah; Bethul (ibid., 4) is Chesil; and “Beth-lebaoth and Sharuhen” (ibid., 6) are the same as Lebaoth and Shilhim mentioned here, for the pronunciation of names of cities and persons frequently varies, as is well known to anyone who examines the variants found in the Book of Chronicles. From what I understand of the words of the Sages, Kenah, Dimonah, and Adadah were one city: the principal city was called Kenah, while its surrounding areas were called Dimonah and Adadah. Similarly, Ziklag, Madmannah, and Sansannah were also one city: the principal city was called Ziklag, while its surrounding areas were called Madmannah and Sansannah. Likewise, the phrase “Hazor-hadattah and Kerioth-hezron, which is Hazor” does not add to the count, but explains Hazor: all these—Hazor-hadattah, meaning “the new enclosure,” and the settlements of Hazor—were included within Hazor. Scripture gives this identifying description because there was another Hazor in Naphtali (below, 19:36), namely the Hazor mentioned above in chapter 11. Lebaoth and Shilhim, which the commentators count as two cities, were likewise one, as I proved in discussing Simeon’s inheritance, where Beth-lebaoth and Sharuhen are mentioned as one; see there. Accordingly, there were precisely twenty-nine cities, no more. This enables you to understand the remarkable discussion in the Talmud (Gittin 7b): “Rav Huna bar Natan said to Rav Ashi: What is the meaning of the verse, ‘Kenah, Dimonah, and Adadah’? He replied: Scripture is enumerating the towns of the Land of Israel. He said to him: Do I not know that it is enumerating the towns of the Land of Israel? Rather, Rav Geviha of Argiza explained its meaning: Anyone who bears resentment against another but remains silent—the One Who dwells eternally executes judgment for him. Rav Ashi asked: If so, should ‘Ziklag, Madmannah, and Sansannah’ be interpreted similarly? He replied: Had Rav Geviha of Argiza been here, he would have offered an explanation. Rav Aha of Bei Haleza explained it thus: Anyone who has a complaint concerning food against another but remains silent—the One Who dwells in the burning bush executes judgment for him.” If you plow with my heifer, you will discover their riddle. The Sages knew that Kenah, Dimonah, and Adadah constituted one city together with its districts, and they therefore sought to explain why Scripture enumerated here the districts and outlying areas of Kenah, although they were not included in the number of cities—something it does nowhere else. Thus, when Rav Ashi answered Rav Huna bar Natan, “Scripture is enumerating the towns of the Land of Israel,” Rav Huna replied, “Do I not know that it is enumerating the towns of the Land of Israel?” His meaning was: Nevertheless, there must be a reason why Scripture counts here the small towns that are not included in the total. Rav Geviha supplied the reason: In that generation, the name of the city Kenah together with those of its districts was commonly used as a mnemonic and allusion to a moral teaching. Scripture therefore mentioned Kenah in the form in which people habitually referred to it together with its districts, thereby recalling the moral lesson associated with it. Rav Ashi then asked that Scripture similarly enumerates Ziklag together with Madmannah and Sansannah—one city and its districts—and therefore a reason was also needed for mentioning those districts. Rav Aha then came and supplied the moral teaching that they likewise associated with the names of Ziklag and its districts.
text.1_, 14_Chapter, 62_Verse, 0_Comment: And the Jebusites. I have discussed and properly resolved the apparent contradiction between this passage and the Book of Judges, chapter 1, in my commentary there (verse 8).
text.1_, 15_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And it went out. Luz was not situated directly opposite Mount Bethel, but lay farther inward toward the south, for Scripture says (18:12), “and its extremities were at the wilderness of Beth-aven,” indicating that the transverse boundary line ended there. Since the boundary passed from there toward Luz, Luz must have been situated inward to the south. Therefore, Scripture says, “and it went out from Bethel to Luz.” Luz belonged to Joseph.
text.1_, 15_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: And it passed. In a straight line.
text.1_, 15_Chapter, 1_Verse, 2_Comment: To the longitudinal border. That is, to the lengthwise boundary itself, which was Benjamin’s northern border, at Ataroth-addar (ibid., verse 13). Scripture specifies “the longitudinal border” because another Ataroth lay on the transverse boundary, on the eastern side of Joseph’s inheritance, as stated in verse 7: “It descended from Janoah to Ataroth.”
text.1_, 15_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And it descended westward. From there, the boundary descended westward as far as the Great Sea.
text.1_, 15_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And they inherited. The children of Ephraim received a separate lot, and the half-tribe of Manasseh received a separate lot. Scripture calls them a single lot only because their territories emerged adjacent to one another within the same region. Here it explains that Manasseh and Ephraim inherited, each according to a separate lot.
text.1_, 15_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And it was. From this general territory, which extended across the entire width of the Land of Israel from east to west, the children of Ephraim received the eastern half, while Manasseh received the western half. However, within Manasseh’s half there were also certain cities set apart for the children of Ephraim, as Scripture enumerates here.
text.1_, 15_Chapter, 4_Verse, 1_Comment: “And the territory of” the children of Ephraim—and the boundary was. Because Scripture enumerates two types of territory here, it first says, “And the territory of the children of Ephraim,” meaning everything belonging to them, including the cities set apart for them. It now begins to describe the boundary of their principal inheritance on the eastern side, which belonged exclusively to Ephraim; in verse 8 it will describe the cities set apart for them.
text.1_, 15_Chapter, 4_Verse, 2_Comment: The boundary of their inheritance on the east. That is, their territory occupied the eastern half of the land’s length, while the western half belonged to Manasseh.
text.1_, 15_Chapter, 4_Verse, 3_Comment: From Ataroth-addar to Beth-horon. This constituted the width of their inheritance from south to north. Both Lower Beth-horon and Upper Beth-horon belonged to Ephraim, as stated in I Chronicles 7:24.
text.1_, 15_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And it went out. On the northern side of the boundary—that is, from its northeastern corner at Upper Beth-horon—the boundary extended outward, widened, and proceeded westward as far as Michmethath.
text.1_, 15_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: And the boundary turned. Scripture now describes the northern boundary line from Beth-horon to the far eastern end. The boundary turned eastward, meaning toward the east, for here it is being traced from west to east, and the line proceeded by turning in two directions—the meaning of “turned”—in the shape of the letter dalet. It explains how: the line proceeded diagonally from Beth-horon as far as Taanath-shiloh, which lay on the border opposite Bethel to its north, as stated in Judges 21:19. This line ran from west to east. From there, it passed it and came east of Janoah: the line proceeded from north to south until it passed along Janoah’s eastern side. This enables you to understand the teaching of the Sages (Zevachim 118b): “In three places the Divine Presence rested, and all were within Benjamin’s portion.” How could Shiloh have been within Benjamin’s portion? Shiloh was north of Bethel, so Joseph’s territory seemingly intervened between them. However, according to what was explained above, the territory from Taanath-shiloh and Jericho eastward did not belong to Joseph. From there, a strip belonging to Benjamin extended along the entire eastern side of Joseph’s inheritance as far as Shiloh, and the Tabernacle was erected upon this strip. This also explains the verse: “Behold, there is an annual festival of Hashem in Shiloh, which is north of Bethel, east of the road that ascends from Bethel to Shechem” (Judges 21:19). They celebrated this festival east of Shiloh, along that road, which belonged to Benjamin. The Benjaminites were therefore permitted to seize wives there from among the dancing women, since those women had entered the territory of their inheritance.
text.1_, 15_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And it descended, etc. The entire boundary here proceeded diagonally, until the northern boundary line met the southern line extending from the waters of Jericho. Thus, Scripture says, “and it met Jericho,” for there it met the first boundary line, leaving Ephraim only a narrow strip extending to the Jordan. We now know Ephraim’s boundaries on all four sides: on the south, from Ataroth-addar to the Jordan; on the north, from Beth-horon to the Jordan; on the west, from south to north, from Ataroth-addar to Beth-horon; and on the east, the two boundary lines met diagonally, leaving only a narrow strip. In addition, Ephraim possessed the territory extending northward from Beth-horon to Michmethath.
text.1_, 15_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: From Tappuah. Scripture now enumerates the cities set apart for the children of Ephraim within Manasseh’s territory on its southern side. The territory westward from Ataroth-addar and below belonged to Manasseh, and Ephraim’s continuous boundary had ended. Thus, the entire western half extending from Beth-horon—apart from the strip reaching to Michmethath—and westward from Ataroth-addar as far as the sea belonged to Manasseh. Only at Tappuah, situated on Manasseh’s southern side, did the cities set apart for Ephraim begin. They are called “set apart” because Ephraim’s continuous territory had already ended, and the land between Ataroth and Tappuah belonged to Manasseh. “The land of Tappuah” means that the district north of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, as explained below (chapter 17), whereas Tappuah itself belonged to Ephraim. From there, the boundary of the cities set apart proceeded westward to the Brook of Kanah—that is, along the brook’s southern side, for its northern side belonged to Manasseh, as explained below (17:10)—and extended as far as the sea. The entire territory south of it belonged to Ephraim, and therefore Gezer also belonged to Ephraim.
text.1_, 15_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And the cities. The verse should be read: “This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Ephraim,” etc., “together with the cities” that were set apart. That is, Scripture has explained both the inheritance of the tribe of Ephraim, which formed one continuous territory in the eastern part of Joseph’s inheritance and whose boundaries were described in verses 5–7, and the cities set apart for Ephraim, which were separated from that territory by Manasseh’s inheritance and lay in the southern part of the western region of Joseph’s inheritance.
text.1_, 15_Chapter, 8_Verse, 1_Comment: All the cities. All the cities in this region, together with their dependent villages. The word mivdalot (“set apart”) has the same meaning as muvdalot, with a shuruk.
text.1_, 15_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And they did not dispossess. For Gezer belonged to Ephraim and was among the cities set apart for them.
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: For he was Joseph’s firstborn. Scripture explains why Manasseh was divided into two halves. Because he was Joseph’s firstborn, he was prominent, renowned among the mighty, and numerous in population. Therefore, Machir his firstborn—who was a man of war—received Gilead and Bashan. The Sages likewise received the tradition that the tribe of Manasseh was divided in two because Joseph had caused the tribes to tear their garments. Scripture explains why Ephraim’s tribe was not divided, but Manasseh’s was: for he was Joseph’s firstborn.
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And it was. Accordingly, the inheritance described here belonged to those who remained. Among them were six male ancestral houses, as indicated by “the males according to their families.” In addition, there were female heirs, as Scripture proceeds to explain regarding Zelophehad.
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Among their father’s brothers. The Sages explained (Bava Batra 118b) that in addition to receiving Zelophehad’s inheritance, since he had been among those who left Egypt, they received together with Zelophehad’s brothers a share in Hepher’s inheritance. Thus, Scripture says, “among their father’s brothers.”
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Ten. Six portions were allotted to the six ancestral houses, while Zelophehad’s daughters received four portions, as the Sages explained (Bava Batra 118a). According to the plain meaning, the ten portions were: 1) from Michmethath to En-tappuah; 2) the land of Tappuah as far as the Brook of Kanah; 3) from the Brook of Kanah northward along the brook as far as the sea; 4) Beth-shean and its towns; 5) Ibleam and its towns; 6) Dor and its towns; 7) En-dor and its towns; 8) Taanach and its towns; 9) Megiddo and its towns; and 10) the three regions. Thus, there were ten districts, each constituting its own distinct tract and measured portion.
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: For the daughters. According to the Sages’ interpretation, Scripture explains that the total of ten included the portions received by Zelophehad’s daughters. According to my interpretation, it explains why so many separate tracts were necessary: because daughters too inherited among the sons.
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: Those who remained. I have established that notar, “that which remains,” denotes what is secondary. Above (verse 2), Scripture called all the children of Manasseh “those who remained,” because Machir, by virtue of his valor, had taken his portion first. Here it calls the children of Machir “those who remained” because they were few in comparison with the six ancestral houses.
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: From Asher. For Asher lay north of Manasseh. The transverse boundary separating Ephraim from Manasseh extended from Ataroth-addar to Beth-horon, except that near Beth-horon a strip belonging to Ephraim extended farther westward as far as Michmethath, as explained above (16:5–6). From Michmethath in the north, the boundary line proceeded from north to south as far as En-tappuah. The entire territory from Ataroth-addar to Tappuah in the south, enclosed within the line running from Michmethath to Tappuah, belonged to Manasseh. Thus, Manasseh’s territory separated Ephraim’s main boundary from the cities set apart for Ephraim.
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: To Manasseh. The northern breadth of Manasseh’s territory, extending from Michmethath to the sea, belonged entirely to Manasseh. The southern breadth, however, extending from Tappuah to the sea, was divided: its northern half belonged to Manasseh, while its southern half belonged to Ephraim, where the cities set apart for Ephraim were located.
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 7_Verse, 1_Comment: The land of Tappuah. The region north of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh.
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 7_Verse, 2_Comment: But Tappuah. The city itself, which lay on the southern side along Manasseh’s border, belonged to the children of Ephraim.
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And it descended. Likewise, the southern boundary, divided between Manasseh and Ephraim, descended as far as the Brook of Kanah. There, south of the brook, these cities belonged to Ephraim among the cities of Manasseh. That is, these were the cities set apart for Ephraim already mentioned above (16:8). The territory north of the brook belonged to Manasseh as far as the Great Sea.
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Southward. That is, as far as the sea the territory remained divided: the region southward belonged to Ephraim, while the region northward belonged to Manasseh, and the sea formed the western boundary of both.
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 9_Verse, 1_Comment: And with Asher. Having described Manasseh’s southern boundary—which initially belonged exclusively to Manasseh from Ataroth-addar to Tappuah, while from Tappuah to the sea it was shared with Ephraim—and having already indicated the general southern boundary shared by the children of Joseph at the beginning of chapter 16, Scripture had not yet described Manasseh’s northern boundary. It therefore states that on the north Manasseh bordered Asher, which lay north of Manasseh, as explained below (19:14). On the east, the line running from north to south along Manasseh’s eastern side began at Michmethath, which projected northward beyond Ephraim’s border. Consequently, above Michmethath lay the territory of Issachar, which bordered Ephraim on the east, as explained below (19:17).
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And there were. In addition, Manasseh possessed further territories within the neighboring tribes of Issachar and Asher.
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 10_Verse, 1_Comment: The three regions. That is, three adjoining districts forming a single province, which was therefore called “the Three Regions.”
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: But they were unable. Manasseh’s territories within Issachar and Asher were given to them only afterward, when Joshua told them, “its extensions shall be yours,” as related in the following verses. Nevertheless, the children of Manasseh were unable to dispossess the inhabitants, etc.
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Why have you given me an inheritance of only one lot? I have already explained that although separate lots were drawn for Ephraim and Manasseh, they nevertheless received one tract and one general territory, which was merely divided into two portions. We also explained (at the beginning of chapter 14) that the lot indicated only where each tribe’s territory would be located; afterward, Joshua could enlarge or reduce its portion according to the tribe’s population. The children of Joseph were as numerous as the population of two tribes, thereby fulfilling Genesis 48:5:
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 13_Verse, 1_Comment: And I am a numerous people. According to the number of individuals, their allotted territories should have been doubled.
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said. He answered them: It is impossible to add to your inheritance by giving you land outside your territory, for Joshua could assign you land only within your own region, not within another tribe’s boundary. But since you are a numerous people, take axes and cut down the forest, and the land now occupied by forest trees will become fields of grain. Thus, he said:
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 14_Verse, 1_Comment: Go up into the forest and clear land for yourself there. That is, there you shall create new land filled with fields and vineyards by cutting down the trees and uprooting them. For Mount Ephraim is too confined for you—it presses upon you, as in Joshua 10:
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 14_Verse, 2_Comment: “And it did not hasten to set for approximately a whole day”)—it awaits you to clear it and make it inhabited land.
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And the children of Joseph said. They answered him: Your proposal that we clear the hill country and convert its forest into inhabited land will not suffice, for the hill country will not be enough for us, since our population is still too numerous.
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 15_Verse, 1_Comment: Second, all the Canaanites dwelling in the valley have iron chariots. They live beyond that hill country, and it would be better for the forest to remain as a barrier between us and them, preventing them from advancing and ravaging the land with their instruments of destruction.
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: And Joshua said. Joshua then saw that it was necessary to enlarge their territory by adding cities from Asher and Issachar—Beth-shean and the other cities that he added to Manasseh, as explained above (verse 11). He said to them: Since you possess two advantages—first, you are a numerous people in quantity; and second, you possess great strength in quality and might—therefore, you shall not have only one lot; that is, you may add territory to your allotted portion.
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: For the hill country. First, because you are a numerous people, the hill country shall be yours to meet your needs; although it is forested, you shall clear it and build inhabited cities there.
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 17_Verse, 1_Comment: Second, because you possess great strength, its extensions shall be yours. I grant you also the territory beyond the hill country—namely, the valley and the cities within the portions of Asher and Issachar that were enumerated above (verse 11). Those tribes will not object to my reducing their inheritance, for the Canaanite possesses iron chariots and is strong in his own right; they themselves cannot dispossess him and will rejoice that you will drive him out. This explains what Scripture stated above (Joshua 17:11):
text.1_, 16_Chapter, 17_Verse, 2_Comment: And Manasseh possessed territories within Asher and Issachar—yet even they did not dispossess the Canaanites from them.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And there remained. Judah and Joseph received their portions first because the royal line and the two Messiahs were destined to arise from them. The remaining tribes had not yet received their portions by lot.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: How long will you be negligent in going to possess it? For Hashem had told Joshua above (13:1–6): “You have grown old,” etc.; “I Myself will dispossess them; only divide it as an inheritance.” Thus, Hashem made their dispossession of the remaining peoples dependent upon the land first being apportioned, so that each tribe would know its own portion. By failing to cast lots for the tribal territories, they were therefore negligent in going to possess the land. Abarbanel explains that until then they had been unwilling to divide the land because they feared that afterward each tribe would refuse to help the others dispossess the inhabitants of their respective portions. They preferred that everyone first conquer the entire land together and divide it only afterward. Judah and Joseph alone requested their portions first because their hearts were courageous among the mighty. Therefore, Joshua said, “How long will you be negligent?”
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Provide for yourselves. Know that there is a distinction between one who causes a lot to fall and one who shoots or casts it. Shooting or casting describes the act from the perspective of its point of origin: a person casts or shoots an object from his hand, without regard to the place upon which it will land. For the latter perspective, Scripture employs the expression “causes to fall”—that is, he causes the lot to fall upon one of those participating in the lottery. Both expressions are therefore appropriate to any lottery. From the perspective of casting the lot from one’s hand, it may be said that he “cast a lot”; from the perspective that his casting necessarily causes it to fall upon one of the participants, it may be said that he “caused the lot to fall”—that is, he brought about its fall. Thus, Scripture says, “They cast pur, that is, the lot” (Esther 3:7), and “they cast lots” (I Chronicles 26:13; Nehemiah 11:1). This applies to a lot whose outcome occurs by chance. With a providential lot, however—such as Joshua’s lotteries, concerning which “the lot is cast into the lap, but its every judgment is from Hashem”—the person merely casts the lot, while Hashem causes it to fall upon the proper place. Therefore, regarding such lotteries Scripture says, “This is the land that shall fall to you as an inheritance” (Numbers 34:2), and “the portions of Manasseh fell” (above, 17:5). It attributes the falling to the lot itself rather than to the person, because the person merely casts it from his hand; he does not truly cause it to fall upon the proper place. Know also that there is a further distinction between one who casts a lot and one who shoots a lot. One who casts does not aim at a particular point; wherever the object falls is where it falls. One who shoots, however, aims at a particular target, like an archer who consistently shoots toward a mark. Accordingly, the language of shooting is inappropriate for ordinary lotteries, since the person cannot aim at the place where the lot will fall, for its fall is accidental and unknown to the one conducting the lottery. Only here (verse 6) does Scripture use the expression, “and I will shoot a lot for you,” because Joshua had in fact received a tradition identifying each tribe’s portion and boundaries, including how and where its lot would fall. Thus, Jacob and Moses, in their blessings, blessed each tribe in accordance with the territory it would inherit: “Zebulun shall dwell by the seashore” (Genesis 49:13); “for they shall draw from the abundance of the seas” (Deuteronomy 33:19); and concerning Joseph, “Blessed by Hashem is his land” (ibid., 13); and similarly with all the tribes. Joshua was therefore truly shooting the lot toward a target, not merely casting it. Although outwardly he appeared to be conducting a lottery without knowing where each lot would fall, in truth he directed it through his Divine inspiration so that it would strike its target—the territory already known to him through tradition. This is the meaning of the verses here. Joshua disclosed this matter to the children of Israel, telling them to appoint three men from each tribe. They would arise, traverse the land, and describe it according to their inheritance. That is, I know that the Divine Spirit will manifest itself through the work of these emissaries, causing them to describe the land in accordance with the inheritance designated by Hashem. Therefore, he said:
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And they shall appear to divide it. The reflexive form may denote an apparent or pretended action, as in “There is one who appears to make himself rich” and “one who appears to make himself poor” (Proverbs 13:7). Thus, it will appear outwardly as though they themselves are dividing the land into seven portions, whereas in truth the division will occur of itself in accordance with Hashem’s will. Scripture then explains why it was to be divided into only seven portions: Judah shall remain, etc. Judah’s boundary, which occupied the Negev, and Joseph’s boundary, which occupied the northern part of the southern region, would not change; each would remain within its existing boundary. Only seven tribes therefore remained to receive their territories by lot.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And you. Nevertheless, you must not rely upon the miracle; rather, you must actually record the land, so that it will appear that you are the ones describing it.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: And I will cast the lot for you here. I too will direct the lot—for, as I have already explained, shooting means striking a deliberately chosen point. That is, the lot will fall upon the place where it truly ought to fall, in accordance with what had already been made known to me by tradition.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: For the Levites have no portion. Scripture explains why the land was divided into only seven portions: Levi had no territorial portion, and three tribes had already inherited east of the Jordan, in addition to Judah and Joseph, who were mentioned in verse 5.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: And Joshua commanded those who went. Although Joshua had informed the children of Israel that every detail of the undertaking was ordained by Hashem, and that the entire determination of the lot and inheritance came from Him, he nevertheless instructed the emissaries to proceed like ordinary people—traveling, acting, and dividing the land through their own free choice.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 7_Verse, 1_Comment: Go, etc., describe it, and return to me. Likewise, he did not tell them that he would direct the lot toward its target, but said, “Here I will cast a lot for you,” because outwardly he would cast it in the ordinary human manner, without knowing or deliberately determining where it would fall. The question that arises here—how they divided the remaining land into seven portions when Simeon’s inheritance was taken from Judah’s territory—will be explained below (chapter 19).
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And he cast. The lot indicated the location of each tribe’s territorial boundaries.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 9_Verse, 1_Comment: And Joshua apportioned it. Afterward, Joshua apportioned the land according to the number of individuals, as I explained above (chapter 14).
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: On the northern side. Along the boundary of the children of Joseph described above (16:1–3).
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 11_Verse, 1_Comment: From the Jordan. Scripture enumerates the boundary from east to west.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 11_Verse, 2_Comment: On the north. It follows that Jericho belonged to Benjamin. Scripture, however, says, “to the slope of Jericho,” because the fertile district of Jericho, situated east of the city, was not given to Benjamin at that time, as we will explain below.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 11_Verse, 3_Comment: And it ascended through the hill country. This was Mount Bethel, which belonged to Benjamin, proceeding westward.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 11_Verse, 4_Comment: And its extremities were. There the straight boundary line ended, and the line turned inward toward the south, as explained above (16:2) and below (verse 22). Above (7:2), Scripture says, “Ai, which is beside Beth-aven, east of Bethel.” Thus, the Beth-aven near Ai was also east of Bethel. We must therefore say that Mount Bethel lay east of the city of Bethel, while the wilderness of Bethel extended westward from Beth-aven. Consequently, Mount Bethel lay east of the wilderness of Beth-aven, even though the city of Bethel itself lay west of Beth-aven; for otherwise, the verse there implies that Bethel was near Ai and, correspondingly, near Beth-aven.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: And it passed from there. The boundary turned inward toward the south.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 12_Verse, 1_Comment: To the southern slope of Luz. Thus, Luz lay outside the boundary line and belonged to Joseph.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 12_Verse, 2_Comment: It is Bethel. This was the place that Jacob named Bethel, not the Bethel near Ai, which belonged to Benjamin. When I Chronicles 7:28 states that Bethel belonged to Ephraim, it refers to Bethel-Luz.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 12_Verse, 3_Comment: Upon the mountain to the south. It follows that Lower Beth-horon belonged to the children of Joseph. Therefore, Scripture says above (16:3), “as far as the border of Lower Beth-horon.”
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And the boundary curved around. The boundary encircled the mountain on three of its sides, which is the meaning of ve-ta’ar, “and it curved around.”
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 13_Verse, 1_Comment: And it turned, etc., from the mountain. At the mountain’s lower slopes, the boundary turned southward in the shape of the letter dalet. The line then proceeded from north to south and ended at Kiriath-baal, which belonged to Judah. This also defines Benjamin’s western border from north to south: it extended from Mount Beth-horon at the northwestern corner to Kiriath-jearim at the southwestern corner.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And the southern side. Scripture enumerates the southern boundary from west to east.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 14_Verse, 1_Comment: From the southern edge of Kiriath-jearim, as stated above (15:9) and explained there (verse 10).
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 14_Verse, 2_Comment: And it went out to the spring. The boundary extended southward and widened there. For in describing Judah’s border, Scripture says that it “went out” from the spring of the waters of Nephtoah toward the cities of Mount Ephron, where it extended northward.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: To the edge, etc. The eastern edge.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 15_Verse, 1_Comment: Southward. It follows that the slope of the Jebusite—that is, Jerusalem—belonged to Benjamin.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: And it curved around northward and went out to En-shemesh. The boundary line extending from En-rogel to En-shemesh departed southward from its straight course; therefore, Scripture says, “and it went out.” Upon reaching En-shemesh, it encircled En-shemesh on three sides; therefore, it says, “and it curved around northward.” It then went out southward a second time, as I explained above (15:7).
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: And it passed. As I explained above in the description of the inheritance of the children of Judah.
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: This is the inheritance of the children of Benjamin according to its boundaries. In describing the inheritance of each of the tribes in chapter 19, Scripture says, “This is the inheritance of the children of Simeon according to their families,” and it uses the same formulation for Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan. Concerning Judah, however, it says (15:12), “This is the boundary of the children of Judah all around,” and later (15:20), “This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Judah.” In Judah’s case, Scripture initially described only the boundary, not the inheritance itself, because the children of Simeon later received part of Judah’s inheritance. Accordingly, verses 1–12 enumerate only Judah’s border and territorial limits, and therefore Scripture says, “This is the boundary of Judah.” Beginning with verse 20, it enumerates the cities individually and therefore says, “This is the inheritance.” Concerning Benjamin, however, Scripture describes both the border and the inheritance, since no other tribe received territory within it. It therefore says, “This is the inheritance,” referring to the individual cities, and “according to its boundaries,” referring to the territorial limits. With the other tribes, whose borders were not described in complete detail and whose cities alone were enumerated, Scripture simply says, “This is the inheritance.”
text.1_, 17_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: Fourteen cities. Yet when counted individually, only twelve are found. The commentators explain that Zela-haeleph represents two cities, as does Gibeath-kiriath. In my opinion, however, Scripture omitted from the detailed list Anathoth and Almon, which are enumerated among Benjamin’s Levitical cities (21:18). It likewise appears that Zela-haeleph was a single city, since Zela is vocalized with a patach, indicating the construct state; the same applies to Gibeath-kiriath.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Beer-sheba. Mentioned above (16:28). There was another Beer-sheba belonging to Judah (I Kings 19:3), which is not mentioned among the boundaries of the land.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: And Sheba. It is not mentioned there, nor in I Chronicles 4:28. And Moladah. Mentioned above (15:26).
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 2_Verse, 1_Comment: And Balah. This is Baalah, mentioned there (verse 29), and Bilhah in Chronicles (ibid.).
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And Eltolad. Mentioned there (verse 30), and called Tolad in Chronicles.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 3_Verse, 1_Comment: And Bethul. This is Chesil, mentioned there in the same verse, and it is called Bethuel in Chronicles.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Ziklag. Mentioned in both places; see what I wrote concerning it above.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 4_Verse, 1_Comment: And Beth-marcaboth and Hazar-susah. They are not mentioned in the account of Judah’s inheritance. In Chronicles, they are called Beth-marcaboth and Hazar-susim.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And Beth-lebaoth and Sharuhen. These are Lebaoth and Shilhim (there, verse 32). Chronicles instead calls them Beth-biri and Shaaraim, reflecting a still greater change in pronunciation.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: Thirteen cities. Yet when counted individually, fourteen are found. It is difficult to say that Beer-sheba and Sheba were one city, for Scripture’s practice here is to enumerate three cities in each verse and place the remaining cities in the final verse. If Beer-sheba and Sheba were one city, it should therefore have listed Beer-sheba, Sheba, Moladah, and Hazar-shual in a single verse, as Chronicles indeed does. Rather, as I proved above (15:32), Beth-lebaoth and Sharuhen were one city. The meaning is Beth-lebaoth together with the area extending before the city. Therefore, it is called above “Shilhim,” related to the expression “Your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates” (Song of Songs 4:13), referring to the cultivated fields extending before the city. Here it is called “Sharuhen,” because those fields subsequently ceased to exist, leaving only an extension attached to the city. By the time the Book of Chronicles was written, gates had been constructed there before the city, and it was therefore called “Shaaraim.” Ziklag was counted among Simeon’s cities only until the days of David, for afterward it was given to the kings of Judah, as stated in I Samuel 27:6. This explains the statement in Chronicles (ibid., verse 31): “These were their cities until the reign of David.”
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: Ether and Ashan. Mentioned there (verse 42). Chronicles enumerates Etam, Ain, Rimmon, Tochen, and Ashan. Etam is Ether, while Tochen was an additional city built later.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: As far as Baalath. That is, the areas surrounding the cities extending as far as Baalah contained settlements called Beer and Ramath-negev. Therefore, Chronicles mentions only “as far as Baal” without listing them separately.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And it was. Zebulun’s territory lay at the northwestern extremity of the Land of Israel. Its boundary began at a point in the land’s northwest, where the city of Sarid was situated.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And it ascended. Scripture enumerates the western boundary from north to south.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 10_Verse, 1_Comment: It ascended westward. Toward the sea. On this side, it reached Dabbesheth and reached the brook east of Jokneam, for Jokneam belonged to Zebulun (below, 21:34). The brook lay west of Jokneam and marked the end of this boundary at Zebulun’s southwestern corner. Some identify it as the Kishon River.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And it turned back. Scripture now enumerates the northern boundary from west to east.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 11_Verse, 1_Comment: At the border of Chisloth-tabor. There this boundary line ended. From there it extended southward along the eastern side, proceeding from north to south toward Daberath, which belonged to Issachar. At that point Zebulun bordered Issachar on the east, for both Tabor and Daberath belonged to Issachar. From there, it ascended to Japhia, likewise proceeding from north to south.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: And from there it passed eastward. Along the eastern side, the boundary passed the city of Gath-hepher, the hometown of the prophet Jonah, and the city of Eth-kazin. And it went out. From there it extended eastward to the city of Rimmon, curved around it on three sides, and then turned back from east to west toward the city of Neah. It was called Rimmon-hamethoar, “Rimmon that was curved around,” because Zebulun’s boundary encircled it; the city projected eastward from the boundary like a horn.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And it turned. The boundary turned around the city of Neah on two sides, in the shape of the letter dalet, while Neah itself remained outside the boundary line. It then passed north of Hannathon, which likewise lay outside the boundary. Here Scripture enumerates the southern boundary from east to west.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 13_Verse, 1_Comment: And its extremities were at the Valley of Iphtah-el. There this boundary line ended.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: There the boundary turned inward and proceeded through Kattath—which is Kitron, mentioned in Judges 1:30—as far as Bethlehem. From there it extended opposite the initial boundary, namely the brook east of Jokneam. Thus, Zebulun’s boundaries on all four sides have been described.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 14_Verse, 1_Comment: Twelve. These were Sarid, Maralah, Jokneam, Japhia, Gath-hepher, Eth-kazin, Rimmon, and the five cities listed in verse 15. Concerning Dabbesheth, Scripture says that the boundary “reached” it, indicating that it was not included within Zebulun’s territory. I have already explained that Daberath belonged to Issachar; and the Valley of Iphtah-el was a valley, not a city.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: To Issachar. Issachar’s inheritance lay north of Ephraim and east of Manasseh. The projection of Ephraim’s territory that extended along its northwestern side as far as Michmethath lay southwest of Issachar, as explained above. Michmethath was opposite Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim (17:7), while the Valley of Jezreel lay in the plain opposite the hill country of Ephraim, as is evident from the passage above (ibid., verse 16). Thus, Scripture says:
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: And their boundary was toward Jezreel. This was Issachar’s southern boundary on its western side. The cities of Jezreel and Chesulloth stood at the southwestern corner of its territory. From there, the boundary line turned from south to north along its western side, encompassing the places listed in verses 19–21. When it reached the northern side and proceeded from west to east, then:
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: The boundary reached Tabor. This was opposite Chisloth-tabor in Zebulun’s territory, mentioned above (verse 12). Alternatively, Tabor may be the name of a city, as stated in I Chronicles 6:62: “Tabor and its pasturelands.”
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 21_Verse, 1_Comment: And the extremities of their boundaries were. That is, the two boundary lines on the north and south both ended at the Jordan. Below we will explain that Issachar’s territory did not actually extend to the Jordan itself; rather, the boundary lines from the two sides met one another there, as with Joseph’s territory. The area immediately adjoining the Jordan belonged to Naphtali, as will be explained.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: And their boundary was. Asher’s territory lay alongside Manasseh’s border, as explained above (17:11), and west of Issachar’s border. Scripture first enumerates its southern boundary from east to west, along Manasseh’s border: there were Helkath and Hali. The southern boundary began at Helkath, which stood at Asher’s southeastern corner.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 24_Verse, 1_Comment: Beten and Achshaph. All these cities, as far as Mishal, stood along the southern boundary in the order listed here, from east to west.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: And it reached Carmel by the sea. Where the boundary ended at the Great Sea, it terminated beside Carmel on the south, while Shihor-libnath, near the sea, lay on Asher’s northern side. Thus, Asher’s southern boundary extended from Helkath to the sea near Carmel, while its western boundary followed the sea from Carmel to Shihor-libnath. The commentators write that Shihor-libnath is the name of a river. To distinguish it from the River of Egypt, which is called simply Shihor, this one was called Shihor-libnath. It is now known as the Belus. In ancient times, materials for making glass were found there, as related in the chronicles of the kingdom of Tyre, and it may have been called Libnath after white glass.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: And it turned back. From Shihor-libnath, which stood at the northwestern corner, the boundary turned from west to east. This describes Asher’s northern border, which extended from Shihor to Beth-dagon and afterward reached Zebulun, whose territory lay north of Asher. Thus, Scripture says, “and the Valley of Iphtah-el to the north,” meaning that it lay north of Asher’s boundary. Scripture already explained (verse 14) that the Valley of Iphtah-el lay on Zebulun’s southern boundary, where Zebulun bordered Asher. Afterward came Beth-emek and Neiel, which likewise stood along that line from west to east.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 26_Verse, 1_Comment: And it went out. After Neiel, the boundary line extended from south to north as far as the northern extremity of the Land of Israel, where Cabul was located. Thus, Scripture says, “on the left,” meaning on the left side of the Land of Israel—that is, the north. Accordingly, the line passed along the entire eastern boundary of Zebulun. Some explain that Cabul was the city that Solomon gave to Hiram, who called the surrounding region the Land of Cabul after its capital city, Cabul (I Kings 9:12). (28) And Ebron. There, in the north of the Land of Israel, the boundary passed Ebron and Rehob as far as Great Sidon, which likewise belonged to Asher, as stated: “Asher did not dispossess the inhabitants of Acco or the inhabitants of Sidon” (Judges 1:31). Acco lies in the north of the Land of Israel, as explained at the beginning of tractate Gittin. This was not the Sidon near Tyre, but another Sidon.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: And the boundary turned back. At Sidon, the northern boundary ended, with Sidon situated at Asher’s northeastern corner. The boundary then turned from north to south, marking Asher’s eastern side as far as Ramah and the fortified city of Tyre, which stood at Asher’s southeastern corner; the fortified city of Tyre itself belonged to Naphtali. This was not the great city of Tyre on the seacoast, which, as is known, had not yet been built at that time. Some explain that it was a fortress built upon a high rock or crag.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 28_Verse, 1_Comment: And the boundary turned back to Hosah. From there, the boundary began to turn from east to west, proceeding toward Hosah, which lay to the west, and from there to the region of Achzib.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 28_Verse, 2_Comment: And from the region of Achzib its extremities were at the sea. That is, the boundary proceeded toward Helkath and from there to Carmel by the sea. Thus, Scripture has described Asher’s boundaries on all four sides.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 28_Verse, 3_Comment: And Ummah. From Achzib southward were these additional cities:
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 28_Verse, 4_Comment: Twenty-two cities. These were the four cities listed in verse 25; Elimelech, Amad, and Mishal; Beth-dagon, Beth-emek, Neiel, and Cabul; the five cities in verse 28; Ramah, Hosah, and Achzib—for the fortified city of Tyre belonged to Naphtali—and the three cities listed in verse 30.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 32_Verse, 0_Comment: And their boundary was. Every part of the Land of Israel that still remained after the aforementioned divisions belonged to the children of Naphtali, except for Dan’s territory in the west. Along the Jordan, the entire width of the land facing the river remained unassigned. For we have already explained (16:7) that Joseph’s eastern boundary lines met one another diagonally near the waters of Jericho and did not extend as far as the Jordan. Likewise, although Benjamin’s eastern boundary ascended from the Jordan toward the northern slope of Jericho, Benjamin possessed only the territory from Jericho onward. As the Sages said (Sifrei on Numbers, paragraph 81), the fertile district of Jericho was not apportioned among the tribes, and Benjamin did not receive it until the days of David or Solomon, when the Temple was built within Benjamin’s portion. Similarly, Issachar, whose territory came after Benjamin’s and concerning whom Scripture says, “the extremities of their boundary were at the Jordan,” did not extend to the Jordan itself. Thus, the entire eastern strip of the Land of Israel along the Jordan remained for Naphtali; see what I wrote above (16:6). This explains the statement here that Naphtali bordered Judah at the Jordan toward the sunrise. Accordingly, the eastern side of Naphtali’s territory extended along the entire length of the Jordan, while opposite it, on the western side, its boundary extended from Heleph, from the oak at Zaanannim, as far as Lakkum. All this described its western side, while on the east, “its extremities were at the Jordan,” for the Jordan bounded its eastern territory.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 33_Verse, 0_Comment: And it turned back. On the northern side, Naphtali’s boundary extended from east to west as far as Aznoth-tabor. And it went out. It extended still farther northward until reaching the northern part of the Land of Israel, where Hukkok was situated. Zebulun’s northern boundary had ascended from Sarid to the border of Chisloth-tabor and from there extended southward toward Daberath, which belonged to Issachar, as explained above (verse 12). Consequently, the area to the left of the line running directly toward Chisloth-tabor, extending as far as the extreme north of the Land of Israel, remained unassigned; likewise, the region from Daberath northward to the northern extremity of the land remained unassigned. Naphtali’s boundary descended into this territory and encompassed everything remaining north of Zebulun as far as the northern extremity of the Land of Israel. This explains the statement here that Naphtali bordered Zebulun on the south. We have also explained (verses 27–28) that Asher’s inheritance included a strip east of Zebulun extending to the northern extremity of the Land of Israel, and that this boundary turned from Ramah to the fortified city of Tyre, proceeding from north to south. Both Ramah and the fortified city of Tyre belonged to Naphtali (verses 35–36). Accordingly, as Naphtali’s boundary descended westward, it passed through Ramah and the fortified city of Tyre from south to north, with Asher lying west of Naphtali. Thus, Scripture says that Naphtali bordered Asher on the west. It follows that the cities mentioned along Asher’s northern boundary were not situated at the absolute northern extremity of the Land of Israel; beyond them lay an additional strip belonging to Naphtali, through which Naphtali’s boundary descended and encircled Zebulun on the north. Otherwise, it would be impossible for Naphtali’s boundary to extend north of Zebulun without interruption.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 37_Verse, 0_Comment: Nineteen cities. These were the fifteen cities enumerated among the fortified cities, together with Adami-nekeb, Jabneel, Lakkum, and Hukkok, making nineteen in all. Heleph and the oak were names of places, not cities.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 40_Verse, 0_Comment: And the boundary of their inheritance was. Dan received the western portion of Benjamin’s general region, for Benjamin had received only the eastern half of the territory extending from east to west. Dan received the western half, together with the area where Judah’s territory extended northward and thereby narrowed Benjamin’s western boundary.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 46_Verse, 0_Comment: And it went out. Because the tribe of Dan inherited at the extremity of the Land of Israel along the frontier, they were unable to dispossess the Amorites, as stated in Judges 1:34. Thus, Scripture says, “the territory of the children of Dan went out from them.” That is, they did not take possession of their territory, because the Amorites would not allow them to descend into the valley. This is explained in Judges 18: “For until that day no inheritance had fallen to him among the tribes of Israel.” This means that Dan’s inheritance did not fall within the territories of the other tribes, but at the western extremity along the frontier. Therefore, the children of Dan went up and fought against Leshem, which lay in the east of the Land of Israel. This occurred during the period of the Judges, and Leshem is the city called Laish there.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 48_Verse, 0_Comment: And they finished assigning the inheritances. This refers to the first division, which was conducted by lot. As we explained above (chapter 14), there were two stages of division. First came the lottery, which determined the territory of each tribe; concerning this, Scripture says here, “And they finished assigning the inheritances.” Second came the apportionment according to population, which Joshua performed by enlarging or reducing each tribe’s portion according to its size. Concerning this, verse 51 says, “And they finished dividing the land.” Immediately after the lots were drawn, but before the land was divided according to population, they gave Joshua an inheritance. Scripture explains why:
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 49_Verse, 0_Comment: They gave it to him according to the word of Hashem. Therefore, Joshua’s inheritance was assigned in conjunction with the lottery, which likewise operated according to the word of Hashem. They did not wait until the second stage of division, which was conducted by Joshua, for Joshua would then have possessed the authority to assign the land to himself. This is the meaning of the statement in Bava Batra 121b: “‘Only by lot shall the land be divided’—this excludes Joshua and Caleb.” Although the detailed apportionment according to the number of individuals was not determined by lot—and for this reason Raavad asks in Shittah Mekubbetzet on Bava Batra 121b: According to his own view that only the tribal territories were determined by lot, not the individual portions, why was it necessary to exclude Joshua and Caleb, who were private individuals?—nevertheless, before the second division had been completed and the share due to each individual had been determined, it was impossible to assign portions to Joshua and Caleb in advance without a special apportionment. Their portions therefore had to be assigned according to the word of Hashem. One might consequently have thought that this too was done by lot. Scripture therefore explains that they gave Joshua the city that he requested, something impossible through a lottery and possible only through the direction of a prophet. Likewise, Caleb received Hebron at his own request and before the detailed apportionment.
text.1_, 18_Chapter, 50_Verse, 0_Comment: And they finished dividing. This was explained in verse 50.
text.1_, 19_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Designate. The Sifrei (Parashat Masei) explains that Israel was not obligated to set apart the cities of refuge until after the conquest and settlement of the land, as it is written: “When Hashem your God cuts off the nations,” etc., “and you possess their land,” etc. (Deuteronomy 19:1). Therefore, Hashem did not command Joshua concerning them until the division of the land had been completed.
text.1_, 19_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Unintentionally, without knowledge. In the portion of Masei (Numbers 35:11), Scripture says “unintentionally,” whereas in the portion of Shoftim (Deuteronomy 19:4) it says “without knowledge.” The Sages explained (Makkot 7b): “‘Unintentionally’ excludes one who acted deliberately; ‘without knowledge’ excludes one who intended his action.” Therefore, both expressions are used here. God willing, I have explained the laws of this passage in my commentary on the Torah.
text.1_, 19_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And they consecrated. Regarding the question of how the two and a half tribes could have provided three cities of refuge—the same number as the nine and a half tribes—Ramban answers that the Levitical cities also afforded refuge. There were forty-two ordinary Levitical cities, making forty-eight together with the six cities of refuge. Thus, each tribe provided an average of four cities, amounting to ten cities from the two and a half tribes; and they indeed provided this number, as stated in chapter 21. If one asks why the two and a half tribes were not nevertheless required to provide more Levitical cities, since the ordinary Levitical cities afforded refuge only to one who entered them knowingly, Ramban answers that most Levites dwelt in the Land of Israel, since residence there was more fitting for them because of their service in the House of God.
text.1_, 19_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: The designated cities. The word mu’adah follows the same grammatical pattern as musadah, “founded,” indicating that these cities were specially designated as gathering places for anyone who had unintentionally killed a person.
text.1_, 20_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And the lot came out. The command was: “From the numerous you shall take more, and from the few you shall take less” (Numbers 35:8). Accordingly, Judah and Simeon provided nine cities, most of them from Judah, for only the city of Ain is found within Simeon’s inheritance, since the portion of the children of Judah was larger than theirs; whereas Naphtali provided only three cities. Just as in the apportionment of the tribal inheritances the lot first determined the general territory of each tribe, after which Joshua apportioned the land according to the tribe’s greater or smaller population, based upon his assessment, as explained above (chapter 14), so too here the lot first determined the territory from which each Levitical family would receive its cities. It assigned the sons of Aaron their territory among three tribes—Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin—for the names of these three tribes shone forth from the Urim and Thummim when the lot of the sons of Aaron was drawn. Those conducting the lottery divided the children of Levi into four groups: the sons of Aaron, the remaining sons of Kohath, the sons of Gershon, and the sons of Merari. They then cast lots for each group to determine from which tribes its cities would be taken. The lots came out appropriately, in accordance with each group’s degree of sacred distinction. Just as among the organs of the body, every organ situated closer to the heart is more distinguished and possesses a purer constitution, so the sons of Aaron, who were closest to the Tabernacle and the Temple, received their lot within Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin, whose territories surrounded the Temple. For this reason, they also remained continually attached to the kingdom of the House of David. Next in rank were the remaining sons of Kohath, who likewise dwelt close to the heart and were charged with the sacred service: they carried upon their shoulders the Ark, the Table, and the sacred vessels. Their portion therefore fell within Ephraim, Dan, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. Joseph’s inheritance adjoined Benjamin’s inheritance, while Dan’s inheritance lay behind Benjamin’s; thus, they sheltered the Temple beneath their wings and remained close to its territory. After them came the sons of Gershon, who carried the Tent of Meeting, its curtains, and its covering. These correspond to the flesh that covers the inner organs surrounding the heart. They received cities from Issachar and Asher, both of which lay beyond Joseph—Issachar to its east and Asher to its west—and from Naphtali, which likewise adjoined them and bordered the territories of Benjamin and Joseph on the east along the length of the Jordan, together with Manasseh’s inheritance in Bashan. Although that territory lay across the Jordan, it shared a certain connection with Manasseh’s other half in the Land of Israel and was related to it by virtue of their constituting one tribe. The sons of Merari, who occupied the outermost position and carried the Tabernacle’s boards, bars, pillars, and sockets—corresponding to the body’s skin and bones—received cities from Reuben and Gad outside the Land of Israel and from Zebulun, which lay at the far northwestern extremity of the Land of Israel. Concerning all the other families, Scripture says that they received cities “by lot”; only regarding the sons of Merari does it omit this phrase (verse 7). It also says “to the sons of Merari” without the conjunction “and,” because once the sons of Merari remained last, no separate lottery was necessary: they necessarily received cities from the three tribes upon which no lot had yet fallen. Therefore, Scripture introduces them without the conjunction “and,” since they did not receive their cities through a lot cast specifically for them. After the lottery had determined the general territory of each family, Joshua apportioned and designated the particular cities according to the greater or smaller population of each tribe. Therefore, Scripture first says, “The lot came out for the families of the Kohathites,” etc., and relates how the lottery assigned each family its proper territory. Afterward, it says:
text.1_, 20_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: And the children of Israel gave, etc. Afterward, they assigned the specific cities according to the greater or smaller population of each tribe, giving larger or smaller cities accordingly. Thus, the words “and they gave,” etc., “the cities,” refer to the particular assignment of the individual cities.
text.1_, 20_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And they gave them Kiriath-arba, etc.—and to the sons of Aaron, etc. Scripture seeks to explain why Judah and Simeon provided nine cities, whereas every other pair of tribes provided only eight—four cities from each tribe, except for Naphtali. Since Caleb had received an especially large personal portion, he too was required to give a city to the Levites, as stated: “Each man shall give of his cities to the Levites in proportion to the inheritance he possesses” (Numbers 35:8). Hebron possessed so many villages and fields that, proportionately, Caleb himself was required to contribute the equivalent of one-fourth of a tribe’s contribution—namely, one city. He therefore gave Hebron, while the city’s fields and villages remained his. This introduction explains that, from Judah’s inheritance, the Levites received one city separately from Caleb’s personal portion. Judah and Simeon then provided eight additional cities, making nine together with Hebron. Thus, Scripture says, “And to the sons of Aaron the priest they gave,” meaning together with Caleb’s contribution. Although most of these cities were taken from Judah rather than Simeon, this was because Simeon inherited within Judah’s territory, as explained above, so the two tribes formed a single inheritance.
text.1_, 20_Chapter, 33_Verse, 0_Comment: Those who remained. This may be understood according to what was explained above (verse 4): the sons of Merari are called “those who remained,” meaning that they were secondary in relation to the tribe of Levi as a whole, like the skin and bones that form an outer covering around the fruit and the heart. Similarly, the other Kohathite families are called “those who remained” in comparison with the sons of Aaron, the priests, as stated in verse 20. The sons of Merari are also called “those who remained” because they were left after the lots had first been drawn for the sons of Kohath and Gershon, so no separate lot needed to be drawn for them, as explained above (verse 4). Therefore, Scripture repeats the designation “those who remained” concerning them in verse 38, for they were “those who remained” from both of these perspectives.
text.1_, 20_Chapter, 40_Verse, 0_Comment: And He gave. After recounting the conquest and division of the land, Scripture states that seven things were fulfilled for Israel. First, “He gave”: He gave them the land as a gift, as He had promised the patriarchs. Second, “and they possessed it”: this refers to the dispossession and conquest of their enemies during the seven years of conquest, for yerushah denotes the transfer of an inheritance from the possession of the one who formerly held it into the possession of the heir. Third, “and they dwelt in it”: during the seven years in which the land was divided, each person took possession of his own portion. (42) Fourth, “And Hashem gave them rest on every side”: the wars against their enemies ceased. Fifth, “not a man stood”: even when their enemies fought against them, they could not remain standing, but fell before them. We have already explained the distinction between “no man positioned himself before them” and “no man stood before them.” The first means that no one challenged them to battle at all; this was not the case here, for kings did come and wage war against them. The second means that one who positioned himself to fight could not maintain his position, for “they bowed and fell.” Sixth, their enemies’ defeat was not natural; rather, “Hashem delivered all their enemies into their hand” through miracle and Providence. (43) Seventh, “Not one thing failed.” All the other benefits and successes that Hashem had promised them in the Torah through Moses likewise came to pass.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: You have observed. The condition that Moses made with the children of Reuben and Gad required only that they march armed before their brethren until the conquest was completed. Moses, however, added a command that they remain there until after the division of the land as well, as explained above (1:13). Thus, Joshua said, “You have observed everything that Moses commanded you.” Second, “and you have obeyed my voice.” He now explains what he meant by “You have observed everything that Moses commanded you”: namely, that:
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: You have not forsaken your brethren these many days. That is, throughout the seven years of conquest and the seven years of division. The words “and you have obeyed my voice” mean, “and you have kept the charge of Hashem’s commandment.” Joshua had no authority to impose new commandments upon them beyond the Torah of Moses; he could only issue instructions that safeguarded the Torah’s commandments—that is, protective boundaries and safeguards. Thus, Scripture says, “You have kept the charge of Hashem’s commandment.” (4) And now Hashem has given rest. As stated, “until Hashem gives rest to your brethren as He has to you” (Deuteronomy 3:20). (5) Only. Since their territory was separated from the Land of Israel, they required greater vigilance there.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(7–9) Why does Scripture repeat that Joshua sent them away and blessed them, and then again that he sent them away and blessed them? What relevance does the statement that Moses had given half of Manasseh an inheritance in Bashan have here, when this was already known? And why does it say that they departed from Shiloh? It should first have stated that Joshua summoned them to Shiloh.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: And also when he sent them away. Since the tribe of Manasseh had been divided into two halves, they required an additional, separate blessing. (8) With abundant possessions. For the children of Reuben and Gad had possessed abundant livestock, but the half-tribe of Manasseh had not.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 6_Verse, 2_Comment: Divide it. That is, divide it with your brethren who remained behind to guard your cities, for only forty thousand of them crossed the Jordan (above, chapter 4), fewer than one-third of their number in the portion of Pinchas. Abarbanel explains that the spoils captured by the children of Israel were certainly divided among the tribes. The children of Reuben and Gad could therefore carry home the spoils they had acquired. The portion of the half-tribe of Manasseh, however, was intermingled with that of the tribe’s other half, so Joshua had to instruct them to divide the spoils with their brethren. This is why Scripture first states that Moses had given one half of the tribe of Manasseh an inheritance in Bashan, etc. Consequently, although Joshua had sent them away, etc., he nevertheless had to tell them: “Return with abundant possessions,” etc.; “divide the spoil of your enemies with your brethren”—that is, with the other half of the same tribe. These are Abarbanel’s words. Accordingly, the phrase “they returned and departed” may mean that because the half-tribe of Manasseh had to remain in Shiloh while the spoils were divided, the children of Reuben and Gad also waited for them; afterward, they all departed from there together.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And they returned. Joshua summoned them to his city, Timnath-serah, in the hill country of Ephraim, and sent them away from there. They did not proceed eastward from there to cross the Jordan; instead, they went to Shiloh, which lay at the northern edge of Joseph’s inheritance, to pray there at the Sanctuary of Hashem and to take leave of the Israelites assembled there. This demonstrated that their hearts had not withdrawn from the sanctity of Hashem’s Tabernacle or from the unity of the Rock of Israel—the opposite of what Israel later suspected concerning the altar. Therefore, Scripture precisely says, “from the children of Israel, from Shiloh.”
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(10–12) Why does Scripture redundantly say, “the region of the Jordan that is in the land of Canaan”? Likewise, why does it say, “opposite the land of Canaan, in the region of the Jordan, on the side belonging to the children of Israel”? And why does it state twice, “The children of Israel heard”?
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 9_Verse, 1_Comment: Which is in the land of Canaan. Scripture relates that they built the altar on the Canaanite side, west of the Jordan. This testified that they did not intend to separate from Israel, for had that been their intention, they would have built it on the eastern side. Second, the altar’s structure testified that it had been built only for appearance, not for burnt offerings or sacrifices: it was exceedingly high and had no steps, demonstrating that its builders did not intend to offer sacrifices upon it, but only to make it a sign, memorial, and marker.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And they heard. The children of Israel heard and concluded that they had built an altar resembling the well-known altar at Shiloh—that is, patterned after it—and that they had built it opposite the land of Canaan in order to draw the hearts of the children of Israel on this side of the Jordan toward that altar as well.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And they heard. That is, because of this, they did not judge them favorably but accepted the accusation that judged them guilty. And they assembled for war. That is, they gathered an army in case it became necessary to fight; therefore, Scripture does not use the preposition “against.”
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: And they sent. To warn them first, in the hope that they might repent. Phinehas. Since their act appeared to involve both sacrilege against Hashem and treachery against Israel, they sent Phinehas to rebuke them concerning the offense against Hashem.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 12_Verse, 1_Comment: And ten leaders. To remonstrate with them concerning the offense against Israel.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(16–20) What sin was there in this altar that caused Israel to prepare for war against them? The verses are repetitive: first they cite the sin of Peor as evidence, and afterward the sin of Achan. What did they intend by their great prolixity, multiplying words without end?
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 15_Verse, 1_Comment: What is this trespass? Since they did not know whether the altar had been built for idolatry or for offering sacrifices to Hashem, they argued against both possibilities. First, if it was intended for idolatry, what is this trespass? It is surely a grievous trespass to turn away today from following Hashem—today, while all the signs and wonders He performed for you are still before your eyes. Nor have you merely turned away from Him passively; you have committed an overt act by building yourselves an altar for idolatry. This constitutes rebellion today against Hashem—open rebellion, transgression, and denial of Hashem.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: Was it too little? They said: If you ask, “Why do you contend on Hashem’s behalf?” know that your act will bring harm upon the entire nation, just as the sin of Peor caused two forms of harm. First, it caused lasting harm for generations, from which we have not purified ourselves to this day. Second, it caused immediate harm, for the plague struck the congregation of Hashem, and those who had not sinned were punished because of those who had.
