text.1_, 21_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: And you. Accordingly, if you turn away today from following Hashem and repeat this folly, the same two forms of harm will result. First, you will rebel today against Hashem, which is itself an immediate and exceedingly grave evil. Second, tomorrow He will be angry with the entire congregation of Israel: His anger will fall not upon you alone, but upon the whole congregation of Israel; nor will it last only today, but also “tomorrow”—that is, it will continue for a long time.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: But. Second, they now argued against the other possibility—that the altar had been built for Hashem. If you say that the land of your possession is impure and therefore unfit for offering sacrifices, and that you consequently built this altar on the western side of the Jordan to offer sacrifices to Hashem upon it, this too constitutes rebellion: against Hashem, Who commanded that sacrifices be offered not upon a private altar but only at His Tabernacle; and against Israel, because it divides their collective unity, which requires them all to serve the one God together in one house rather than splitting into two groups with two altars. Thus, they said, “Cross over for yourselves into the land of Hashem’s possession, where Hashem’s Tabernacle dwells,” so that you may unite with us both in possessing the holy land and in worshiping Hashem at His Tabernacle and House.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 18_Verse, 1_Comment: Do not rebel against Hashem, and do not cause us to rebel. For this would constitute rebellion both against Hashem and against Israel. Abarbanel explains the passage similarly. Nowhere else is the verb “to rebel” joined to the direct-object marker et, except here, because rebellion ordinarily applies only to a servant rebelling against his master, not to one half of a nation rebelling against the other. This rebellion, however, would create a division affecting both sides, so that we too would be drawn into rebellion against Israel’s unity as the nation became divided. Since you would cause separation and rebellion on our side as well, Scripture says, “and do not cause us to rebel.”
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: Did not. If you ask, “Why do you contend on Hashem’s behalf?” know that this too will bring collective harm upon the entire nation, as experience demonstrated with Achan, who trespassed against the devoted property. He sinned against property consecrated to the Sanctuary, for the silver and gold he stole were sacred to the Sanctuary. This resembles your own sin, which is likewise directed against the Sanctuary. Consider what happened to us: wrath fell upon the entire congregation of Israel, and he was not the only man to perish for his sin. Because a single member of the nation sinned, wrath and the concealment of the Divine countenance came upon the entire nation, and Hashem’s Providence departed from them. Consequently, Achan was not the only one to die, because this was not a directly inflicted punishment, in which case only the sinner himself would have been punished; rather, it was the concealment of the Divine countenance from the entire community, as explained above (7:12–13). If one man caused the Divine countenance to be hidden from the entire community, how much more so now, when the sinners comprise two and a half tribes, will Hashem withdraw His Providence from the entire congregation.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(21) Why did they not answer Phinehas?
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 20_Verse, 1_Comment: And they spoke to the heads, etc. They did not respond directly to Phinehas, who had come to rebuke them for their presumed trespass against Hashem, because if they cleared themselves of the lesser accusation of treachery against Israel, the first and graver accusation would automatically fall away.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(22–29) How, in their view, would this altar prevent the western tribes from saying in the future to their descendants, “You have no portion in Hashem”? On the contrary, just as this altar aroused suspicion against them now, it would arouse the same suspicion in future generations, who might cite it as proof that the eastern tribes had no portion in the altar at Shiloh. Why did they repeat, “God, Hashem—God, Hashem”? Why did they repeat both “if in rebellion” and “if in trespass”? And the entire lengthy statement, in which they repeated the matter several times, requires explanation.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 21_Verse, 1_Comment: God. In response to the suspicion that the altar was intended for idolatry, they declared, “God, God, Hashem”—there is no other besides Him. In response to the suspicion that it was intended for offering sacrifices to Hashem, they said: “God, God, Hashem—He knows” the truth already, and “Israel shall know” the truth when they see that we offer no sacrifices upon it. They then confirmed their words with an oath and an imprecation:
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 21_Verse, 2_Comment: If in rebellion. That is, rebellion against the unity of Israel, corresponding to the second suspicion.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 21_Verse, 3_Comment: Or if in trespass against Hashem. Corresponding to the first suspicion.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 21_Verse, 4_Comment: May He not save us, etc. May He cast us away from His presence.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: To build. This explains their words, “if in trespass against Hashem”: if we built ourselves an altar in order to turn away from Hashem—that is, to practice idolatry. Corresponding to “if in rebellion,” they explain: “if to offer upon it burnt offerings or meal offerings,” etc., thereby separating ourselves from the Tabernacle at Shiloh. In either case, may Hashem Himself exact punishment from anyone who has done such a thing.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: But if not. The altar’s construction arose entirely from anxiety concerning a matter that we feared might confront us in the future. This also means that we were anxious about precisely the matter of which you now suspect us—separating ourselves from the congregation of Israel and from Hashem’s Tabernacle. The truth is exactly the opposite: we acted out of concern that this very separation might arise in the future, when your children will say to our children, etc., “You have no portion in Hashem.” Since the Jordan separates us from you, our territory is outside the Land of Israel, where many commandments do not apply. Such statements might influence our children’s hearts until they cease to fear Hashem.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 25_Verse, 1_Comment: Let us now make for ourselves. A marker and faithful sign that we, like you, are children of the living God, by building the altar—not for burnt offerings or sacrifices; that is, an altar whose structure was designed solely as a visible monument, not for offering burnt offerings or sacrifices, as stated in verse 10: “an altar great in appearance.”
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 25_Verse, 2_Comment: For it is a witness. It will serve as a witness between us and you throughout all generations.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 25_Verse, 3_Comment: To perform the service of Hashem before Him with our burnt offerings, etc. This altar would testify that an altar standing outside Hashem’s Tabernacle is unfit for sacrifices, because Hashem’s service may be performed only before Him at His Tabernacle. Consequently, your children will not say tomorrow to our children, “You have no portion in Hashem,” as Scripture proceeds to explain.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 27_Verse, 0_Comment: And we said. That is, we declared immediately at the time of its construction:
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 27_Verse, 1_Comment: And it shall be, if they say, etc., then we shall say: See the replica of Hashem’s altar that our fathers made. That is, observe its structure, which was fashioned in a manner demonstrating that it was intended solely for display, not for offering sacrifices upon it. Moreover, our fathers made it—meaning all Israel—because by not protesting its construction, they consented to it and thereby made it a witness between us and you.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 28_Verse, 0_Comment: Far be it from us. After explaining that their intention in constructing the altar was for it to serve as a witness for future generations, they added that there was even less reason to suspect them of wrongdoing, for this very altar made such an act far from them. That is, the altar itself—whose form showed that it was made only for display, not for sacrifice—made it far from us to rebel against Hashem. It would itself testify against us that sacrifices may be offered nowhere except upon the altar of Hashem our God before His Tabernacle.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 30_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(31) The structure of the verse is exceedingly difficult. Before they built the altar, did Israel have any doubt that Hashem was among them?
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 30_Verse, 1_Comment: Today we know. Phinehas began to reassure them, saying that he himself had never doubted the matter. Since they saw that Hashem dwelt among Israel and had not hidden His countenance from them, they knew that these tribes had not committed this trespass against Him. The verse should be understood as follows: “Today—because Hashem is among us—we know that you have not committed this trespass against Hashem.” The words “because Hashem is among us” form a parenthetical statement explaining that they knew the eastern tribes had not trespassed precisely because Hashem remained among them.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 30_Verse, 2_Comment: Then you would have removed. That is, had you committed such a grievous trespass, you would then have removed and separated the children of Israel from the hand of Hashem and His Providence. The expression derives from “God took away your father’s livestock” (Genesis 31:9). Since Hashem’s hand remains among us and performs wonders, we know today that you have not trespassed. Phinehas meant that he had never doubted them at all; they had come only to learn the reason for their action and to remove a potential stumbling block for future generations.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 32_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(33) What is noteworthy about the fact that they no longer spoke of going up against them for war, once they had vindicated themselves and their innocence had become clear as daylight?
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 32_Verse, 1_Comment: And the matter pleased, etc. Scripture informs us that their decision to march against them for war did not arise from any hatred, jealousy, or animosity in the hearts of the tribes of Hashem toward their brethren. On the contrary, it arose from their great love for them and their desire to turn them back from sin. Therefore, they rejoiced over the explanation and blessed God. Had they come against them out of hostility, they would not have rejoiced upon discovering that they now lacked any cause to fight them. Scripture further explains, “and they did not speak,” etc., “of destroying” the land: even when they first set out, they had neither said nor intended that they would destroy the land, but only that they would turn their brethren back from sin. They therefore rejoiced and blessed God when the tribes’ righteousness emerged as brightly as daylight.
text.1_, 21_Chapter, 33_Verse, 0_Comment: And they called. The children of Reuben and Gad named the altar according to the purpose for which it had been built: to serve as a witness that Hashem alone is God, the one God besides Whom there is no other, and that they would never exchange the worship at His altar for worship in another place or of another god.
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: For its elders. These were the Sanhedrin.
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: And for its heads. The heads of the tribes.
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 1_Verse, 2_Comment: And for its judges and its officers. Those appointed in each and every city.
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 1_Verse, 3_Comment: And he said to them. The substance of Joshua’s address was this: After seeing that many peoples whom Israel had not dispossessed still remained in the land, Joshua recognized two possible courses. Israel could either make covenants and intermarry with them until they became one nation, thereby eliminating the hostility between them, or wage war against them until they dispossessed them; otherwise, it would be impossible for Israel to dwell peacefully in the land. He feared that after his death Israel would be afraid to provoke war against them and would choose the first course. He therefore came to warn them against this with sound reason and understanding. Thus, he said, “I have grown old” and can no longer go out to war. Nevertheless, it was not I who conquered them through my own strength, for:
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And you have seen all that Hashem your God did to all these nations. He performed great signs and wonders, through which you clearly recognized that it was not my own power that achieved this victory for you, but that Hashem your God is the One Who fights for you. He is eternal and will not die. Therefore:
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(4) According to the commentators’ explanations, this passage contains several repetitions and presents its ideas in a disorderly sequence. The specific difficulties will become evident from the commentary.
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 3_Verse, 1_Comment: See, I have allotted to you. I have already fulfilled the responsibility that depended upon me: allotting the inheritance so that each person would know his portion. Thus, Hashem had said, “You shall cause this people to inherit” (above, chapter 1), and, “I Myself will dispossess them before the children of Israel; only divide it as an inheritance” (above, 13:6). Joshua then specifies the territories he had allotted: first, from the Jordan, including all the nations that I cut off—those dwelling in the southeastern region near the Jordan, whom he conquered during his lifetime; and second, the territory extending to the Great Sea, etc., which he had not conquered, as explained above (chapter 13).
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And Hashem your God, etc. That is, once I have allotted the land as an inheritance, only the conquest remains. Even after my death, your God lives, and He will drive them away, etc., as He promised you. Joshua says, “He will drive them away,” concerning the nations he had already conquered, some of whom had abandoned their lands, such as the Girgashites: Hashem would drive them away so that they would never return. He says, “and He will dispossess them,” concerning those whom he had not yet conquered. This, however, required the condition that Israel observe the Torah. Thus, he says:
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And you shall be very strong to observe. This refers to the negative commandments.
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 5_Verse, 1_Comment: And to perform. This refers to the positive commandments, etc. It is the same command that Hashem gave Joshua above (chapter 1) as a condition of the conquest. Now that you will conduct the warfare, this command rests upon you.
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: So as not to. By observing the words of the Torah, you will necessarily take care not to associate or intermarry with “these” remaining nations, concerning whom the Torah issued its prohibition. The word “these” is repeated because it refers to two groups: the nations that had been conquered and those remaining unconquered, as explained above (verses 4–5). Therefore, verse 12 says, “the remnant of these nations—these that remain.” I have explained the distinction between yeter, “remnant,” and she’er, “that which remains.” Yeter denotes what was left incidentally; this refers to the conquered nations, some of whose people happened to survive. She’er denotes what was intentionally left; this refers to the nations that had not been conquered, whom Hashem deliberately left to test Israel, as stated in Judges 3:1.
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: And by the name. That is, by refraining from intermarriage with them, you will avoid progressing to increasingly severe prohibitions: first, mentioning the names of their gods; more seriously, swearing by their names; still more seriously, worshiping them; and most seriously, bowing down to them, one of the four forms of idolatrous service punishable by death. Joshua’s essential point is that the negative command implies its converse: if Israel intermarries with them, they will first mention the names of their gods, afterward swear by them, then worship them, and finally bow down to them.
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(8–10) According to the commentators, who interpret the words “but rather” as meaning “only,” the statement “and Hashem dispossessed,” etc., has no connection with what precedes it. Likewise, the statement “one man pursued a thousand” has no relationship to the passage. And according to their interpretation, the verb “pursued” is in the future tense but must be understood as referring to the past.
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 7_Verse, 1_Comment: For. Joshua now begins to explain the benefit or harm that would result from the two alternatives described above. Lest they say to themselves, “Why should we continually provoke wars? Would it not be better to make a covenant with these nations?” he says: Know that if you cling to Hashem your God—the word “if” introduces a condition—as you have done to this day, continuing to cling to Him as before, then just as you have seen with your own eyes the benefit that He dispossessed great and mighty nations before you, so it will be in the future: one man among you will pursue a thousand, because Hashem your God is the One Who fights for you. This is the benefit you will receive if you cling to Hashem, which includes refraining from intermarriage with the nations He prohibited.
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And you shall take great care. Joshua now explains the harm that would result from the second course. You must guard yourselves carefully against the danger it will bring, and thereby take care to love Hashem. For perfect love requires one to hate those who hate the one he loves, as it is written, “Do I not hate those who hate You, O Hashem?” (Psalms 139:21).
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: For if you indeed turn back. From loving Him.
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 11_Verse, 1_Comment: And you cling to the remnant of these nations. This is impossible so long as you love Hashem. Twofold harm will then come upon you: first through natural causes, and second through Divine Providence. Joshua begins by explaining the natural harm:
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Know for certain. That is, you can recognize for yourselves that Hashem will no longer dispossess them. Therefore, know that they will become a snare and a trap for you in matters of religion and faith.
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 12_Verse, 1_Comment: And scourges in your sides. When an enemy attacks you from the side, these nations will turn against you.
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 12_Verse, 2_Comment: And thorns in your eyes. Even in times of peace, they will pierce your eyes through jealousy, hatred, and hostility.
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 12_Verse, 3_Comment: Until you perish. Through natural causes, for it is impossible that perfect love and a faithful covenant should exist between you and them.
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And behold. Joshua now explains the harm that will come upon them through Divine Providence, for Hashem will punish them for this conduct. He first presents evidence from the favorable promises that had already been fulfilled. Thus, he says, “Behold, I am going the way of all the earth.” Nevertheless, you will remain under Hashem’s Providence, both for good and for harm, because Hashem’s promises will not cease to operate with my death. Now infer the fulfillment of the adverse warnings from that of the favorable promises already fulfilled. Thus, he says, “You know today with all your heart that not one thing has failed of all the good things” Hashem promised. He repeats the idea to convey two points. First, “all have come upon you”: not one promised benefit was absent. Second, “not one thing has failed from them”: every benefit came in all its particulars, not merely in part. In other words, they all came in their full number, and each one came in its complete quality.
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And it shall be. You should therefore understand from this that just as every good thing has come upon you, so will He bring upon you every harmful thing when you transgress the covenant of Hashem. Even if, according to the natural order, you ought to endure, Hashem’s anger will then burn against you, and He will punish you through Divine Providence.
text.1_, 22_Chapter, 14_Verse, 1_Comment: And you shall perish quickly. Through Hashem’s hand and His punishment, which are not bound by time, nature, or their causal processes. Therefore, corresponding to his earlier statement, “until you perish,” meaning naturally over an extended period, Joshua now adds two points: first, “until He destroys you,” through providential devastation and annihilation; and second, “you shall perish quickly.” He also teaches another distinction between the arrival of good and the arrival of evil. When Hashem promises good, He declares it decisively, so that His utterance itself completes the matter; the good comes of itself, for “He spoke, and it came to be.” His decree of evil, however, is not absolute but conditional upon their failure to repent. It must therefore be actively brought upon them, since it does not come of itself. Thus, Scripture says: “Just as every good thing has come upon you” of itself, “so Hashem will bring upon you every harmful thing,” because the latter will not come of itself.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(2–4) What did Joshua intend by this introduction? What significance is there in stating that Terah was the father of Nahor? How was Abraham’s begetting Ishmael an act of increasing his offspring or a particular benefit? And likewise, what benefit was there in Isaac’s begetting Esau?
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 1_Verse, 1_Comment: Thus says Hashem. From Adam until Abraham, the chosen quality and the Divine influence rested only upon individuals. They constituted the heart and fruit, while the rest of humanity was like husks. From the time that the sun of Abraham’s righteousness began to shine, however, Hashem desired that the Divine influence rest upon a multitude: first the tribes, then the seventy souls, and afterward an entire nation with whom Hashem spoke face to face. The patriarchs and their descendants therefore had to undergo numerous processes of refinement and trials, so that the dregs would be purified, the husks removed, and the whole would become heart, fruit, and the choicest oil, as the Kuzari explains at length. This is what Joshua explains here. He told them: Your ancestors were not inherently fit for the Divine influence. They were unfit because of their location, for “your fathers dwelt beyond the River,” whereas the only place suited to producing grapes and sacred, praiseworthy fruit is the Holy Land. They were also unfit by lineage and origin, for “Terah was the father of Abraham and the father of Nahor.” Abraham was surrounded by thorns: beside him stood Nahor, and at his root stood Terah. Nor were they fit through their own spiritual preparation, for “they served other gods.”
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And I took. Scripture first explains the effort Hashem made to prepare Abraham for the Divine influence with respect to his location, corresponding to the statement, “They dwelt beyond the River.” When the owner of a garden sees a choice sapling planted in barren soil amid a field of stones, he removes it from its place and replants it upon a fertile hillside. Likewise, “I took Abraham from beyond the River and led him throughout all the land of Canaan,” a place suited to Divine Providence and prophecy. Through his journeys throughout the land, Abraham was also tested, refined in the crucible of trials, and proven worthy. Regarding the second matter—his purification from the defects of his ancestry and lineage, corresponding to “Terah was the father of Abraham”—Hashem accomplished this through the words, “and I multiplied his offspring.” Through this, the dregs and impurities were separated into Ishmael, while Isaac emerged as pure gold. Thus, “I gave him Isaac,” for Isaac alone was designated as Abraham’s sacred and praiseworthy fruit. Yet Isaac too contained a measure of impurity, which was separated through Esau. Thus, Scripture continues:
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And I gave Jacob and Esau to Isaac. Through this, Esau absorbed all the impurity. Therefore, “I gave Mount Seir to Esau,” for it was suited to his portion.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 3_Verse, 1_Comment: But Jacob and his children. From then on, they were prepared for the great Divine influence, but they still required refinement in the third respect mentioned above: they had to become worthy through their own spiritual preparation, corresponding to the statement, “They served other gods.” Therefore, they went down to Egypt, which served as an iron furnace that purified their material nature through the harshness of their servitude. Through this, they were prepared to become the people of Hashem, so that henceforth the Divine Presence would rest not merely upon individuals but upon multitudes, and not intermittently but continually.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And I sent. Scripture now recounts the Exodus, when the Divinely appointed time arrived for this awesome influence to rest upon Israel. First, Hashem chose emissaries worthy of accomplishing this great event: Moses and Aaron. Second, He chose means suited to this purpose: “and I afflicted Egypt” through wonders, signs, and miracles. Thus, He says, “according to what I did in its midst.” And afterward—that is, after all the wonders through which Israel recognized Hashem’s power and might—“I brought you out.”
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And I brought out. I desired to perform still more miracles so that you would have no doubt whatsoever concerning My power and Providence. Therefore, even after I brought your fathers out of Egypt, you came to the sea so that the Egyptians would pursue you. All this was brought about by Me so that you would believe in Me, as it is written, “Israel saw,” etc., “and they believed in Hashem” (Exodus 14:31).
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And He placed darkness. Until they descended into the sea. This produced two contrasts. First, you were saved while they drowned. Second, darkness covered them, whereas your eyes saw. The term ma’afel, “darkness,” differs from ofel: it denotes something that darkens and conceals the light—namely, the cloud and darkness that obscured the Egyptians’ vision while illuminating the night for Israel. Yet although your eyes saw what I did in Egypt, you still did not believe in Me with complete faith. Consequently, you dwelt in the wilderness for many days. I had to lead you about in the wilderness for forty years in order to cleanse you from the impurity of Egypt, as it is written: “I led you forty years in the wilderness,” etc.; “but Hashem did not give you a heart to know,” etc., “until this day” (Deuteronomy 29:3–4).
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: And I brought you to the land of the Amorites. Two types of warfare were then waged against you. First came warfare through human strength: “They fought against you, and I delivered them into your hand.” Second came warfare through means beyond nature, as Scripture proceeds to say:
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And Balak arose and waged war against Israel. Scripture explains that his warfare was not conducted with sword and spear, but by the fact that he sent for Balaam and summoned him to curse you.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: But I was unwilling to listen to Balaam. Through this, I delivered you from that form of warfare as well.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(11) Did the inhabitants of Jericho not refrain from fighting altogether, as is evident from Scripture?
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 10_Verse, 3_Comment: And they fought. Afterward, the lords of Jericho fought against you. This designation refers to the kings who subsequently assembled to avenge Jericho, as related above (chapter 9). The Girgashite is not listed there but is listed here because the Girgashite initially joined the assembly, but afterward became afraid, withdrew, and departed for Africa, as will be explained.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 10_Verse, 4_Comment: And I delivered. That is, I delivered some of them into your hand—namely, all those enumerated except the Girgashite—while others, namely the Girgashite:
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(12) This verse appears out of sequence. Joshua is now speaking about Israel’s entry into the land, whereas he already discussed the war against Sihon in verse 8.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 11_Verse, 1_Comment: And I sent the hornet, and it drove them out before you. This refers to the Girgashites’ departure for Africa. Scripture explains what this “hornet” was: “the two kings of the Amorites—not by your sword,” etc. That is, the report that you had conquered the two Amorite kings not by your sword or bow but through Hashem’s deliverance acted like a hornet: they became terrified by this report and fled from their land to Africa.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(14) Why does Joshua say, “Serve Hashem,” twice?
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 13_Verse, 1_Comment: And now, fear Hashem. After all these acts of kindness, fear Hashem, etc. Joshua commanded them to fear Hashem with awe of His exaltedness, not merely fear of punishment, and to serve Him in sincerity and truth: not with false service, which is the opposite of truth, and not in expectation of reward, as in the teaching, “Do not be like servants who serve the master on condition of receiving a reward” (Pirkei Avot 1:3), which is the opposite of sincerity. He therefore stipulated, “and remove the gods,” because it is impossible to serve Hashem in partnership with another; one must serve Him alone. Thus, he again says, “and serve Hashem,” meaning Him alone, without associating any other with Him, for one who associates another with Hashem does not truly serve Him.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And if it is displeasing in your eyes to serve Hashem. If your hearts produce poison and wormwood, leading you to believe that certain matters are governed by nature and the celestial order, and you therefore desire to engage in other forms of worship that, in your opinion, will assist you in attaining natural or astrologically determined success:
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 14_Verse, 1_Comment: Choose for yourselves today. That is, if so, you must abandon Hashem entirely, for it is impossible to serve Him together with another. You must then choose between two alternatives. Either you believe that the celestial order governs you according to your ancestral origin beyond the River; if so, serve the gods that your fathers served beyond the River. Or you believe that the celestial order governs you according to its influence upon the land in which you dwell; if so, serve the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell. But as for me and my household, we will serve Hashem, for we believe that we are subject to no angelic prince, constellation, star, or force of nature, but to Hashem alone.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And the people answered. They declared that they would not forsake Hashem and gave four reasons. First, because of the obligation resting upon them: “For Hashem our God is the One Who brought us and our fathers up,” etc. Through this, He acquired ownership of their very persons, making them His servants, for they had been slaves in Egypt, and one who redeems a slave from his master’s house acquires him for himself. This is why the Exodus from Egypt is given as the reason for many of the commandments: through it, Israel became subject to the Master Who brought them out of the house of bondage. Second, because of awe of His exaltedness: “Who performed before our eyes these great signs.” Through them, they recognized His power and ability to overturn the celestial order. Third, because of the benefit they received, as they said, “He protected us throughout all the way that we traveled.” He guarded them both by supplying their needs in the wilderness and during their wars against the nations, as a man guards his son. Why, then, should they forsake the Source of living waters? Fourth, because of fear of harm, as they continued:
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: And Hashem drove out all the peoples, etc., the inhabitants of the land, from before us. Consequently, if we behave like those peoples, the land will likewise vomit us out, as it is written: “Let not the land vomit you out when you defile it, as it vomited out the nation that preceded you” (Leviticus 18:28). Their answer also corresponded directly to Joshua’s alternatives. Against his suggestion that they serve the gods worshiped beyond the River and in Egypt, they replied that Hashem had brought them out of Egypt, while Egypt’s gods had not saved their worshipers. Against his suggestion that they serve the gods of the Amorites, they replied that Hashem had driven out the Amorite people as well.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(19) What did Joshua mean when he told them that they would be unable to serve Hashem? What was the substance of their dispute, which on its surface appears devoid of reason or meaning? What did the people add in their second response beyond what they had said initially, causing Joshua then to accept their words and say, “You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen Hashem”? Had they not already chosen Him in their first response?
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: For you will forsake, etc., and He will turn and harm you and destroy you after He has benefited you. The very good that you hoped to obtain through your worship will readily become the source of sickness and affliction. Joshua also said that precisely because Hashem had benefited them through His Providence, which was closely attached to them, this itself required that He turn and harm them through that same Providence if they forsook Him. This would not have been so had He never benefited them and had they remained subject merely to nature. Thus, it is written: “You alone have I known from all the families of the earth; therefore, I will visit upon you all your sins” (Amos 3:2). Hashem’s intimate knowledge and particular Providence attached to His people necessarily entail providential punishment as well.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: And they said, “No.” That is, we do not intend to serve Hashem for the sake of reward or punishment; rather, “we will serve Hashem” for His own sake. Therefore, they did not now say, “We will serve Hashem our God,” as they had initially. The possessive expression “our God” denotes His relationship with His creatures—benefiting or harming them according to their deeds—as I have explained elsewhere. They now clarified that they would serve Him for His own sake, not on condition of receiving a reward.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: And Joshua said, “You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen Hashem for yourselves.” That is, you have chosen Him through rational and deliberate choice, not from unrestrained personal desire—for one who serves because of reward or punishment does not act through rational choice, as I have explained elsewhere. Their choice was “Hashem, to serve Him,” not to serve themselves. One who serves for reward or from fear of punishment does not truly serve Hashem, but himself; you, however, have chosen primarily to serve Him, not to obtain personal benefit.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: And now. Since you have undertaken to serve Him because of His exaltedness:
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 22_Verse, 1_Comment: Remove the “foreign gods” that are among you. That is, remove every idolatrous thought from your hearts.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 22_Verse, 2_Comment: And incline your hearts toward Hashem. Because He is the God of Israel—that is, because He exercises Providence over Israel. Therefore, they are the portion of His inheritance and are not subject to any angelic prince or star. I have established that whenever the name “God” appears with a possessive relationship to Israel, it denotes the bond and attachment He has with Israel, through which He watches over them with particular Providence. For this reason, they are forbidden to associate any other power with Him in worship, although the descendants of Noah were not prohibited from doing so, because Israel is uniquely His portion. Thus, although Joshua had initially told them not to serve Him for the purpose of reward or punishment on account of His being “the God of Israel”—the One Who rewards and punishes—they must nevertheless serve Him because of this relationship. Since He exercises particular Providence over them, they may not associate the worship of any other being with Him.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: And the people said. Therefore, they declared, “We will serve Hashem our God” without associating any other power with Him.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 23_Verse, 1_Comment: And we will obey His voice. Without expectation of reward or fear of punishment, but solely to obey whatever He commands because it is the commandment of God. (25) And he made. Joshua made a covenant with them because they willingly undertook to serve Hashem perfectly, without ulterior motive.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 23_Verse, 2_Comment: And he established for them a statute and an ordinance. Joshua instituted regulations and laws for them according to the needs of the land, as the Sages described regarding the ordinances enacted by Joshua (Berakhot 48b; Eruvin 17a).
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: And he wrote. Joshua recorded these matters as part of his book, as the Sages said, “Joshua wrote his book” (Bava Batra 14b), and joined it to the Book of God’s Torah so that it would become part of the Holy Scriptures.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 25_Verse, 1_Comment: And he took a large stone. Since the Torah scroll was kept with the Ark—either inside it or beside it, according to the respective views of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Judah (Bava Batra 14b)—Joshua wished to designate a place in the Sanctuary for his own book. He therefore erected a large hollow stone to serve as a chest and repository for it, and set it up beneath the terebinth that was in the Sanctuary at Shiloh.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment:
Questions
(27) Why did Joshua designate the stone as a witness?
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 26_Verse, 1_Comment: And Joshua said, etc., “Behold, this stone.” That is, the stone together with the book contained within it.
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 26_Verse, 2_Comment: Shall be a witness among us. As Moses said, “Take this Book of the Torah and place it beside the Ark of the Covenant of Hashem, and it shall be there as a witness against you” (Deuteronomy 31:26). Joshua likewise designated his book, deposited within the stone, as a witness concerning two matters. First, “among us,” thereby including himself together with them:
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 26_Verse, 3_Comment: For it has heard all the words of Hashem. That is, within it were contained all the words that Hashem had spoken to us—the words of Hashem recorded throughout this book—as well as Joshua’s present address, which began, “Thus says Hashem.” Second, “it shall be a witness against you, lest you deny”, like one who summons a witness so that the other party will be unable to deny the matter in his presence. Although they were then in Shechem, Joshua fashioned the hollow stone there and placed his book within it; from there, he transported it to the Sanctuary at Shiloh and set it up. The terebinth was certainly outside the Sanctuary, since it is forbidden to plant any tree within the Sanctuary precincts. This indicated that Joshua’s book did not possess the same status as the Torah scroll in every respect. Alternatively, this “terebinth” was made of stone in the form of a tree, like the stone projections described in Ezekiel 40:9, and stood within the Sanctuary itself. For this reason, the noun’s vocalization changes from a tzere to a patach, as in “for you shall be like a terebinth” (Isaiah 1:30).
text.1_, 23_Chapter, 31_Verse, 0_Comment: And the bones of Joseph, etc., became an inheritance for the children of Joseph. The children of Joseph took possession of the righteous man’s remains, which became an inheritance to them. They regarded it as a precious inheritance that they had merited to have the righteous Joseph buried within their portion. They likewise endeavored to have Eleazar buried within their territory. When Eleazar died, they consecrated the Hill of Phinehas as a devoted field, which by law belonged to the priest serving in that watch; it therefore fell to Phinehas, enabling him to bury Eleazar there. Thus, both Joseph’s grave and Eleazar’s grave were situated within the inheritance of Joseph’s descendants in the hill country of Ephraim.
